Analyze Your Housing Stock and Different What if Scenarios Using Excel — Analyze Your Housing Stock and Different "What-If" Scenarios Using Excel

Building stock analysis involves collecting and assessing the characteristics of a set of buildings within a defined area. It includes analyzing data about the buildings, such as their physical attributes, energy performance, and occupancy patterns. Analyzing these things can help support policy planning and decision-making related to energy efficiency, energy affordability, and grid impacts.

A typical analysis starts with defining the goal and scope (e.g., retrofits to cut building consumption by X%) and a geographic boundary (e.g., a state, city, or low-income housing only within a county). Then data is collected/generated and amalgamated, often from multiple sources such as tax assessor records, surveys, and energy audits. ResStock can support or even sidestep this typically time- and labor-intensive data collection step by providing housing data aggregated from multiple national datasets. Additionally, ResStock data offers simulated data for estimating the energy performance baseline and energy savings from a broad range of energy efficiency retrofit measures.

The following steps are a starting point for using ResStock data in a residential building stock analysis. If you use ResStock for your residential building stock analysis, spend more time planning out specific questions and goals that you have for your analysis.

We will do a simple analysis to understand some of the characteristics of single-family detached homes in Colorado and identify the energy and utility bill impacts of deploying high-efficiency cold-climate heat pumps with electric back up to all eligible single-family detached homes in the state.

ResStock publishes national level datasets containing the energy baseline and a set of energy efficiency measures on the [Open Energy Data Initiative (OEDI) website](https://data.openei.org/s3_viewer?bucket=oedi-data-lake&prefix=nrel-pds-building-stock). The documentation for each release is on our website, and near each release you will see a Technical Documentation button. We recommend browsing the documentations so that you can choose the dataset that can best answer your questions. The datasets can vary in the type of housing upgrades, weather years, model assumptions, reporting metrics, and more. Below is a screenshot showing an example of where our documentation is located for our 2024.2 dataset.

How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples — How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples

The Data Viewer is a tool that can show annual and timeseries data with premade visuals that can be downloaded. This tutorial will show you how to get 1,000 samples in the Data Viewer using the End Use Savings Shapes 2022.1 Release, representing 242,000 dwelling units. For more information on the number of samples that should be used in an analysis, see the *How Many Samples are Required for this Analysis* explanation on the Resources page.

**To illustrate the capabilities of the Data Viewer, the question we want to answer is: How much annual energy could be saved if all dwelling units in Littleton, Colorado, had the basic enclosure package applied?**

For this example, we are doing a city-based filter, but the same procedure applies for any down selection in the Data Viewer. This includes other geographies, building characteristics, or demographics.

On the [ResStock datasets page](https://resstock.nlr.gov/datasets), scroll down to End Use Savings Shapes 2022.1 Release. Notice that the fourth column has Data Viewer Links by state. Click on the first line option, which is "by state."

![](../../../assets/images/resstock-home-page.png)

A separate tab will appear that will ask you to log in with a free account. At first, there will be a map of the United States. From here, you can select a state.

separate tab will appear that will ask you to log in with a free account. At first, there will be a map of the United States. From here, you can select a state.

The Data Viewer shows three types of information: 1) bar charts, 2) timeseries, and 3) histograms. For this example, we will be using Colorado as the starting point.

![](../../../assets/images/type-state.png)

**Step 1: Type "Colorado" into the Type a Location Box**
Now, you can see that bar charts, timeseries, and histograms are all available to analyze.

![](../../../assets/images/bar-timeseries-histogram-colorado.png)

For this example, our analysis question is: How much annual energy could be saved if all dwelling units in Littleton, Colorado, had the Upgrade 1: Basic Enclosure Package applied?

ResStock recommends a minimum sample size of 1,000 for most applications to minimize the error. For the 2022.1 dataset, those 1,000 samples represent 242,000 dwelling units.

To make sure we have 1,000 samples, we will first look at Histograms, which tell us how many dwelling units are in the location.

**Step 2: Click Explore Histograms**

This is what the homepage of Explore Histograms looks like.

![](../../../assets/images/click-explore-histograms.png)

many dwelling units are in the location.

**Step 2: Click Explore Histograms**

This is what the homepage of Explore Histograms looks like.

![](../../../assets/images/click-explore-histograms.png)

Notice at the top there are dropdown menus to choose fuel type, upgrade name, and output metric for the histogram. In this case, we are looking at all fuel types and only dwelling units eligible for the basic enclosure upgrade, the output metric is annual energy consumption, and it is for the whole state of Colorado. The bottom of the screen displays the histogram with annual energy consumption [Wh] on the x-axis and # (number) of dwelling units on the y-axis.

Now, we have results for the impact of the upgrade package for the whole state of Colorado, but how do we select only Littleton? To do this, we will add a "Filter" for City.

**Step 3: Click + Add Filters**

Click on the "+Add Filters" button in the middle-left of the screen (bracketed in red here).

![](../../../assets/images/explore-add-filters.png)

**Step 4: Filter to Littleton**
Click "City", and then choose CO, Littleton from the alphabetical list. Once you choose CO, Littleton it should appear as a check in the upper right corner. Then, click Save Filters.

![](../../../assets/images/choose-littleton.png)

Littleton from the alphabetical list. Once you choose CO, Littleton it should appear as a check in the upper right corner. Then, click Save Filters.

![](../../../assets/images/choose-littleton.png)

After clicking "Save Filters," an orange button pops up on the right that says the results are out of date. This means that the displayed histogram does not yet incorporate our filter.

**Step 5: Apply Filter to Results**

Click "Results Out of Date, Click to Reload Results" to make sure our filters are appropriately applied.

![](../../../assets/images/update-results-littleton.png)

Now, the number of dwelling units has gone from 1.2 million dwelling units in the first column to about 2,000 dwelling units.

![](../../../assets/images/2000-y-axis-littleton.png)

This is how you can tell the filter has been applied.

**Step 6: Verify Dwelling Unit Count**
Add together the number of dwelling units from each column to check if there are 242,000 dwelling units. Hover your mouse over each column to see how many dwelling units there are in each column.

![](../../../assets/images/hover-dwelling-unit-count.png)

Hovering over each of the columns gives you the values below and the total: _1,937 + 4,358 + 4,358 + 3,874 + 3,148 + 1,211 + 1,695 + 484 = 21,065_

over each of the columns gives you the values below and the total: _1,937 + 4,358 + 4,358 + 3,874 + 3,148 + 1,211 + 1,695 + 484 = 21,065_

For this example of CO, Littleton there are 21,065 dwelling units present, **less than 10% of the recommended 240,000 dwelling units**. Now, we need to find ways ways to expand our sample either by geography or other characteristics to get to our target sample size.

**Step 7: Identify Nearby Geographies That Can Be Included in the Analysis**

For this analysis, we decide to expand our sample by including the nearby areas. First, click _Edit Filters > City_ and scroll to _Colorado_ to see what other geographies can be chosen from the list. Then, pulling up Google Maps and searching for Littleton, CO shows that some nearby cities that are also in the City list include Englewood, Lakewood, Centennial, Highlands Ranch, Arvada, Denver, and Westminster.

In this case, we use personal experience combined with the mapping to select cities from the list above. Most of these cities are suburban areas of the Denver metro area, with lots of single-family detached housing. We decide not to include Denver because it is more densely populated, and is likely to have more multifamily housing than Littleton. Use your best personal judgement when expanding your geography or other filters to include more samples.

**Step 8: Add In Another City**
We start by adding in  Englewood, to see if that gives us sufficient dwelling units. The City filter should already be pulled up from Step 7. Choose CO, Englewood from this list. Now, there should be two cities with check marks at the top. Choose Save Filters and remember to click the Results Out of Date, Click to Reload Results button to make sure our filter is applied.

![](../../../assets/images/add-englewood.png)

**Step 9: Recalculate Dwelling Units**
Like Step 6, add together the number of dwelling units to check if there are 242,000 dwelling units. With these two cities chosen, there are 36,803 dwelling units. We have almost doubled the number of dwelling units, but we are still not close to the recommended 242,000 dwelling units.

**Step 10: Continue Sample Expansion**
Continue adding cities from those identified in Step 7 until there are 242,000 dwelling units. After adding in Littleton, Englewood, Lakewood, Centennial, Highlands Ranch, Arvada, and Westminster there are finally 271,671 dwelling units. We are finally above the recommended 242,000 dwelling units!

adding in Littleton, Englewood, Lakewood, Centennial, Highlands Ranch, Arvada, and Westminster there are finally 271,671 dwelling units. We are finally above the recommended 242,000 dwelling units!

Now that the area has been defined, we look at annual energy savings if these dwelling units had the basic enclosure applied.

**Step 11: Pull Up Bar Charts**
Hit the back button on your browser and click _Explore Bar Charts_.

![](../../../assets/images/explore-bar-charts.png)

![](../../../assets/images/base-bar-chart.png)

On the Bar Charts page, the top section is similar to Histograms with fuel type, upgrade, output, location, and filter button. The middle section is the legend which color codes end uses. Hovering your mouse over one end use will highlight it on the two graphs below.

The bottom left graph shows the Annual Energy Consumption in Watt hours [Wh] for the Baseline scenario and the upgrade, which in this case is the Basic Enclosure. The bottom right graph calls out the Annual Energy Savings [Wh] by end type.

The example right now is for all of Colorado, but our main question is how much annual energy could be saved if all dwelling units in Littleton, Colorado, had the Basic Enclosure package applied?

text:
How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples — How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples

example right now is for all of Colorado, but our main question is how much annual energy could be saved if all dwelling units in Littleton, Colorado, had the Basic Enclosure package applied?

**Step 12: Downselect to Our Sample Area**
Add in the location filters that we determined with the Histogram charts in Step 10. Use the _Add Filters_ button and the orange update results buttons just as we have in similar steps. Your screen should look like the figure below.

![](../../../assets/images/bar-chart-cities-added.png)

**Step 13: Determine Energy Savings for Littleton**
Determine what the annual energy savings are for just Littleton by normalizing the results. The results shown in the histograms currently represent the savings from 271,671 units in different geographic locations, but Littleton only has 21,065 dwelling units eligible for the basic enclosure upgrade (from Step 6). The baseline energy consumption (i.e., the energy before an upgrade) is approximately 7.75 TWh, and the basic enclosure energy consumption is approximately 6.5 TWh for all 271,671 dwelling units in the expanded sample. You can scale the sample to the target geography using the following calculation:

_Energy Use Target Area = Energy Use Sample x (Dwelling Units in Target Area/Dwelling Units in Sample)_

For our example, to calculate the baseline energy use for Littleton using our larger sample:

metadata.doc_title: How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples
metadata.section: How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples

text:
How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples — How To Use The Data Viewer With Enough Samples

Use Target Area = Energy Use Sample x (Dwelling Units in Target Area/Dwelling Units in Sample)_

For our example, to calculate the baseline energy use for Littleton using our larger sample:

_Baseline Littleton = 7.75 TWh sample x (21,065 units Littleton/271,671 units sample) = 0.60 TWh = 600 GWh_

We take the 7.75 TWh used in the baseline, multiply it by the number of applicable units in Littleton (21,065) and divide it by the number of dwelling units in our sample (271,671). The resulting calculations show that before an upgrade, the applicable dwellings in Littleton use 0.60 TWh or 600 GWh.

_Upgrade Littleton = 6.5 TWh sample x (21,065 units Littleton/271,671 units sample) = 0.50 TWh = 500 GWh_

Similarly, we can find the energy use in Littleton by swapping the 7.75 TWh of the sample baseline for the 6.5 TWh of the sample basic enclosure case. After upgrading all 21,065 units, ResStock estimates that these homes in Littleton will use 500 GWh. This means that Littleton can save approximately 100 GWh of energy annually if all applicable Littleton dwelling units upgraded to the Basic Enclosure.

that these homes in Littleton will use 500 GWh. This means that Littleton can save approximately 100 GWh of energy annually if all applicable Littleton dwelling units upgraded to the Basic Enclosure.

In the example above, we expanded the sample size by including surrounding areas. Similar expansion could be done based on other characteristics, such as pulling in homes of similar ages or with other relevant characteristics. The steps of the analysis remain similar---figure out an expansion strategy, check sample size, and then scale results based upon the ratio of dwelling units in the target area to the dwelling units in your sample.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly marketready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end -use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Heating, Ventilation, and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Load Flexibility.

The HVAC load flexibility measure modifies the heating and cooling thermostat set points before peak periods to preheat or precool the building or during peak periods to shift load away from peak periods. In real deployments of demand flexibility via smart thermostats, the dispatch is typically limited to a handful of days per year to avoid customer fatigue. But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched nearly every day in the modeled dataset . Although the profile on any given day is realistic, the full annual load profiles do not reflect the realistic dispatch of HVAC load flexibility . Details on the appropriate use of the load profiles can be found in this document.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1 Technology Summary

Renewable energy is increasingly being adopted for electricity generation. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that the share of U.S. power generation from renewables will increase from 21% in 2021 to 44% in 2050 (EIA, 2022). This projected increase consists mainly of new wind and solar power, but wind and solar power are inherently variable energy sources, which poses a challenge for grid stability and control compared to fossil fuelbased power generation. For instance, solar power generation fluctuates with the time of day and weather, whereas wind energy is influenced by seasonal and atmospheric conditions. These fluctuations require sophisticated grid management to ensure a stable electricity supply.

Flexible loads help balance supply and demand, especially as renewable energy increases. Many utility companies operate demand response programs. These programs range from interruptible service programs targeting large commercial and industrial customers, to rebates given to large customers for voluntary peak hour load reductions, to direct control of water heaters and airconditioning compressors (Ryan Hledik A. R., 2022). Utilities such as Duke Energy (2024a), Xcel Energy (2024), and Pacific Gas and Electric Company (2024) enable demand response through time-based pricing where electricity rates vary by the time of day. By charging higher rates during peak hours and lower rates at other times, customers are encouraged to shift their usage to off-peak hours.

Residential buildings account for a substantial share of U.S. electricity demand, representing 38% of the total electricity consumption in 2023 (EIA, 2024), making this sector the largest of all sectors. Demand flexibility within the residential building stock is crucial to achieving demandside load flexibility, which can help balance grid loads. Within the residential sector, most load flexibility potential is found within the heating and cooling end uses because of the inherent thermal energy storage capability of the building's heated or cooled mass.

This measure models the use of smart thermostats to achieve demand flexibility in residential buildings by controlling their heating and cooling systems. This document describes the technology in general, describes how it is modeled in ResStock ™ , and reviews results at a high level.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

According to Stewart (2023):

A smart thermostat is an internet-connected device that controls home heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) equipment and can automatically adjust temperature set points to optimize performance and achieve energy savings. Smart thermostat features often include two-way communication, occupancy detection (such as geofencing and occupancy sensors), schedule learning, and seasonal optimization algorithms. Smart thermostats can control most conventional HVAC systems including central air conditioners, heat pumps, and forced air furnaces.

Within the context of demand flexibility programs, the internet-connected feature of a smart thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their demand response program. These thermostats adjust customer home cooling set points by 1°F -4°F for up to 4 hours when there is a risk of an electricity shortage, as determined by Xcel Energy.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or 'on -peak window,' is the window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time immediately preceding the peak period.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2.1 Load Shifting

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shifting ' represents DR [demand response] that encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with daily patterns of solar energy generation.'

For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window, conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2.2  Load Shedding

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shedding ' describes loads that can be curtailed to provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events. '

For this analysis, load shedding is accomplished by decreasing the heating set point and increasing the cooling set point of the building during the on-peak window. This allows the temperature to drift beyond the original set point during the on-peak window, trading decreased thermal comfort for reduced peak load. How quickly the temperature drifts to the modified set point will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, and the infiltration.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2.3  Set Point Change and Magnitude

Different durations of pre-peak load shifting and different set point offsets for load shifting or load shedding can be applied by HVAC load flexibility programs. For a mild impact on residents, a shorter on-peak duration (e.g., 2 hours) with a small set point offset during the onpeak hour (e.g., 2°F) can be used. In contrast, for the maximum load change, a longer pre-peak period (e.g., 4 hours) with larger set point adjustments, such as a low precooling set point (e.g., 60°F) and/or a high on-peak cooling set point (e.g., 80°F), may be applied.

Table 1 outlines the pre-peak and on-peak durations as well as the set point offsets used in existing smart thermostat programs. Typically, on-peak periods last 1 -4 hours, and the set point is adjusted by 1 -4°F during peak periods to align with residents ' comfort preferences. Loadshifting preheating or precooling strategies are not widely adopted in the current programs surveyed for this analysis. These findings broadly match the findings reported in a 2024 market overview of demand flexibility programs (Sean Murphy, 2024).

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2.4 On-Peak Hour Identification

When analyzing the impact of load flexibility, it is necessary to define the target time periods when demand flexibility will be dispatched to reduce load. These time periods are commonly referred to as on-peak hours. On-peak hours can be identified in different ways, depending on the goal. For instance:

- Reducing system net load: Grid-wide net load data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest demand, and demand flexibility can be dispatched to help lower overall system peak power generation requirements.
- Responding to time-of-use pricing: Utility rates for individual customers can be analyzed to identify times with the highest electricity prices. This is only applicable for customers with time-of-use rates. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to reduce individual customer utility bills.
- Minimizing grid operation costs: Grid-wide operational cost data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest operational costs, which could be dependent on system

peak demand, renewable generation, and local or distribution-level peak power. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to help reduce overall system operation costs.

The primary use for the results from this analysis is to feed into a national-scale energy system analysis that extends to 2050. The hypothesis is that demand flexibility will play a more important role further in the future; therefore, for this measure, the goal is to quantify load flexibility's technical potential to reduce net system load in 2050. Cambium is a dataset of load profiles based on assumed changes to the power sector over time (Gagnon, et al., 2024). It provides future load projections and related metrics. The MidCase scenario within Cambium adopts central estimates for key inputs, including technology costs, fuel prices, and demand growth. One important note is that the Cambium data do not consider future changes in load profiles due to wide-scale electrification, such as the addition of electric vehicles or heat pumps. Future work intends to update these load profiles and reassess the peak period definitions.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 1.2.5 Dispatch Strategy

In historic deployments, thermostat-based demand response is typically only dispatched 15 -25 days per year to avoid customer fatigue (Xcel, 2021) (Austin Energy, 2024). But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched every day in the modeled dataset . The dispatch strategy is modified for shoulderseason days where heating or cooling load is assumed to be minimal, defined by an average daily temperature greater than 50°F and less than 68°F. On those days, load shifting (done via precooling or preheating) is not dispatched, but load-shedding events are dispatched. The method for choosing this temperature range is described in section 4.2 Initial Sensitivity Analysis. Because of the unrealistically high number of days that demand flexibility is dispatched in this upgrade, the results must be used thoughtfully. One approach is to use daily profiles from the baseline for most days of the year and to splice in daily profiles from the upgrade for days when the intent of the analysis is to dispatch demand flexibility. Similarly, annualized energy consumption or energy savings metrics should not be used because of the overrepresentation of dispatch .

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 2 ResStock Baseline Approach

The baseline assumption for thermostats in ResStock is a range of heating and cooling set points and setbacks or setups derived from the Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, which vary based on climate zone, building type, HVAC type, and tenure (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023). These set points are assumed to apply year-round. Approximately one-third of dwelling units are assumed to have heating and/or cooling thermostat setbacks or setups, where the set point is changed by the homeowner during part of each day. The distribution of set points in the building stock is shown in Figure 1. ResStock makes no explicit assumption about whether these setbacks or setups are achieved using manual adjustment, a programmable thermostat, or a smart thermostat. In practice, demand response programs typically incentivize or directly pay for customers to install smart thermostats as a condition of program participation.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 3.2  ResStock Workflow

Figure 2 illustrates the modeling approach used to integrate a load flexibility measure into ResStock. This measure modifies the existing building energy model thermostat set point schedules during the pre-peak and on-peak periods only. For times outside of the event, the existing thermostat schedules in the model are unchanged. If the baseline thermostat set point schedules indicate that the dwelling unit is already in a setback or a setup state, the demand flexibility thermostat change still applies.

The load flexibility scenario (which includes the pre-peak duration and the set point offset values) serves as input for the measure, allowing customized controls. The input values used for this measure are explained in section 3.3 Input Variables.

Figure 2. Modeling approach for running a load flexibility measure in ResStock

Values for on-peak hours for summer months, winter months, and intermediate months are provided at the state level in an input file. The load flexibility measure first retrieves the heating and cooling set point schedules specific to each individual dwelling unit. It then modifies these schedules by adjusting the set points by an offset during the designated pre-peak and on-peak periods. This approach ensures that each unit's load flexibility aligns with its original comfort settings while providing targeted adjustments to reduce energy use during peak demand times. A minimum heating set point of 55°F and a maximum cooling set point of 82°F ensure that extreme discomfort is avoided. If the set point change would cause a heating set point higher than the original cooling set point or a cooling set point lower than the original heating set point, the set point adjustment is limited to avoid this condition. These thresholds and exceptions were chosen based on engineering judgment and only apply to a small percentage of dwelling units.

To prevent the creation of a new peak caused by the coincident return to normal set point temperatures, the load flexibility measure introduces a random shift to each dwelling unit's demand response start and stop time. The maximum allowable shift is defined in the scenario design, allowing each unit to randomly adjust its response start time within this range. For example, with a maximum random shift of 30 minutes and a 15-minute simulation time step, the potential random shift values are -30 minutes, -15 minutes, 0 minutes, 15 minutes, and 30 minutes.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.1  Single-Building Examples

We performed an initial ResStock test run to validate the operation of the load flexibility measures. This was a test run performed before the final input values were established, which is why some values differ from the final selection. The test run was performed using 50 models spread across the nation with two scenarios (also called upgrades):

- Upgrade 1: load shifting plus load shedding -a pre-peak duration of 2 hours, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during both the pre-peak and on-peak period
- Upgrade 2: load shedding only -no pre-peak load shifting, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during the on-peak period.

We can see that for upgrade 1, there is both a pre-peak and peak offset, with the peak period being 18:00 to 19:00. For upgrade 2, there is no pre-peak offset. Both show the expected temperature offset of 2°F.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.2.1 Quantifying Demand Flexibility Impacts

Traditional energy efficiency measures are often evaluated based on how much energy or utility bills they save on an annual basis. Because the goal of demand flexibility is to modify the load profile for a small number of days per year, metrics that evaluate the ability to modify the load are more useful than annualized energy consumption impacts.

There are many ways that the peak load impact of demand flexibility can be quantified. For this analysis, we adopted the demand decrease percentage (D3) metric, as defined by (Jingjing Liu, 2022). This metric is defined as:

The D3 metric can be computed for a single building or a group of buildings in aggregate. It can also be computed for the whole building load or for individual end uses.

This metric is defined as:

The D3 metric can be computed for a single building or a group of buildings in aggregate. It can also be computed for the whole building load or for individual end uses.

This metric was adopted because it quantifies the impact for a single demand response event (in our case, each day where demand response is dispatched), but it can easily and meaningfully be summarized over multiple events. For example, the mean or quartile values can be used to describe how the impact changes during a year, a season, or a month. This is particularly useful when the demand flexibility impacts are later used as the input to other models seeking to represent demand flexibility but that do not endogenously represent building physics. Examples of such models include Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's DR-Path (Brian Gerke, 2019) and the Brattle Group's Load Flex model (Ryan Hledik A. F., 2019).

Because the goal of this analysis is to feed results into downstream modeling efforts, we calculated the D3 metric for the aggregate load of groups of buildings of a common type located in a common geography.

Figure 8 shows how the D3 metric varies with different pre-peak durations for cooling load flexibility on the hottest day of the year for each state. We used an approximate 20% reduction for the 2°F offset and an approximate 40% reduction for the 4°F offset. Although only the peak offset without any precooling can provide a significant percentage reduction, pairing that with precooling can push the reduction even further -more so in some states than others. Also, the longer the duration of precooling, the higher the percentage reduction, with the highest reduction coming from 4-hour precooling.

Figure 9 shows the same metrics calculated year-round. That is, we calculated the average cooling energy consumption during the peak period for the whole year for both the baseline and the upgrade, and we calculated the difference as a percentage reduction. Some states have more percentage savings year-round than their hottest day, whereas others have less. Regardless, most show a positive correlation with the duration of the pre-peak period (at all offset levels) except for a handful of states that show a surprising negative correlation. We examined the results with the largest negative correlation -an identification with a 6°F pre-peak offset to investigate how a larger precooling duration (or having precooling at all) could result in a higher load during the peak.

The answer is in how the precooling and preheating was initially implemented. In the sensitivity analysis, we always chose to either precool or preheat, depending on the daily average temperature. If the daily average temperature was less than 66°F, we classified that as a heating day, otherwise we classified the day as a cooling day; however, this might not always work neatly. For some days in shoulder season with mostly low temperatures during the morning but a hot afternoon, we classified the day as a heating day even though the building needed more cooling than heating; therefore, we mistakenly preheated a building that needed precooling (or at least not preheating).

Figure 10 shows an example of a heating day misclassified as a cooling day for a single model. The day was misclassified as a heating day, and preheating was performed from 14:00 to 18:00, resulting in a large reduction in cooling load later in the day because the preheating increased both the heating and the cooling set points 2 ; however, once the peak period begins at 18:00, the increased cooling set point is reset to normal, resulting in increased cooling energy consumption. Essentially, we tried to preheat when precooling would have been appropriate, resulting in increased load during the peak. The solution was to avoid preheating or precooling when the average daily outdoor temperature is near the threshold (66°F) because it is hard to predict whether precooling or preheating would be the more appropriate action. In the final run, we implemented this correction.

Figure 11 shows minimal cooling below an average daily temperature of 10°C (50°F), and Figure 12 shows minimal heating above an average daily temperature of 25°C (68°F). Based on these results, in the final implementation, we precooled only if the daily average temperature is above 68°F, and we preheated only if the daily average temperature is below 50°F. We did not need to follow these thresholds for load shedding -decreasing the heating set point and increasing the cooling set point during the peak period will reduce the demand regardless of the building having a cooling or a heating load.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.3  Final Sensitivity Analysis

After further reviewing the real-world demand response programs and reviewing the initial sensitivity analysis results, we narrowed the analysis space. First, we narrowed the offset to only 2 -4°F, and then we limited the precooling windows to 1 hour and 4 hours. More details can be seen in Table 7.

In this round, we also introduced a random shift. This was used to reduce the 'snapback , ' or rebound, seen after the peak period when all thermostats reset to the normal set point at the same time. A maximum random shift of ± 30 minutes will make some buildings start their peak period up to 30 minutes early or up to 30 minutes late (i.e., the shift can be anything ranging from +30 minutes, to +15 minutes, to 0 minutes, to -15 minutes, to -30 minutes). This random shifting was assigned on a building-by-building basis, not on a per-event basis. In a real deployment, this staggering of individual homes could be accomplished through a combination of intentional control, inherent time delays, and equipment states found across the portfolio at any point in time.

Table 7. Test Run Specification for Final Sensitivity Analysis

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.5  Stock-Level Results

A test run with 30,000 samples was conducted. The state-level D3 metrics are calculated in the following five steps:

1. Filter out samples that have electric heating and samples that have cooling separately.

2. Aggregate state-level heating (or cooling) time series for both the baseline and savings from upgrades.
3. Calculate the percentage reduction in heating or cooling during the peak periods for each day.
4. Remove days where heating (or cooling) savings during peak periods are zero, indicating that the thermostat demand flexibility measure is not applicable on those days.
5. Compute the mean, along with the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles for the remaining days.

The results for the single-family detached across the five upgrades are shown in Figure 15 -Figure 19. States not shown in the figures either lack relevant data due to an insufficient sample size or do not have the specific end use (heating or cooling) savings.

Figure 15 shows an approximate 40% winter and 30% summer reduction in peak load from load shedding for 4 hours with a 2°F offset. As expected, Figure 16 shows an approximate 15% winter and 10% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 4 hours with a 2°F offset. This lower reduction relative to Figure 15 is expected because the thermal inertia does not carry through the entire 4-hour peak window. Figure 17 shows an approximate 60% winter and 50% summer reduction in peak load from load shedding for 4 hours with a 4°F offset. This deep reduction is expected because of the significant depth of the set point change. Figure 18 shows an approximate 30% winter and 20% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 4 hours with a 4°F offset. As expected, this reduction is larger than the reduction shown from load shifting with a 2°F offset because the deeper set point change for 4 hours allows more charging of the building thermal mass, allowing reduced space conditioning during more of the 4-hour peak window. Last, Figure 19 shows an approximate 10% winter and 5% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 1 hour with a 2°F offset. text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.6  Limitations and Concerns

In this measure, demand response is dispatched every day. This is done to evaluate and estimate the potential impact of demand response over a wide range of day types and weather conditions. For this reason, although the individual day-level results for this measure are realistic, the annual energy consumption savings are not consistent with the current dispatch practices, and they should not be used directly . Instead, users interested in estimating annual energy impacts should splice daily time-series results from the baseline model (without demand response) and the time-series results from the upgraded model (with demand response) in the target proportion.

impacts should splice daily time-series results from the baseline model (without demand response) and the time-series results from the upgraded model (with demand response) in the target proportion.

This measure is applied to all dwelling units with electric heating or cooling to investigate load flexibility potential; however, only a subset of these units is ideally suited for this measure. Units already equipped with smart thermostats have a lower barrier to entry into a demand response program. This measure assumes that units without a smart thermostat would be equipped with one as part of the installation process. Alternately, utilities could ask customers to manually adjust thermostats for a small number of events per year, but the participation of such a program would be important to establish. If one wishes to study the impact of the partial penetration of smart thermostats or less than 100% participation in the demand response program, they should take a subset of buildings from the upgrade and take the rest from the baseline.

In previous calibration efforts, the building energy models used in ResStock have shown a temperature decay that is faster than empirical data. To better match the empirical data, ResStock uses an increased thermal capacitance multiplier for the air inside the dwelling units. This could still result in temperature decay profiles that are faster than reality, meaning that this analysis could underestimate the duration of the load reduction before the adjusted thermostat set point is reached. If the root cause is an underestimate of the thermal mass, the results could also underestimate the amount of time required to effectively preheat or precool the dwellings.

set point is reached. If the root cause is an underestimate of the thermal mass, the results could also underestimate the amount of time required to effectively preheat or precool the dwellings.

The models used in ResStock represent the building stock circa 2018 using weather from 2018, but the goal is to estimate the potential of demand flexibility in 2050. Based on the slow speed of retrofits in the building stock and the slow uptake of envelope upgrades, the use of today's building stock is believed to be an acceptable limitation. The impact of not using future weather projections is more difficult to assess. On one hand, average temperatures are not expected to change dramatically by 2050. On the other hand, extreme temperatures, which might or might not be coincident with the peak periods, could change more dramatically.

temperatures are not expected to change dramatically by 2050. On the other hand, extreme temperatures, which might or might not be coincident with the peak periods, could change more dramatically.

This measure relies on the inputs for on-peak hours during summer, winter and intermediate seasons. We selected a grid peak load reduction approach for the year 2050 as the target of this study. This could create higher customer costs or grid operation costs, depending on the utility rate design and other factors. The choice of future load scenario in Cambium and the fact that the future load profile does not include wide-scale electrification could also significantly impact the timing of the peak periods. An analysis of these factors would require modeling the future power system, including the dispatch of demand response resources. That modeling is beyond the scope of this analysis.

Finally, the choice of pre-peak and on-peak durations and the set point offset are applied uniformly across the entire building stock; however, optimal settings likely vary, depending on the climate and the building 's characteristics. For example, a long pre-peak duration might not be effective for dwellings with poor exterior insulation because they tend to lose heat quickly.

text:
HVAC Demand Flexibility with On-Peak Load Shedding of 2F offset — 4.7  Future Work

The results provided in this analysis could be expanded in several ways. First, determining the peak period windows for targeting the load reduction could be based on different future load profiles -in particular, load profiles assuming major electrification of vehicles and space heating. If those load profiles significantly shift the timing of the peak load window, performing new analysis might be warranted. If the timing of the windows shifts only minimally, the uncertainty due to other future changes might outweigh the uncertainty in these results. Second, these results could be recreated using a future building stock. In 2050, some dwellings that exist in today's ResStock model will have been demolished, whereas others will have been retrofitted with new equipment, and new dwellings will have been built. All these changes could impact the results. If deep energy efficiency with significant building envelope improvements is widely adopted, the thermal response of the dwellings might change. Last, a further comparison of the thermal decay of the ResStock models to empirical data could be performed. Ideally, this comparison would result in improvements to the ResStock models. How much these changes would affect the presented results is unclear.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Executive Summary

This report documents the development and simulation of the Electric Vehicle (EV) Adoption with Level 1 (L1) Charging measure within ResStock™. ResStock is a physics-based, bottom-up modeling tool designed to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock and estimate building energy use and bills for scenarios at both regional and national scales.

The EV Adoption with L1 Charging measure adds one EV and one L1 charger to every occupied dwelling unit. This approach models a future scenario to capture the effects of widespread EV adoption and L1 charging on the residential energy sector. Results show that full adoption increases national residential site energy use by approximately 7.2%, driven entirely by additional EV charging demand. The broad applicability of the measure allows users to combine results with the baseline and other EV scenarios to simulate different levels of adoption and participation. These custom scenarios can be designed to model EV technology penetration and behavior, and leverage ResStock granularity to construct adoption scenarios based on housing attributes or occupant demographics.

scenarios can be designed to model EV technology penetration and behavior, and leverage ResStock granularity to construct adoption scenarios based on housing attributes or occupant demographics.

This measure provides a method for analyzing the interactions between residential energy demand and transportation electrification. By aligning charging behavior with other occupantdriven loads, users can evaluate strategies to balance household energy needs with grid reliability. The results highlight the growing influence of EV adoption on residential energy consumption and the importance of planning for increased electricity demand as the transportation sector electrifies. As EV adoption expands and charging technologies advance, this work supports data-driven decisions that promote a more efficient, resilient, and affordable energy future.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Measure Motivation

Utilities, auto manufacturers, charging providers, and EV supply equipment manufacturers are working together to develop technologies (such as smart chargers) and services (such as time-of use rates) that enable efficient EV-grid integration. With potential continued EV adoption (over 10% of sales in the United States in 2024 [IEA 2025] and 25.3% of sales in California [California Energy Commission 2025] in 2024), coordination between the residential energy sector, transportation sector, and electric grid will play a key role in maintaining affordability and reliability. Without such coordination, increases in peak demand may require costly grid upgrades, increase electricity prices, and increase the risk of outages or degraded service.

metadata.doc_title: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging
metadata.measure_name: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Measure Motivation

affordability and reliability. Without such coordination, increases in peak demand may require costly grid upgrades, increase electricity prices, and increase the risk of outages or degraded service.

This ResStock ™ (Reyna et al. 2025) measure assigns one EV and an L1 charger to each occupied dwelling unit model that does not own an EV in the baseline scenario. We apply only to units without an existing EV so that Level 2 (L2) chargers are not downgraded to L1 and households with L1 chargers in the baseline result in no change. By modeling widespread adoption of EVs and chargers, ResStock users can combine models from both the baseline and the measure to create their own unique EV saturation scenarios. This allows nuanced scenarios in which only segments of households adopt EVs or shift their charging load. Such a method can be used to model EV and charger adoption scenarios and examine the resulting energy and power impacts on the residential building sector. The simultaneous charging of EVs at multiple dwelling units in this measure can also quantify the potential stress that a local electric grid may incur during peak charging hours.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 2.1  Introduction to Electric Vehicles in ResStock

EVs are an increasingly important component of residential energy demand, with charging behavior often correlated with other household loads due to shared occupancy and behavioral patterns. The current ResStock baseline reflects 2023 EV saturation levels, which corresponds to a small number of representative dwelling unit models with EVs (1.05% of all datapoints). For each EV-owning dwelling unit, ResStock assigns specific vehicle properties, driving behavior, and charging behavior dependent on location, demographics (income and tenure), or occupancy - factors that also influence other household load profiles. While the baseline includes a limited number of EVs, ResStock's EV measures enable scenario analysis of future adoption and charging patterns.

This measure comprises two components: adoption of an EV and adoption of an L1 charger. EV charging power in ResStock depends on the vehicle charger type, while EV charging demand depends on characteristics of the EV and driver behavior. When an EV is assigned to a dwelling unit in ResStock, the characteristics of the vehicle, driving behavior, and charging behavior are predetermined in the sampling routine, using distributions sourced from the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) and other datasets (Speake et al. 2025).

and charging behavior are predetermined in the sampling routine, using distributions sourced from the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) and other datasets (Speake et al. 2025).

ResStock leverages physics-based modeling, where high-level EV and driving behavior ResStock inputs are translated to EnergyPlus inputs to model the charging energy demand of an individual dwelling unit, as shown in Figure 1. The ResStock baseline is consistent with EV saturations from 2023, which corresponds to a small number of representative models with EVs. The ResStock EV characteristics that inform the energy model and influence the charging energy demand include the (1) EV battery/vehicle type, (2) annual vehicle miles traveled (VMT), and (3) at-home charging fraction. The battery/vehicle type determines EV efficiency and battery capacity, while VMT influences the time spent driving, which in turn determines charging demand. The at-home charging fraction describes the share of the vehicle's electricity demand met by the residential charger. These inputs are assigned to all households in the ResStock baseline regardless of whether the EV is modeled. The charger type is not predetermined for all dwelling units and is instead explicitly defined in a measure. The EV charger power is assumed constant; however, the timing and duration of charging events are highly variable across models due to varying vehicle parameters, driving behaviors, and occupancy patterns. The underlying EV model accounts for charging and discharging losses by scaling the driving power with ambient temp

Baseline EV charging availability schedules indicate when a vehicle is plugged in and available to charge. These schedules are determined by the dwelling unit's occupancy schedule, whereas the periods of active charging are dependent on the availability schedule and the EV's state of charge (SOC). EV charging availability schedules in ResStock are generated stochastically based on the presence of an individual occupant assigned as the driver. During an 'away period' for the driver, the vehicle is assumed to be driven immediately after the occupant leaves and just before they return home. While the baseline charging availability schedule is dependent only upon the driver's occupancy status, the duration and magnitude of charging energy depend on the VMT, the charger power, vehicle properties, and fraction charged at home, as discussed further in Section 4.1. The driving schedules are dependent on stochastic occupant behavior, but do not explicitly capture seasonal variations in travel.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 3  Applicability

The 'EV Adoption With Level 1 Charging' measure applies to all occupied dwelling units in the baseline scenario without EV ownership. This logic corresponds to 86.8% of the existing housing stock. Only a single EV is adopted per dwelling unit, as modeling multiple vehicles is not currently supported. This measure design allows flexibility when analyzing scenarios of adoption. For example, a user can select a percentage of a specific segment to adopt this measure while using the results from the baseline simulation for the remaining models. Units in multifamily buildings are included in the measure. Although multi-family households may not own the charging infrastructure or see its impact on their utility bills in practice, we model them consistently with other housing types, treating EV energy as a direct household energy cost. We also assume that multi-family chargers are always available, which may not be true in practice, and therefore the charging event durations may not reflect actual events.

metadata.doc_title: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging
metadata.measure_name: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 4.1  Methodology

To model baseline residential EV charging demand in ResStock, our approach: (1) characterizes regional inputs that affect EV battery parameters, driving behavior, and charger characteristics; (2) assigns these inputs as arguments to individual dwelling unit models; (3) generates occupancy-driven charging and discharging schedules; and (4) simulates building energy models with integrated EVs. We associate each EV with an at-home charger, and report only the charging energy of the dwelling unit, as charging energy away from home is not modeled. No vehicle-to-building energy exchange is considered in ResStock. To apply this measure to the baseline, we repeat Steps 2-4 using updated inputs to assign EV ownership and charger.

More detailed information regarding baseline EV modeling and scheduling in ResStock can be found in Speake et al. (2025), which describes the EV stock characterization, model input generation, battery modeling, and analysis of baseline results.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Electric Vehicle Stock Characterization

Included in the baseline ResStock inputs are probability distributions that describe the likelihood of EV-related attributes being assigned to dwelling units. These EV-related inputs are part of ResStock's broader stock characterization process, which defines detailed building, occupant, and technology characteristics for the U.S. residential building stock (see Section 3 Reyna et al. [2025] for more detail). EV input distributions are sampled to produce EV ownership profiles for each building model. The baseline of ResStock assigns each dwelling unit a value for EV ownership, the at-home charging fraction, the vehicle type that provides the battery capacity and efficiency, and the VMT per year. If a dwelling unit has an EV, an EV charger is applied, and its power draw is determined based on the charger level. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles are not currently modeled in ResStock.

The ResStock EV implementation draws data from the TEMPO ™  model (Muratori et al. 2021), EIA RECS 2020 (U.S. EIA 2020), the National Household Travel Survey (Federal Highway Administration 2022), vehicle registration data from Experian 1 , the No Place Like Home study (Ge et al. 2021), and the Autonomie model 2 . The distributions of these options reflect 2023 saturation levels of EV technology and operation in the United States, ensuring that EV-related measures capture expected diversity 3 . All dwelling units are sampled with percentage of vehicle charge at home, a vehicle type, and a VMT. These options are only relevant in the baseline for dwelling units with an EV but are used to define vehicle and driving characteristics for dwelling units that adopt an EV in this measure. text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Vehicle Schedules

We generate two EV schedules as inputs to the vehicle battery model, (1) a charging availability schedule, which indicates when a vehicle is plugged in and available to charge, and (2) a driving schedule, during which the EV battery is discharging energy. Both schedules are derived from the dwelling unit's occupancy schedule, and the driving schedule also depends on the assigned ev\_hours\_per\_week argument. The durations of charging energy events are dependent on the charging availability schedule and the SOC. Figure 3 shows a snapshot of relevant schedules for a single EV driver. The schedules values represent the fraction of each 15-minute timestep during which the event occurs, and values less than one correspond to events shorter than 15 minutes.

4 See Section 3 of Speake et al. (2025) for more detailed information on EV stock characterization in ResStock

Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Vehicle Schedules

EV plugged-in schedule, charging power, driving schedule, and driver occupancy schedule

![Image](94459_images/image_000004_081d9b6686e8cf141807f9c4cdb8292111a6e7e19aa2f2c962d6dd6754c13cd7.png)

The durations of driving periods scale with the occupant's weekly driving hours and are proportionally adjusted with the duration of the away period. On average, higher-mileage drivers have shorter away periods in which they are not driving. We assume a constant driving speed but scale the discharge power based on the ambient temperature, as discussed in the following subsection. The charging schedule is similarly based on occupancy, where the baseline behavior assumes that the vehicle is plugged in when the occupant arrives home. In the figure, the charging availability schedule overlaps the occupancy schedule except for the time step where occupancy is partial (between 0 and 1). A partial occupancy time step, in which the occupant is home for only part of the 15-minute time step, would ideally reflect both charging and discharging. However, ResStock models these events entirely as discharging, as the underlying EnergyPlus ® battery model can only be charged or discharged in a time step. This limitation may cut short or delay charging by up to 15 minutes; however, that is preferable to underestimating discharging, where events are shorter and changes in the duration would have a much larger impact on the total discharge energy-and, consequently, the charging energy.

preferable to underestimating discharging, where events are shorter and changes in the duration would have a much larger impact on the total discharge energy-and, consequently, the charging energy.

The charging availability schedule shown in the figure indicates when the vehicle is plugged in and eligible to be charged, whereas the actual charging, i.e., energy consumption, is handled by the battery model. Once charging begins, the only parameters that influence the timing and the magnitude of energy use are the charger power and the battery SOC. When charging availability schedule has a value of 1, the EV will charge at a constant power (1.6 kilowatts for L1 charger)

until the maximum SOC is reached, at which point no further charging load occurs, regardless of the schedule. The behavior can be observed in Figure 3 prior to 10:30 and after 18:30 where charging power consumption remains zero despite charging availability schedule being 1. It can also be seen that the charging power remains constant at 5.69 kW when the vehicle is being charged - the slight depression during the second event where the charging power is below 5.69 kW is because in the underlying model charging doesn't occur for the full 15 minutes before charging stops after reaching the maximum SOC.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Electric Vehicle Modeling

The charging availability and driving schedules are aligned with the stochastic occupancy model (based on American Time Use Survey data) in OpenStudio-HPXML. We calculate the total hours driven per week using the ev\_average\_mph (calculated from Federal Highway Administration [2022]) and ev\_miles\_per\_year arguments from the 'Electric Vehicle Battery' and 'Annual Miles Driven' input files, respectively, which inform the charging and discharging schedule generation. The battery model takes care of the actual power draw during the charging and discharging periods. An example of what these schedules look like is presented in Figure 3. The charging schedule algorithm assumes that the occupant plugs in their vehicle as soon as they arrive home and keeps it plugged in until they leave. Thus, the charging availability schedule is identical to the occupancy schedule of the driver, but the schedule of actual charging typically differs. This scenario makes the battery eligible to be charged anytime the EV is at home if the SOC is below the maximum level. Whether the charging happens and at what power level is managed by the battery and charger modeling. Additionally, not all EV owners are modeled as charging exclusively at home. The 2020 RECS included a question about what fraction of charging is done at home, with the options being 100%, 80% to 99%, 60% to 79%, etc., which was transl

metadata.doc_title: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging
metadata.measure_name: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Electric Vehicle Modeling

modeled as charging exclusively at home. The 2020 RECS included a question about what fraction of charging is done at home, with the options being 100%, 80% to 99%, 60% to 79%, etc., which was transl

ated to a ResStock input file and sampled to assign the 'Home Charging Fraction' input. This input scales the average energy consumption rate of the battery model, ensuring that the resulting charging energy reflects only the portion of charging that occurs at home. The charging power remains fixed regardless of the at-home charging fraction, and only the vehicle discharge power is affected. The underlying assumption in using this approach is that 2020 RECS respondents implement the fraction of their charging in terms of energy, as opposed to time.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Electric Vehicle Modeling

vehicle discharge power is affected. The underlying assumption in using this approach is that 2020 RECS respondents implement the fraction of their charging in terms of energy, as opposed to time.

EV charging and discharging energy are modeled within OpenStudio-HPXML, which leverages a lithium-ion battery model in EnergyPlus ® . The 'Electric Vehicle Charger' input directly influences charging power draw, which is assigned a constant value dependent on the charger level. The L1 charger type in this measure has a power draw of 1.6 kilowatts. The other ResStock inputs in Table 2 influence the average EV energy consumption rate as well as the duration of driving events, which will reflect in the duration and energy demand of charging events. The 'Home Charging Fraction' input adjusts for the actual charging energy provided by the at-home charger, however, we do not directly alter the number charging events but instead scale the average EV energy consumption rate.

The average EV energy consumption rate can be considered the average driving power output under design conditions. For each household, this output is calculated by:

metadata.doc_title: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging
metadata.measure_name: Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — Electric Vehicle Modeling

EV energy consumption rate.

The average EV energy consumption rate can be considered the average driving power output under design conditions. For each household, this output is calculated by:

1. Determining the expected annual EV energy consumption (kilowatt-hours) by multiplying the EV energy efficiency (kilowatt-hours per mile) by the annual miles (miles)
2. Calculating the average EV energy consumption rate by dividing the annual discharge energy (kilowatt-hours) by the number of hours driven per year.

Although we do not include all time-dependent variables impacting discharge events, we do incorporate a model that adjusts the average EV energy consumption based on the dwelling unit site ambient temperature at each time step. Ambient temperature plays a large role in EV energy usage, attributed primarily to the climate control systems of the vehicle cabin and battery. We deploy a curve of the discharge power versus ambient temperature 5 in the EnergyPlus Energy Management System 6  to capture the higher energy demand associated with cold-weather operation relative to mild or hot weather.

The 'EV Adoption With L1 Charging' measure assigns the 'Electric Vehicle Ownership' parameter to 'Yes' and the 'Electric Vehicle Charger' as 'Level 1,' while the remaining EVrelated inputs are assigned during the baseline sampling routine as described in this section and detailed further in Speake et al. (2025). This approach preserves both the diversity and the expected dependencies that influence vehicle type and operation.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 4.2  Modeling Limitations

The modeled EV charging energy may not always align with the driving demand, as it is constrained by the charging schedule and charger type. Different combinations of EV-related inputs can thus lead to a discrepancy between charging demand and charging availability. This approach can result in reduced charging energy, which is quantified with a custom output variable 'unmet driving hours', in which the EV is scheduled to be in use but does not have the required SOC to complete its driving hours. Unmet driving hours are seen in larger proportions in dwelling units with L1 chargers that lack the higher power input of L2 chargers, and charge mostly at home. Section 5 includes figures of the prominence of unmet driving hours in this measure. Unmet driving hours can be an important metric when designing vehicle and charger adoption scenarios. Input combinations with a higher number of unmet driving hours may be less realistic and, as a result, may be given less weight in scenario design.

designing vehicle and charger adoption scenarios. Input combinations with a higher number of unmet driving hours may be less realistic and, as a result, may be given less weight in scenario design.

We assume a direct relationship between home occupancy and driving/charging events, which results in similar daily schedules throughout the year, with distinct patterns for weekdays and weekends. While this simplifies modeling, it may underpredict or overpredict individual charging or discharging events, as real-world behavior is more variable. Similarly, we apply the 'fraction charged at home' input directly to the discharging power, reducing charging loads evenly across the year. While this might be realistic for some drivers who split their charging between home and other locations, others may instead scale their number of at-home charging events, where only certain days are used to charge at home. In this case, our approach captures the annual demand but may underestimate the magnitude or duration of individual charging events. This simplification may also lead to underestimation or overestimation of unmet driving hours, which in practice depend on alignment between charging locations and at-home hours.

This measure assumes a distribution of energy consumption rates and capacities that align with the current baseline EV stock, as set by the 'EV Battery' input. This measure may potentially overpredict the energy demand if EV technology makes advancements in efficiency and capacity over a certain adoption period. This current snapshot of battery efficiency and capacity may also overpredict unmet driving hours compared to future EV technologies with higher efficiencies. Additionally, ResStock limits dwelling units to a single EV, which is reasonable for capturing aggregate trends but may underestimate peak charging power in households with multiple EVs. As EV adoption scales, capturing these dynamics will be increasingly important for accurately modeling demand spikes and infrastructure needs.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 5  Results

This section provides an overview of results from the 'EV Adoption With L1 Charging' measure package and the baseline scenario. The results are presented to illustrate the measure's performance and ensure confidence in its implementation, not to reflect a realistic scenario on its own. The measure is designed to offer the users flexibility when combined with the baseline or other measures. As such, results presented here should be interpreted with caution.

Although this section presents the energy and unmet driving hour impacts of the measure, the full set of outputs available in the dataset includes annual and time series charging energy, charging emissions, utility bills, and EV schedules. Section 5.1 shows the overall stock energy consumption, Section 5.2 displays the unmet driving hours, and Section 5.3 shows samples of time series data.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 5.1  Annual Stock Energy Consumption

Figure 4 presents the distributions of annual ResStock energy usage for the baseline and the measure at the national level. With broad adoption of EVs and L1 chargers (86.8% of the housing stock), the national site energy usage increases by 7.2%, which is entirely driven by increases in EV charging electricity demand. Figure 5 shows annual stock energy consumption by Building America climate zone. Stock energy consumption expectedly increases with the 'EV Adoption With L1 Charging' measure package in all climate zones. While EV charging loads are influenced by outdoor temperatures, the effect is much smaller compared to heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) loads. As a result, the measure's percentage of change in total energy usage is mostly driven by the proportion of baseline HVAC energy usage, where milder climates will exhibit a higher percentage energy increase from EV adoption. Increases in total consumption range from 5.3% in the 'Very Cold' climate zone to 10.6% in the 'Hot-Dry' climate zone.

text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 1 Charging — 5.2  Average Unmet Driving Hours

Figure 6 displays the average unmet driving hours for each VMT value and percentage charged at home. Unmet driving hours occur when battery charging is not sufficient for the EV's energy demand and are primarily a result of modeling limitations. The most important factors determining unmet driving hours are charger level, VMT, and percent charged at home. Charger level influences the rate of charging possible, while VMT and percent charged at home determine the amount of charging needed. Figure 6 highlights this trend, where only vehicles with high VMT and a high rate of home charging incur unmet driving hours. The increase in this measure is due to the larger fraction of homes with L1 chargers, which are less likely to meet the vehicle's energy demand. However, vehicles with high VMT are relatively uncommon, and most vehicles in the stock experience no unmet driving hours. Across the entire stock, this measure results in an average of 2.37 unmet driving hours, affecting 6.61% of homes.

Figure 6. Unmet driving hours per EV per year by the EV characteristics 'Annual VMT' and 'Percent Charged at Home' for the baseline scenario and the 'EV Adoption With L1 Charging' measure. Unmet driving hours occur when battery charging is not sufficient for the EV's energy demand.

Figure 7 shows the electricity demand for the state of Colorado over 3 days in the winter (left) and 3 days in the summer (right). The dashed line is the demand from the baseline scenario. This measure results in new electricity peaks coinciding with the average time an occupant returns home and aligns closely with the timing of the baseline daily peaks in both seasons. While L1 charging will have lower peak demand than L2 charging, there is still a significant increase due to the full adoption of EVs in the measure. Note that this measure is not meant to reflect a realistic scenario on its own. Rather, it is designed to offer the users flexibility when combined with the baseline or other measures. text:
Electric Vehicle Adoption with Level 2 Charging — Executive Summary

This report documents the development and simulation of the Electric Vehicle (EV) Adoption with Level 2 (L2) Charging measure within ResStock™. ResStock is a physics-based, bottom-up modeling tool designed to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock and estimate building energy use and bills for scenarios at both regional and national scales.

The EV Adoption with L2 Charging measure adds one EV and one L2 charger to every occupied dwelling unit. This approach models a future scenario to capture the effects of widespread EV adoption and L2 charging on the residential energy sector. Results show that full adoption increases national residential site energy use by approximately 7.2%, driven entirely by additional EV charging demand. The broad applicability of the measure allows users to combine results with the baseline and other EV scenarios to simulate different levels of adoption and participation. These custom scenarios can be designed to model EV technology penetration and behavior, and leverage ResStock granularity to construct adoption scenarios based on housing attributes or occupant demographics.

scenarios can be designed to model EV technology penetration and behavior, and leverage ResStock granularity to construct adoption scenarios based on housing attributes or occupant demographics.

This measure provides a method for analyzing the interactions between residential energy demand and transportation electrification. By aligning charging behavior with other occupantdriven loads, users can evaluate strategies to balance household energy needs with grid reliability. The results highlight the growing influence of EV adoption on residential energy consumption and the importance of planning for increased electricity demand as the transportation sector electrifies. As EV adoption expands and charging technologies advance, this work supports data-driven decisions that promote a more efficient, resilient, and affordable energy future.
