Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Envelope Improvements and Advanced Air Sealing — 3.5 Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the two-stage GHP with envelope improvements and advanced air sealing will have on electrical panels. The modeling assumptions and details about electric panels in ResStock can be found in the single-stage GHP documentation 9 .

First, Figure 10 and Figure 11 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. Figure 10 shows in the first column, 'All', that about 35% of all dwelling units have 0 or only 1 breaker space available. Figure 11 shows in the first column that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock, but that the other 2.3% of electric panels already have an existing capacity constraint.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it's important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil).

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. This results in a time-series profile broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model is intended to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. The methodology and results of the baseline model are discussed in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project 1  (Wilson, et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: advanced air sealing with drill-and-fill wall insulation.

The advanced air sealing with drill-and-fill wall insulation upgrade demonstrated 22% total site energy savings for the U.S. residential building stock (see Figure 3 for more details). These savings are primarily attributed to:

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Drill-and-Fill Insulation

Drill-and-fill insulation is a method used to insulate existing walls. The most common drill-andfill insulation materials are cellulose, fiberglass, and spray foam. For cellulose and fiberglass, there are two main types of drill-and-fill installation: loose fill (also known as blown-in) and dense pack, which requires professional equipment (North 2012). This measure upgrade models cellulose as the drill-and-fill insulation material.

Drill-and-fill insulation can be installed from either the inside or outside of the building. In multifamily buildings, drilling from the outside is more common because it allows occupants to remain in place during the work is being performed, and reduces asbestos risk for installers (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2011) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2019). For these reasons, external drill-and-fill will be the focus of this upgrade. Drilling from the interior may be preferable in certain situations, such as inclement weather, when siding is difficult to remove, or when the home is vacant. Figure 1 shows a photo of a drill-and-fill retrofit in progress.

Figure 1. Drill-and-fill insulation

![Image](96281_images/image_000002_46496dc9dcb6427dbff75f4ddc0358aa8acb60d56420701d57fc4b392b42fde5.png)

Photo by Dennis Schroeder, NLR # 28786

Figure 1. Drill-and-fill insulation

![Image](96281_images/image_000002_46496dc9dcb6427dbff75f4ddc0358aa8acb60d56420701d57fc4b392b42fde5.png)

Photo by Dennis Schroeder, NLR # 28786

In a drill-and-fill retrofit, small round holes (typically 1- to 2-inch diameter) are drilled into the exterior wall of the home between the studs (e.g., every 16 inches) (U.S. Department of Energy 2022). A hose is inserted into the wall, and insulation is then blown in. Both the small round holes and the hose are visible in Figure 1.

the studs (e.g., every 16 inches) (U.S. Department of Energy 2022). A hose is inserted into the wall, and insulation is then blown in. Both the small round holes and the hose are visible in Figure 1.

Exterior wall studs in residential construction commonly have three widths: 2x3, 2x4, and 2x6. The 2x3 and 2x4 studs are more common in mobile/manufactured homes and older residential construction, whereas 2x6 studs are more frequently used in newer residential construction (Krigger 2006) (Kochkin and Wiehagan 2014). Mobile/manufactured homes may use 2x2 studs, but these are typically only for interior walls (Dickerhoof 1977). This ResStock 2025 Release 1 assumes that R-13 insulation can fit within a 2x4 wall. In cases where higher levels of insulation are installed, OS-HPXML selects the appropriate wall construction set to ensure the desired Rvalue is achieved. This may include changing the stud cavity depth -for example, changing a wall from a 2x4 to a 2x6 to meet the requirement. More information on this topic can be found on the ResStock 'Wood Stud Depth and Wall RValue Calculations' page . 2

metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Drill-and-Fill Insulation

depth -for example, changing a wall from a 2x4 to a 2x6 to meet the requirement. More information on this topic can be found on the ResStock 'Wood Stud Depth and Wall RValue Calculations' page . 2

When installing drill-and-fill insulation from the exterior of a building, the cladding material is an important consideration. Exterior wood or vinyl siding is sometimes partially removed to allow holes to be drilled in the exterior sheathing. Wood siding can also be drilled through and then patched. Some types of metal siding may be removable, while others may not be (Allwein and Biddle 2002). In homes with face brick (4-inch) as cladding over wood stud walls, drill-andfill can be performed by drilling smaller holes through mortar joints. Other construction types, such as concrete masonry units (CMUs) or steel framing, are limited to insulation methods other than drill-and-fill for retrofits (U.S. Department of Energy 2019).

Other ways to insulate a wall include adding rigid insulation board to the exterior or interior, or removing interior finishes and adding batt insulation, among others (Baechler, et al. 2021) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2019). Attic, crawlspace, basement, or other building insulation techniques are not covered in this measure. Attic floor insulation for unfinished basements is addressed in a separate measure documentation. 3

Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Drill-and-Fill Insulation

crawlspace, basement, or other building insulation techniques are not covered in this measure. Attic floor insulation for unfinished basements is addressed in a separate measure documentation. 3

There are safety concerns that must be addressed when performing drill-and-fill insulation. The structural integrity of the exterior wall and cladding is important, as is any existing water damage (Pfeiffer 2021). Asbestos is a health and safety concern for insulation installers and is more common in homes built between 1930 and 1970 (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2011). Mold or rotted wood may be found in stud cavities, which could also complicate retrofits (Brozyna and Badger 2013). This is not a complete list of safety concerns that should be addressed before upgrading a building's insulation.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 1.2  Drill-and-Fill Considerations

The thermal resistance of drill-and-fill insulation is measured by its R-value, which represents the material 's ability to reduce heat flow (U.S. Department of Energy 2010). A higher R-value results in less heat transfer. As a retrofit, drill-and-fill wall insulation can achieve up to R-13 cavity insulation in 2x4 exterior stud cavities (3.5 inches at R-3.7 per inch), which is the maximum insulation level modeled in this measure (Holladay 2013).

Wall cavities that are insulated to levels less than R-13 (e.g., R-11, R-7) did not receive the drilland-fill upgrade in this ResStock measure. An experienced drill-and-fill practitioner noted that installing additional drill-and-fill insulation into an already insulated wall could cause the insulation batt to bunch, create uneven insulation levels, and lead to other issues. This is supported by literature on retrofit projects that choose not to perform drill-and-fill insulation on walls with existing insulation below R-13 (Frontier Energy, Inc., Misti Bruceri & Associates, LLC 2022) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2022). However, there is some evidence that drill-and-fill can be applied to walls with existing insulation, but this is not included in this measure (Holladay 2013).

Manufactured housing or mobile homes receive drill-and-fill insulation in this measure only if the walls are uninsulated and wood stud. In practice, this can be extremely difficult and requires caution (Carlson and Bemis 1979) (Judkoff, Hancock and Franconi 1990). As with all ResStock results, this upgrade measure represents theoretical technical potential, and dataset users should independently assess whether this measure is appropriate for their building segment of interest.

Studies often pair air sealing and drill-and-fill insulation and report combined energy savings. One study modeled energy savings from drill-and-fill insulation across different climate zones and found whole-home site energy savings ranging from 8.8% to 13.5% (Polly, et al. 2011). Across the literature, drill-and-fill insulation upgrades are frequently paired with air sealing measures (U.S. Department of Energy 2025) (Brozyna and Badger 2013) (Roberts and Stephenson 2012). More information on air sealing modeling can be found in the advanced air sealing documentation (Phoung, Lou and White 2025).

For modeling purposes, drill-and-fill insulation is assumed to be installed properly to a Grade 1 insulation level. According to the RESNET Grading system, Grade 1 assumes installation follows the manufacturer's instructions and fills the entire wall cavity ( Construction Instruction Experience Center n.d.). However, a field study found that only half of all homes had Grade 1 insulation (North American Insulation Manufacturers Association 2017). In practice, a Grade 1 assumption may be optimistic, and insulation inspection should be conducted carefully (North American Insulation Manufacturers Association 2017). This optimistic assumption about proper insulation installation is a limitation of the work, and may cause modeled results to be different than actual building retrofit results.

In summary, this upgrade measure assumes:

In summary, this upgrade measure assumes:

- Advanced air sealing is applied to dwelling units with ACH50 infiltration rates of 6 or greater. This applies to 92% of all dwelling units and heavily influences the results.
- Drill-and-fill insulation is applied to about 30% of dwelling units only
- Drill-and-fill insulation uses cellulose up to R-13 on exterior above-grade walls that separate conditioned from unconditioned spaces only
- Existing wall cavities with no insulation will receive the insulation, and walls with insulation less than R-13 will not
- Proper installation is assumed, similar to Grade 1 RESNET installation.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 1.3  Advanced Air Sealing Summary

As previously mentioned, drill-and-fill wall insulation is often installed along with air sealing during retrofit projects. Therefore, this drill-and-fill insulation package is modeled with air sealing. Full documentation for the advanced air sealing component of this package is reported separately, but a summary is provided below (Phoung, Lou and White 2025).

Air sealing can take various forms, including weatherstripping, caulking, and spray foam. Two common ways to describe air leakage rates are air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50) and cubic feet per minute at 50 pascals (CFM50). ACH50 is used to compare air leakage rates between dwelling units of different sizes, and this metric will be used in this package.

All dwelling units with an infiltration rate above 6 ACH50 will receive advanced air sealing and then have an infiltration rate of 5 ACH50. This level of advanced air sealing, 5 ACH50, should be considered very aggressive, similar to bringing all residential air leakage down to IECC 2021 new construction levels (3-5 ACH50 depending on climate). In reality, bringing infiltration rates down to this level may require additional enclosure upgrades, such as over cladding of walls, replacing windows, or other techniques that go beyond traditional air sealing practices. This applies to 92% of all dwelling units (Phoung, Lou and White 2025).

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 3 Modeling Approach

This section explains how advanced air sealing with drill-and-fill wall insulation is functionally modeled in ResStock using OpenStudio-HPXML.

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, Fontanini and Parker, et al. 2025). This measure does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model includes conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that represent the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, Fontanini and Present, et al. 2024). These distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock, with each sample an option for each characteristic. ResStock uses the OpenStudio-HPXML (OS-HPXML) workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models that can be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  using an HPXML (Home Performance eXtensible Markup Language) file. The state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository at the time the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created is available on the NLR ResStock Resources page on GitHub. 5

dwelling unit uses slightly more cooling energy in the early morning and very late at night. These values are expected, and the winter morning peak shows a decrease, which is the anticipated result.

In general, the North Carolina model shows that the heating energy of the upgraded building is lower than that of the baseline building on January 1. From roughly noon to 7 p.m., the heating energy of the upgraded building is higher. A closer look at the individual indoor conditioned space temperature results and the outside wet-bulb temperature (not shown) reveals that the interior temperature of the baseline building rises above the setpoint during part of the noon to 7 p.m. period, causing the heating energy to decrease and eventually reach zero. This coincides with the hottest part of the day.

After wall insulation is added and air infiltration is reduced, the interior temperature of the upgraded home remains more constant, so the temperature fluctuates less. As a result, the house stays a bit cooler and does not exceed the heating setpoint, so the heating system must remain on to maintain to the setpoint.

The North Carolina model shows expected cooling results, with the upgraded dwelling unit having a smaller, more rounded peak and overall lower cooling energy than the baseline unit on July 1.

Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 4.1.1 Example Time Series Individual Building Results

North Carolina model shows expected cooling results, with the upgraded dwelling unit having a smaller, more rounded peak and overall lower cooling energy than the baseline unit on July 1.

For the third building, the Arizona model, heating energy is lower in the upgraded scenario than in the baseline scenario on January 1. The heating system turns on a few hours later in the upgraded scenario, indicating that wall insulation and advanced air sealing keep the home warmer during the night and into early morning, so the heat does not need to run until later in the morning. The heating peak is also significantly reduced. Both results are in line with expectations.

Finally, the Arizona model's upgraded cooling energy profile is lower than the profile for all hours on July 1. The curve is smaller and has a lower peak as well. These results are consistent with the other two example buildings and the expected outcomes.

Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 4.2  Stock Energy Impacts for Applicable Dwelling Units Only

This section presents results for the full ResStock 2025 Release 1, which includes 550,000 modeled samples. Advanced air sealing with drill-and-fill wall insulation was applicable to 92% of dwelling units. In theory, advanced air-sealing was applicable to 92.2% of baseline dwelling units, drill-and-fill wall insulation to 31% of baseline dwelling units, and about 30% of units could receive both measures as shown in Table 3. Below are results for only the applicable dwelling units.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 4.2.1  Annual Stock Energy Analysis

The average baseline applicable dwelling unit consumed 24.51 MWh of site energy per year. After air sealing and drill-and-fill wall insulation were applied to applicable units, the average dwelling unit consumed 19.20 MWh of site energy per year. This represents an average 21.7% decrease.

Figure 3 shows the average energy consumption by end use per dwelling unit before and after the upgrade.

Figure 3. Average energy consumption by end use group per applicable dwelling unit

![Image](96281_images/image_000004_34347d7836123add5a60a69e20342925aab67b0d013ea3a83a25053f2b797833.png)

Before the upgrade, the largest two end uses in the average dwelling unit were natural gas heating and electric cooling. Other notable end uses included miscellaneous electric loads, electric appliances, and natural gas hot water heating. Although these patterns remain in the upgrade scenario, total site energy use is 22% lower. Significant savings are seen in heating and cooling end uses, particularly electric heating (35%), natural gas heating (40%), fuel oil heating (41%), propane heating (36%), electric cooling (11%), electric heating fan pumps (37%), and electric heat pump backup (54%). Slight savings are observed in the electric cooling fans and pumps (8%). End uses like water heating, lighting consumption, and miscellaneous electricity remain unchanged.

Figure 4 shows the annual average percent savings per upgraded dwelling unit broken down by original wall type and insulation level.

Figure 4. Average annual dwelling unit percentage site energy savings per applicable dwelling unit wall type and insulation level

The applicability logic states that only uninsulated wood stud walls are eligible for drill-and-fill insulation, whereas all dwelling units with an infiltration rate of 6 ACH50 or higher are eligible for advanced air sealing. This logic is clearly reflected in the results: uninsulated wood stud walls show an average site energy savings of 32%. All other wall type and insulation combinations show site energy savings ranging from 8% to 20%. Note that these results are more heavily influenced by advanced air sealing, as its applicability exceeds 90%, whereas drill-and-fill insulation applies to only about 30% of dwelling units.

Again, Figure 6 shows that dwellings with higher baseline infiltration rates achieve greater energy savings, exceeding 40% when the baseline infiltration is 50 ACH50. This trend continues down to 10 ACH50 but changes when infiltration rates fall below 10 ACH50. Infiltration rates of 2 -5 ACH50 have a higher percentage of savings than rates of 6 -8 ACH50. This is likely due to 2-5 ACH50 dwelling units having a lower annual site energy than other buildings, as seen in Figure 5, so any change to the site energy consumption results in a higher percentage change even if the absolute change is small.

This is expected given the significant reduction in heating energy shown in the end use breakdown. Climate zones 4A, 5A, 6B, and 7A show greater percentage energy savings than the dwelling units in their respective climate zones. Climate zone 7B shows a larger site energy percentage savings than climate zones 7AK and 8AK because climate zone 7B 's results are driven by natural gas heating savings, which are on average more than three times as large as climate zones 7AK and 8AK savings. In addition, climate zone 7AK shows heat pump fan and cooling electricity increasing after the upgrade. These end use increases further add to the difference in total site energy savings experienced between climate zones 7AK and 7B. The difference among the climate zones savings are also influenced by the electricity consumption from the heat pump heating backup. Climate zone 7B shows a 38% savings on average for this end use, while climate zone 7AK only shows a 23% site energy savings, and this end use is not applicable for climate zone 8AK. Advanced Air Sealing with Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation — 4.2.2  Aggregated Power Time Series in Select States During the Peak Day

Colorado was analyzed for the time-series results. Of the 550,000 dwelling units in the national run, 549,971 of them completed simulation. 9,374 of the completed dwelling units in the national run were in Colorado. The power time-series for Colorado is shown in Figure 11. February 20 is the peak power day.

Figure 11. Baseline site daily aggregated average energy consumption time series for Colorado

![Image](96281_images/image_000012_c85e04ec85ddd60ac0aa0d6e751d57ed63cdbca0fc428d77d6bdfbadc8fa53e3.png)

The peak day, February 20, is shown in more detail in Figure 12, with 15-minute power data.

Figure 12. Time series for peak day in Colorado before and after upgrade

![Image](96281_images/image_000013_4ab1b7f951180dd941402c341fa761194a5236b369c5b9c94ac2175fcdb36ed1.png)

The baseline peak power was 12.9 kW per dwelling unit. After advanced air sealing with drilland-fill wall insulation was applied to the dwelling units, the peak power decreased to 10.1 kW per dwelling unit, representing a 15.5% reduction. Notable savings occurred throughout the entire day, including early morning and late at night. The peaks and valleys generally maintained the same shape.

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to energy efficiency retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. This results in a time-series profile broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model is intended to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al., 2022).

Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al., 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: duct sealing and insulation upgrade.

The duct sealing and insulation upgrade demonstrated 7% total site energy savings (240 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 3). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 11% stock natural gas heating savings (129 TWh)
- 11% stock electricity cooling savings (43 TWh)
- 8% stock electricity heating savings (22 TWh).

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1  Technology Summary

Ducts are used to distribute conditioned air throughout a house from a forced-air heating or cooling system, such as a central furnace, central air conditioner, or ducted heat pump. This measure applies duct sealing to all homes that use ducts for air distribution. Sealing ductwork located in unconditioned spaces saves energy, improves thermal comfort, and can even improve indoor air quality by patching return leaks on ducts exposed to pollutants. This increases the efficiency and performance of HVAC systems, allowing conditioned air to be distributed more effectively to where it is needed while keeping it clean and separated from dusty areas.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

It is estimated that 20% -30% of air moving through ducts leaks into unconditioned spaces instead of reaching its intended destination in the home (ENERGY STAR, 2025). This leakage reduces the efficiency of the heating and cooling system. Duct sealing and insulation reduce heat loss through ductwork and the loss of conditioned air to unconditioned spaces, thereby reducing the amount of input energy needed to deliver the desired amount of heating or cooling. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE, 2011), many homes have HVAC ducts located in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawl spaces. For ducts located in conditioned spaces, duct sealing and insulation will have little impact on energy use.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

many homes have HVAC ducts located in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawl spaces. For ducts located in conditioned spaces, duct sealing and insulation will have little impact on energy use.

Ductwork is often hidden in walls, ceilings, attics, basements, or crawlspaces, which can make repairs challenging. However, there are several ways to reduce leakage and improve efficiency. Duct sealing can reduce leakage directly and can be achieved by several actions (ENERGY STAR, 2025): (1) repair damaged or disconnected ducts and straighten out flexible ducts that are tangled or crushed; (2) seal all leaks and connections with mastic, UL-Listed tape, or an aerosolbased sealant; (3) seal all duct boots to the drywall or subfloor; (4) include a new filter as part of any duct system improvement; (5) install a filter slot opening cover where missing or where the existing cover does not provide an adequate seal.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

or subfloor; (4) include a new filter as part of any duct system improvement; (5) install a filter slot opening cover where missing or where the existing cover does not provide an adequate seal.

In addition to sealing, insulating ducts can help reduce heat loss. Duct insulation is typically applied by wrapping fiberglass insulation around the ducts. Other products, such as spray foam, can also be used to insulate ducts, depending on the application and installation requirements. If insulation is poor, the existing wraps are often replaced with more effective material. ENERGY STAR ®  (ENERGY STAR, 2025) recommends insulating ducts in unconditioned areas (such as attics, crawlspaces, and garages) with insulation that has an R-value of R-6 or higher. The National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) Standard Work Specifications require insulating all ducts outside the thermal boundary to a minimum of R-8, and insulating all ducts exposed to the exterior to a minimum of R-12 (NREL, 2025). However, in contrast to ducts located in attics, crawlspaces, or garages, insulating ducts that run within enclosed building envelope cavitiessuch as wall or floor assemblies-can be more challenging. This type of insulation is typically performed as part of broader envelope insulation work.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

HVAC duct insulation requirements depend on duct location and climate zone. According to IECC 2015, supply and return air ducts must be insulated with at least R-6 insulation when located in unconditioned spaces, at least R-8 insulation when located outside the building in climate zones 1 through 4, and a minimum of R-12 insulation in climate zones 5 through 8.

When located within a building envelope assembly, the duct must be separated from the building exterior or unconditioned or exempt spaces by a minimum of R-8 insulation in climate zones 1 through 4, and a minimum of R-12 insulation in climate zones 5 through 8 (IECC, 2015).

After ductwork improvements, duct insulation can vary based on the duct location within a home. However, for modeling purposes, ResStock assumes uniform duct insulation throughout the entire dwelling unit. After improving insulation on HVAC ducts, the final R-value can range from R-4.2 to R-12, depending on factors such as climate, duct placement, and overall system design. According to research by NLR, increasing duct insulation to R-8 is considered a reasonable target (Andrews, 2001).

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

depending on factors such as climate, duct placement, and overall system design. According to research by NLR, increasing duct insulation to R-8 is considered a reasonable target (Andrews, 2001).

This measure assumes insulation is added only to ducts located in unconditioned spaces, wherever accessible (e.g., attics, crawlspaces, or garages). If the ducts are currently uninsulated, they are wrapped with R-12 insulation, such as flexible fiberglass duct wrap or pre-formed insulation. Since IECC requires a minimum of R-6 insulation for ducts in unconditioned spaces (IECC, 2015), ducts that already meet or exceed this standard are not upgraded. Therefore, if the existing insulation is below R-6, the old wrap is removed and replaced with high-performance R12 insulation. Ducts integrated with the building envelope are not modified. For applicable dwelling units, where duct insulation in unconditioned spaces is currently below the IECC requirement, we also assume that ducts integrated with the building envelope assembly fall below code-specifically, less than R-8 in climate zones 1-4 and less than R-12 in climate zones 5-8. Based on these assumptions, this measure assumes = the average duct insulation level across the entire dwelling unit reaches an R-value of R-8 after improvements.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

less than R-12 in climate zones 5-8. Based on these assumptions, this measure assumes = the average duct insulation level across the entire dwelling unit reaches an R-value of R-8 after improvements.

Duct leakage can be defined as a percentage of airflow or as an airflow leakage volume value. The percentage rating is calculated by comparing the duct system's measured leakage rate to the air handler's flow rate. This metric is useful for assessing HVAC system efficiency. The leakage volume value is measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm) airflow leakage per 100 ft 2 of conditioned floor area. It estimates the total air volume leaked from the system, helping to visualize the extent of leakage and estimate the scope of repair work needed. The IECC (2012) limits leakage to 4 cfm per 100 ft 2 of conditioned floor area when the air handler is installed and 3 cfm when it is not installed. Industry standards generally require new duct systems to be sealed to 6% or less leakage, while altered or existing systems may be allowed a leakage rate of up to 15% (Eco Performance Builders, 2025). Therefore, this measure will not seal ducts with a leakage rate of 6% or less.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

leakage, while altered or existing systems may be allowed a leakage rate of up to 15% (Eco Performance Builders, 2025). Therefore, this measure will not seal ducts with a leakage rate of 6% or less.

After improving ductwork, the target for duct leakage after a retrofit is recommended to be 5% (Andrews, 2001). However, many contractors strive for even lower leakage levels. For example, Eco Performance Builders (2025), a retrofit company based in the Bay Area, reports an average duct leakage of under 1% after a retrofit, while PV Heating, Cooling & Plumbing (Peavey, 2025), based in the Atlanta metropolitan area, aims for 4% leakage or less. To reach this target, PV Heating, Cooling & Plumbing technicians seal all duct connections and joints using only duct mastic and high-quality mastic tape. Once a duct leakage test confirms that leakage is below the target threshold, they proceed to insulate the sealed duct areas. Achieving 4% duct leakage requires significant effort. In a typical home, it often takes multiple cycles of sealing and testing to meet this performance standard. Therefore, we assume this measure can achieve a 5% duct leakage rate.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 2  Applicability

The goal of this measure is to achieve 5% duct air leakage combined with R-8 insulation for ducts located in unconditioned spaces. Ducts in the conditioned spaces do not require treatment because their heat loss goes directly to the conditioned space and is therefore not 'wasted'. This measure applies to dwelling units with either duct leakage to the outside greater than 6% or duct insulation less than R-6. Dwelling units with 0% leakage and uninsulated ducts are not included, as these configurations typically indicate that the ducts are located entirely within conditioned spaces and ResStock reflects this assumption. Though, ducts in real homes can pass through both conditioned and unconditioned spaces, requiring section-by-section treatment. Nevertheless, based on these assumptions, this duct sealing and insulation measure applies to approximately 46.3% of the U.S. housing stock, as shown in Table 1.

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3  Modeling Approach

ResStock assigns three characteristics related to air distribution ductwork for each housing unit: whether the unit has ducts, the location of the ducts, and a combined characteristic that includes both the level of duct insulation and the amount of leakage from the ducts to unconditioned space. This measure does not change whether ducts are present or their locations; it only changes the duct insulation and leakage. Air leakage and heat gains and losses are calculated for the fraction of the ductwork outside conditioned space. The primary location of the duct system is sampled from the 'duct location.tsv' file. OpenStudio-HPXML assigns the fraction of the duct area in the conditioned space if the duct location is in unconditioned space. If the number of floors above grade is greater than one, then 25% of the duct surface area is assigned to the conditioned space. OpenStudio-HPXML also assigns fractions of supply/return ducts with rectangular and circular cross-sections, which affects the effective R-value for a given nominal duct insulation R-value.

metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model includes conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that represent the contiguous U.S. residential building stock. These distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock, with each sample assigned an option for each characteristic for every dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudioHPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models that can be simulated with OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  using an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here.

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3.3  Electrical Panel

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025). Duct sealing and insulation do not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so they have no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4  Results

This section first confirms the intended modeling approach for the upgrade by examining individual dwelling models, then shows the results if the upgrade were applied to the entire applicable building stock.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1  Single Building Example

This section analyzes three example dwelling units that received duct sealing and insulation upgrades. Before the upgrades, each unit had uninsulated ducts with 20% leakage to the outside. After the upgrades, duct leakage was reduced to 5%, and R-8 insulation was added. The units are in Hawai'i (climate zone 1A), North Carolina (climate zone 3A), and Alaska (climate zone 8AK), representing a range of climate conditions. The floor areas of these three dwelling units are different. Furthermore, the heating and cooling setpoint temperatures are also different. As a result, the baseline heating and cooling energy consumption can vary across the three example dwelling units, appearing either high or low. This section does not compare absolute energy consumption among these three example dwellings. Instead, it focuses solely on the percentage energy reduction achieved by the duct sealing and insulation.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.1  Individual Building Annual Energy Consumption

Figure 1 shows the annual energy consumption of three example dwelling units before and after duct sealing and insulation upgrades. The upgrades resulted in reductions across several heatingand cooling-related end uses, including heating, cooling, heating and cooling fans/pumps, heating heat pump backup, and associated backup fans/pumps.

The example dwelling unit in Hawai'i (climate zone 1A) uses electricity for both heating and cooling. Its total cooling energy consumption (including cooling and cooling fans/pumps) was reduced from 46.5 MBtu to 38.6 MBtu, representing a 17% reduction. Because heating demand in Hawai'i is negligible, heating savings are not analyzed for this location.

The example dwelling unit in North Carolina (climate zone 3A) also uses electricity for both heating and cooling. Its cooling energy consumption was reduced from 11.3 MBtu to 9.0 MBtu, a 20% reduction. Additionally, total heating energy consumption (heating, heating fan/pumps, heat pump backup, and associated fans/pumps) was reduced from 19.7 MBtu to 14.7 MBtu, a 25% reduction.

The example dwelling unit in Alaska (climate zone 8AK) uses fuel oil for heating and has no cooling system; therefore, cooling savings are not analyzed for this location. Its total heating energy use (heating and heating fans/pumps) was reduced from 167 MBtu to 135.7 MBtu, representing a 19% reduction.

The percentage reduction in energy use for these three example dwelling units is similar to findings from a field study conducted by Jump et al. (1996). In that study, 24 houses in the Sacramento, California, area were tested before and after duct retrofitting. The average air leakage was reduced from 18% to 9% after the retrofit, resulting in an average 18% decrease in HVAC energy use (Jump, Walker, & Modera, 1996).

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time Series

Section 4.1.1 shows that for the example dwelling units, only heating- and cooling-related energy consumption changed as a result of the duct sealing and insulation upgrade. So, this section analyzes 15-minute time-series data for those end uses across the three example units, as shown in Figure 2.  Heating end uses include heating, heating fans/pumps, heating heat pump backup, and associated backup fans/pumps. Cooling end uses include cooling and cooling fans/pumps. January 2 is selected to examine the heating time-series data, while July 2 is selected to examine the cooling time-series data. The duct sealing and insulation upgrade consistently reduce energy use throughout the day in all example dwelling units.

In North Carolina (climate zone 3A), as shown in Figures 2(a) and  2(b), the upgrades significantly lower summer cooling peaks in the afternoon as well as winter heating peaks in the morning and evening.

metadata.doc_title: Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time Series

Carolina (climate zone 3A), as shown in Figures 2(a) and  2(b), the upgrades significantly lower summer cooling peaks in the afternoon as well as winter heating peaks in the morning and evening.

In Hawai'i (climate zone 1A), as shown in Figure 2(c), the upgrades help reduce cooling loads throughout the day. For the example dwelling in Hawai'i, the sudden spikes in cooling energy consumption at 3:15 and 22:15, and the sharp drops at 7:15 and 12:15, are driven by changes in the cooling setpoint temperature. At 3:00 and 22:00, the setpoint decreases-from 67.5°F to 66°F and from 70°F to 67.5°F, respectively-triggering increased cooling energy use over the following 15 minutes. In contrast, at 7:00 and 12:00, the setpoint rises-from 66°F to 68.5°F and from 68.5°F to 70°F-eliminating the cooling demand and resulting in zero energy use for the next 15 minutes.

In Alaska (climate zone 8AK), as shown in Figure 2(d), the upgrades result in a steady reduction in baseline heating energy use across all hours.

Overall, the results demonstrate that duct sealing and insulation upgrades are effective in improving energy efficiency across a range of climates, especially during periods of high thermal demand.

Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.2.1  Annual Stock Energy Analysis

Figure 3 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the duct sealing and insulation upgrade for all homes. The annual stock energy savings is 240 TWh, compared to a pre-upgrade consumption of 3,454 TWh-representing a 7% reduction. Most savings occurred in heating and cooling end uses. These include 8% (22 TWh) electricity heating savings, 11% (129 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 8% (14 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 10% (13 TWh) propane heating savings, 35% (8 TWh) electricity heat pump backup heating savings, 11% (43 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 12% (4 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 13% (9 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings.

However, there is only a small change in hot water-related end uses. When both the water heater and ducts are in the same place (e.g., unheated basement, attic), hot water energy consumption can be slightly affected due to reduced heat transfer from the ducts. Furthermore, changes in indoor temperature also slightly impact hot water energy consumption. Overall, the effect on hot water energy use is minimal-less than 1%.

There is also a very small change in appliance electricity use, primarily due to refrigerators. Refrigerators transfer heat from the interior to the surrounding air. When the surrounding air is cooler, refrigerators operate more efficiently and use less energy. The average indoor temperature over the year decreased slightly from 71.28°F to 71.26°F. This marginal cooling results in a slight reduction in refrigerator energy use. However, the impact is negligible-the change in appliance electricity consumption is 0.01%.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. This results in a time-series profile broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model represents the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are provided in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (NREL, 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

model is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are provided in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (NREL, 2025).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape package: advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing upgrade.

The advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing upgrade achieved 22.6% total site energy savings (780 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 5). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 40% stock natural gas heating savings (458 TWh)
- 36% stock electricity heating savings (92 TWh)
- 21% stock electricity cooling savings (80 TWh).

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1  Technology Summary

This upgrade package, which includes advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing, combines three key areas of a retrofit measures. The goal of these upgrades is to reduce heat losses in winter and retain cool air in the conditioned space during summer. Air sealing alone does not eliminate the need for insulation (DOE, 2025). Insulation and air sealing work best together to improve comfort and energy efficiency. Therefore, they are often implemented as a package to address complementary aspects of a home's energy performance, and their combined effect is much greater than any single measure alone. Together, these upgrades help to lower energy bills, enhance indoor comfort and improve indoor air quality year round.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Air Sealing

Air sealing involves identifying and closing large and small gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the home's primary or secondary pressure boundaries, such as around windows, doors, attic hatches, and plumbing or wiring holes (DOE, 2025). These leaks, whether large or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the workload on the heating and cooling system. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Alliance, 2025). Refer to the air sealing documentation for more information on common leakage points, and best practices for sealing, and prescriptive air leakage rates based on climate zones (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Attic Floor Insulation

Insulating the attic floor reduces heat transfer between the living space and the unconditioned attic. In colder climates, this keeps heat inside during winter. In warmer climates, it helps keep the living space cooler. The effectiveness of insulation is measured by its R-value; a higher Rvalue indicates better resistance to heat flow. Installing insulation in existing homes typically involves blowing loose-fill insulation over the attic floor, especially in unfinished attics. The optimal insulation level depends on the climate zone and the home's existing insulation. Refer to the attic insulation documentation for guidance on recommended R-values and installation approaches (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Duct Sealing and Insulation

Ducts distribute heated or cooled air throughout the house. In many homes, especially older ones, these ducts have leaks that allow conditioned air to escape into unconditioned or semiconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. As a result, the system must work harder and use more energy to maintain the desired temperature. Duct sealing addresses these leaks using mastic, metal tape, or an aerosol-based sealant, depending on the situation. Sealing ducts improves system efficiency, maintains more consistent room temperatures, and enhances indoor air quality by preventing dirty attic or crawlspace air from entering the ducts. Duct sealing can also reduce unintentional pressure imbalances, which may cause indoor air quality or combustion safety concerns. See the duct sealing documentation for more information on methods and materials (Lou & Liu, 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

To maximize energy efficiency and based on building science principles, the correct order for implementing this upgrade package is: (1) advanced air sealing, (2) duct sealing, and (3) attic floor insulation. Reducing air leakage is the foundation of energy efficiency. It helps control indoor temperatures and moisture and improves the effectiveness of insulation and HVAC systems. Sealing leaks before adding insulation ensures the insulation performs as intended. It also makes leaks easier to identify and reduces the burden on field staff, since they are not working around additional insulation. Once air sealing targets are met, it is essential to address the HVAC system by sealing any leaky ducts to prevent the loss of conditioned air, particularly in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. Attic floor insulation should be installed last. While highly effective, it must follow air and duct sealing to avoid covering up critical areas that require sealing and to ensure ducts running through the attic are properly sealed and insulated beforehand.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

effective, it must follow air and duct sealing to avoid covering up critical areas that require sealing and to ensure ducts running through the attic are properly sealed and insulated beforehand.

Therefore, we assume that upgrades will be implemented in the following sequence: Advanced air sealing is applied first to applicable dwelling units, with the goal of achieving 5 ACH50. While some regions require tighter envelopes for new construction, 5 ACH50 reflects the average infiltration rate achieved in empirical studies across representative climate zones and ensures that selected homes do not already comply with 2024 IECC requirements (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a).

After air sealing, HVAC ducts in applicable homes are sealed and insulated to achieve the following:

- A maximum of 5% duct air leakage to the outside
- Duct insulation level of R-8.

Attic floor insulation is the upgraded in applicable dwelling units to the following levels:

- R-49 in climate zone 1
- R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

More details about the modeling assumptions for these three measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 2  Applicability

Advanced air sealing upgrades are applied to dwelling units with infiltration rates greater than or equal to 6 ACH50.

Attic floor insulation upgrades are applied only to dwelling units with unfinished attics (vented and unvented attic types in ResStock). Specifically, upgrades are triggered when attic floor insulation is below the following levels: less than R-49 in climate zone 1 and less than R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

Duct sealing applies to dwelling units with duct leakage to the outside greater than 6% or duct insulation rated below R-6. Dwelling units with 0% leakage to the outside and uninsulated ducts are not applicable, as these configurations typically indicate that the ducts are located entirely within conditioned spaces.

Further details on the applicability criteria and stock saturation for each of these three measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025). Table 1 summarizes the stock saturation for the upgrade package that includes all three measures. This comprehensive package is applicable to approximately 97.9% of the U.S. housing stock. However, most homes receive only one or some of these upgrades. Only 27.8% of homes receive all three upgrades.

Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3  Modeling Approach

The modeling approach of the three individual measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025).

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025). This measures does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1  Single Building Example

This section examines a dwelling unit in Colorado (climate zone 5B) that underwent the envelope package upgrade, which includes advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation. Table 3 presents the housing characteristics of the unit before and after the upgrade. To assess the package's effectiveness, we compared the performance of the unit with the full upgrade to its performance when each of the three individual measures was applied separately.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual Results

Figure 1 shows the annual energy consumption of the example dwelling unit under the full envelope package upgrade and under each of the three individual measures applied separately. Among these four scenarios, heating energy use shows the largest reduction, dropping from 105.5 MBtu in the baseline to 65.3 MBtu with the full upgrade, a 38% decrease. Cooling energy use also decreases slightly, while hot water energy use remains nearly unchanged. All other end uses are unaffected.

The envelope upgrade reduced heat loss from the dwelling, which led to a slight increase in hot water energy consumption. In this example, the water heater is in an unheated basement. By preventing heat loss during winter and retaining cool air during summer, the upgrade improves overall thermal efficiency. However, because the unit is heating-dominated, the reduction in heat loss during winter is more significant than the benefit of retaining cool air in summer. As a result, less ambient heat is released into the unheated basement, causing the water heater to work harder and use slightly more energy to maintain the desired water temperature.

The comprehensive envelope upgrade package reduces the dwelling unit's annual total energy use from 165 MBtu to 122 MBtu, a 26% reduction. In contrast, advanced air sealing, duct sealing and insulation, and attic floor insulation individually reduced energy consumption by 18%, 8%, and 1%, respectively. This demonstrates that the full envelope package maximizes energy efficiency, highlighting the synergistic benefits of combining all three measures.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time-Series Results

Section 4.1.1 shows that only heating- and cooling-related energy consumption changed significantly due to the envelope upgrades. Therefore, this section analyzes 15-minute timeseries data for these end uses under the full envelope package upgrade and each individual measures applied separately. Heating end uses include heating and heating fans/pumps. Cooling end uses include cooling and cooling fans/pumps. January 2 is selected to examine the heating time-series data, while July 2 is selected to examine the cooling time-series data.

Figure 3 shows that each envelope upgrade reduces heating energy consumption compared to the baseline. The combined upgrade package (dark blue line) consistently shows the lowest heating energy consumption throughout the day, indicating cumulative savings from all measures. The sudden drop in heating energy consumption at 2:15 and the rise at 11:15 are caused by changes in the heating setpoint temperature. At 2:00, the setpoint drops from 70°F to 67°F, eliminating the need for heating and resulting in zero energy use from 2:00 to 2:15. At 11:00, the setpoint increases from 67°F to 70°F, triggering a spike in heating energy use from 11:00 to 11:15. After that, heating energy consumption returns to normal.

Figure 3. Heating energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after envelope upgrades

![Image](96347_images/image_000004_e9fec4a58398a737f6a0396026b3a2590e906aff76945c3b6ec05e447f0b8e0e.png)

Figure 4 shows that each envelope upgrade reduces cooling energy consumption compared to the baseline. The combined upgrade package (dark blue line) consistently results in the lowest cooling energy use from 12:45 to 22:00, when cooling demand is high, indicating cumulative savings from all measures. During 0:00-12:15 and 23:30-24:00 when cooling demand is minimal or absent in the baseline model, cooling energy consumption increases after the envelope package upgrade. This increase is due to the reduced air exchange and heat loss resulting from the improved building envelope. In the baseline model, natural cooling occurred during these hours through air leakage and lower outdoor temperatures. After the upgrade, the dwelling unit becomes more airtight and better insulated, reducing passive cooling and resulting in small cooling loads in the upgraded model to maintain indoor comfort.

Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.2.1  Annual Stock Energy Analysis

Figure 5 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for all homes. The annual stock energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 780 TWh, compared to a pre-upgrade average consumption of 3,454 TWhrepresenting a 22.6% reduction. Most savings occurred in heating and cooling end uses. These include 36% (92 TWh) electricity heating savings, 40% (458 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 37% (62 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 36% (47 TWh) propane heating savings, 68% (15 TWh) electricity heating heat pump backup savings, 21% (80 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 39% (14 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 20% (13 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings.

Figure 5. Annual site energy consumption for all homes

![Image](96347_images/image_000006_b56a4bdc5da4a977b1c0c77141b04ef357874aa572cda22d93e62d1a266afd6c.png)

Figure 6 shows the annual site energy consumption per dwelling unit by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for upgraded dwelling units, which include 97.9% of all dwelling units. The average annual energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 5,704 kWh, compared to a pre-upgrade average consumption of 24,849 kWh-representing a 23.0% reduction.

Figure 6. Annual site energy consumption per upgraded dwelling unit

Table 5 shows the annual energy consumption savings percentage per upgraded dwelling unit. As discussed earlier, most savings were observed in heating and cooling end uses. However, there is only a small change in hot water-related end uses. When both the water heater and ducts are in the same place (e.g., unheated basement or attic), hot water energy consumption can be affected slightly due to reduced heat transfer from the ducts. If the water heater is in the attic, it can also be affected by improved attic floor insulation. Additional details are available in the duct sealing and attic floor insulation documentation (Lou & Liu, 2025) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b). Furthermore, indoor temperature changes also influence hot water energy use. Overall, the impact on hot water energy consumption is less than 0.2%.

There is also a very small change in appliance electricity use, primarily for refrigerators. Refrigerators work by transferring heat from the interior to the surrounding air. When the surrounding air is cooler, a refrigerator operates more efficiently and uses less energy. The average indoor temperature over the year increased slightly from 71.28°F to 71.46°F. This slight increase in temperature results in a minor increase in refrigerator energy use. However, the impact is negligible-the change in appliance electricity consumption is 0.21%.

Figure 9 shows the annual energy consumption savings from individual and combined envelope measures, based on 27.8% of dwelling units where all three individual measures apply. When all measures are implemented together, 91.1% of the units experience total savings that are slightly lower than the sum of the individual savings, while 8.9% see total savings that slightly exceed the sum of the individual impacts. The slightly lower savings observed in most units result from overlapping effects among the measures. For example, both attic insulation and advanced air sealing reduce heat loss, but their impacts partially overlap, so the combined effect is not fully additive.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to energy efficiency retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. This results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model is intended to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (NREL, 2025).

Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

model is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (NREL, 2025).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape package-Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, Duct Sealing, and Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation Upgrade.

The Advanced Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, Duct Sealing, and Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation Upgrade achieved 27.2% total site energy savings (938 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 5). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 48% stock natural gas heating savings (556 TWh)
- 43% stock electricity heating savings (110 TWh)
- 24% stock electricity cooling savings (91 TWh).

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1  Technology Summary

This upgrade package which includes advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, duct sealing, and drill-and-fill wall insulation, combines four key areas of a retrofit measures. The goal of these upgrades is to reduce heat loss in winter and retain cool air longer in summer. Air sealing alone does not eliminate the need for insulation (DOE, 2025). Insulation and air sealing work best together to improve comfort and energy efficiency. Therefore, they are often completed as a package to address complementary aspects of a home's energy efficiency, and their combined effect is much greater than any single measure alone. Together, these upgrades help to lower energy bills, improve indoor comfort, and enhance indoor air quality year-round.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Air Sealing

Air sealing involves identifying and closing large and small gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the home's primary or secondary pressure boundaries such as around windows, doors, attic hatches, and plumbing or wiring holes (DOE, 2025). These leaks, whether big or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the work load on the heating and cooling. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Alliance, 2025). Refer to the air sealing documentation for more information on common leakage points, as well as best practices for sealing and prescriptive air leakage rate based on climate zones (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a).

metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Attic Floor Insulation

Insulating the attic floor reduces heat transfer between the living space and the unconditioned attic. In colder climates, this keeps heat inside during winter. In warmer climates, it helps keep the living space cooler. The effectiveness of insulation is measured by its R-value; a higher Rvalue indicates better resistance to heat flow. Installing insulation in existing homes typically involves blowing loose-fill insulation over the attic floor, especially in unfinished attics. The optimal insulation level depends on the climate zone and the home's existing insulation. Refer to the attic insulation documentation for guidance on recommended R-values and installation approaches (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Duct Sealing and Insulation

Ducts distribute heated or cooled air throughout the house. In many homes, especially older ones, these ducts have leaks that allow conditioned air escape into unconditioned or semiconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. As a result, the system must work harder and uses more energy to maintain the desired temperature. Duct sealing addresses these leaks using mastic, metal tape, or an aerosol-based sealant, depending on the situation. Sealing ducts improves system efficiency, maintains more consistent room temperatures, and enhances indoor air quality by preventing dirty attic or crawlspace air from entering the ducts. Duct sealing can also reduce unintentional pressure imbalances, which may cause indoor air quality or combustion safety concerns. See the duct sealing documentation for more information on methods and materials (Lou & Liu, 2025).

metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation

Drill-and-fill insulation is one way to insulate an existing uninsulated wall cavity. It involves drilling small holes into the exterior sheeting or interior wall covering and blowing loose-fill insulation material (such as cellulose or fiberglass) into the cavities between the wall studs (EERE, 2025). This measure upgrade models cellulose as the drill-and-fill insulation material. Drill-and-fill insulation can be completed from the inside or outside of the building. See the drilland-fill documentation for more information on the installation technology and applicable situations (Brossman & Lou, 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

To maximize energy efficiency and based on building science principles, the correct order for implementing this upgrade package is: (1) air sealing, (2) duct sealing, (3) attic floor insulation, and (4) drill-and-fill wall insulation. Reducing air leakage is the foundation of energy efficiency. It helps control indoor temperatures and moisture, and improves the effectiveness of insulation and HVAC systems. Sealing leaks before adding insulation ensures the insulation performs as intended. It also makes leaks easier to identify and reduces the burden on field staff, since they are not working around additional insulation. Once air sealing targets are met, it is essential to address the HVAC system by sealing any leaky ducts to prevent the loss of conditioned air, particularly in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. With both air leaks and ducts sealed, attic floor insulation should be installed. Finally, insulation can be added to uninsulated wall cavities to reduce conductive heat loss.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

attics or crawlspaces. With both air leaks and ducts sealed, attic floor insulation should be installed. Finally, insulation can be added to uninsulated wall cavities to reduce conductive heat loss.

Therefore, we assume that upgrades will be implemented in the following sequence: Advanced air sealing is applied first to applicable dwelling units, with the goal of achieving 5 ACH50. While some regions require tighter envelopes for new constructions, 5 ACH50 reflects the average infiltration rate achieved in empirical studies across representative climate zones and ensures that selected homes do not already comply with 2024 IECC requirements (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a).

After air sealing, HVAC ducts in applicable homes are sealed and insulated to achieve:

- A maximum of 5% duct air leakage to the outside
- Duct insulation level of R-8.

Attic floor insulation is then upgraded in applicable dwelling units to the following levels:

- R-49 in climate zone 1
- R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

Finally, uninsulated wood stud walls are upgraded with cellulose drill-and-fill insulation to reach an R-13 level.

More details about the modeling assumption for these three measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025) (Brossman & Lou, 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 2  Applicability

Advanced air sealing upgrades are applied to dwelling units with infiltration rates greater than or equal 6 ACH50.

Attic floor insulation upgrades are applied only to dwelling units with unfinished attics (vented and unvented attic type in ResStock). Specifically, upgrades are triggered when attic floor insulation is below the following levels: less than R-49 in climate zone 1 and less than R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

Duct sealing applies to dwelling units with duct leakage to the outside greater than 6% or duct insulation rated below R-6. Dwelling units with 0% leakage to the and uninsulated ducts are not applicable, as these configurations typically indicate that the ducts are located entirely within conditioned spaces.

Drill-and-fill wall insulation is applicable to dwelling units with uninsulated wood stud walls.

Further details on the applicability criteria and stock saturation for each of these four upgrades can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025) (Brossman & Lou, 2025). Table 1 summarizes the stock saturation for the upgrade package that includes all four measures. This comprehensive package is applicable to approximately 98% of the U.S. housing stock. However, most homes receive only one or some of these upgrades. Only 9.2% of homes receive all four upgrades.
