Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3  Modeling Approach

The modeling approach of the four individual measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b) (Lou & Liu, 2025) (Brossman & Lou, 2025).

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025). This measure does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual

Figure 1 shows the annual energy consumption of the example dwelling unit under the full envelope package upgrade and under each of the four individual measures applied separately. Among these five scenarios, heating energy use shows the largest reduction, dropping from 105.5 MBtu in the baseline to 39.9 MBtu with the full upgrade, a 62% decrease. Cooling energy use also decreases slightly, while hot water energy use remains nearly unchanged. All other end uses are unaffected.

The envelope upgrade reduced heat loss from the dwelling, which led to a slight increase in hot water energy consumption. In this example, the water heater is in an unheated basement. By preventing heat loss during winter and retaining cool air during summer, the upgrade improves overall thermal efficiency. However, because the unit is heating-dominated, the reduction in heat loss during winter is more significant than the benefit of retaining cool air in summer. As a result, less ambient heat is released into the unheated basement, causing the water heater to work harder and use slightly more energy to maintain the desired water temperature.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing, Drill-and-Fill Wall Insulation, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time Series

Section 4.1.1 shows that only heating- and cooling-related energy consumption changed significantly due to the envelope upgrades. Therefore, this section analyzes 15-minute timeseries data for these end uses under the full envelope package upgrade and each individual measures applied separately. Heating end uses include heating and heating fans/pumps. Cooling end uses include cooling and cooling fans/pumps. January 2 is selected to examine the heating time-series data, while July 2 is selected to examine the cooling time-series data.

Figure 3 shows that each envelope upgrade reduces heating energy consumption compared to the baseline. The combined upgrade package (dark blue line) consistently shows the lowest heating energy consumption throughout the day, indicating cumulative savings from all measures. The sudden drop in heating energy consumption at 2:15 and the rise at 11:15 are caused by changes in the heating setpoint temperature of this example dwelling unit. At 2:00, the setpoint drops from 70°F to 67°F, eliminating the need for heating and resulting in zero energy use from 2:00-

2:15. At 11:00, the setpoint increases from 67°F to 70°F, triggering a spike in heating energy use from 11:00-11:15. After that, heating energy consumption returns to normal.

Figure 3. Heating energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after envelope upgrades

Figure 4 shows that each envelope upgrade reduces cooling energy consumption compared to the baseline. The combined upgrade package (dark blue line) consistently results in the lowest cooling energy use from 12:30 to 22:30, when cooling demand is high, indicating cumulative savings from all measures. During 0:00-12:00 and 23:30-24:00 when cooling demand is minimal or absent in the baseline model, cooling energy consumption increases after the envelope package upgrade. This increase is due to the reduced air exchange and heat loss resulting from the improved building envelope. In the baseline model, natural cooling occurred during these hours through air leakage and lower outdoor temperatures. After the upgrade, the dwelling unit becomes more airtight and better insulated, reducing passive cooling and resulting in small cooling loads in the upgraded model to maintain indoor comfort.

This includes 43% (110 TWh) electricity heating savings, 48% (556 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 48% (79 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 42% (55 TWh) propane heating savings, 72% (16 TWh) electricity heating heat pump backup savings, 24% (91 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 46% (17 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 23% (15 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings.

Table 5 shows the annual energy consumption saving percentage per upgraded dwelling unit. As discussed earlier, most savings were observed in heating and cooling end uses. However, there is only a small change in hot water-related end uses. When both the water heater and ducts are in the same place (e.g., unheated basement, attic), hot water energy consumption can be affected slightly due to reduced heat transfer from the ducts. If the water heater is in the attic, it can be affected by improved attic floor insulation. Additional details are available in the duct sealing and attic floor insulation documentation (Lou & Liu, ResStock 2025 Release 1 SDR Duct Sealing and Insulation Upgrade Documentation, 2025) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b). Furthermore, indoor temperature changes also influence hot water energy use. Overall, the impact on hot water energy consumption is less than 0.1%.

text:
EnergyStar Windows — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al. 2022).

text:
EnergyStar Windows — Executive Summary

is available in (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure-ENERGY STAR ® Version 7.0 Window Upgrade.

The ENERGY STAR Version 7.0 Window Upgrade demonstrated 7% total site energy savings (0.25 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 6). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 12% stock electricity heating savings (1.3E11 kWh)
- 12% stock natural gas heating savings (3.2E10 kWh)
- 10% stock electricity cooling savings (4.0E10 kWh)
- 11% stock cooling fan and pump electricity savings (7.11E9 kWh).

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1  Technology Summary

Windows are an important part of the building envelope. They allow light and heat to pass, allow views of the outside world, and separate the interior conditions of the dwelling from the outdoors. This section will review how windows work and include details about the specific window characteristics included in this measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: EnergyStar Windows
metadata.measure_name: EnergyStar Windows

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

As commonly understood, a window is an area of transparent or translucent material in the wall of a building. The National Fenestration Rating Council (NFRC) is an independent, 501(c)(3) nonprofit certification body for the energy performance of windows, doors, and skylights (National Fenestration Rating Council (NFRC), n.d.). NFRC's technical definition of a window is 'An assembled unit consisting of a frame/sash component holding one or more pieces of glazing functioning to admit light and/or air into an enclosure and designed for a vertical installation in an external wall of a residential building. Includes transoms.' (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2022).

metadata.doc_title: EnergyStar Windows
metadata.measure_name: EnergyStar Windows

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

to admit light and/or air into an enclosure and designed for a vertical installation in an external wall of a residential building. Includes transoms.' (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2022).

Window glazing and window frames and sashes can be made of a variety of materials. Historically, in the U.S., residential windows were made with wood frames supporting a single pane of clear glass. Today, window frames and sashes can be made from wood, aluminum, composite materials, fiberglass, or vinyl (U.S. Department of Energy, 2025). Windows today can have multiple panes of glass separated by gaps, which can be filled with special gases to reduce the heat transfer through the window. The glass can have special coatings on the surface to limit how much visible or infrared light is allowed through (U.S. Department of Energy, 2025). Figure 1 shows cross sections illustrating several different window glazing configurations. Windows with more panes generally allow lower amounts of heat and radiation to come through the window.

Figure 1. Cross sections of single, double, and triple pane windows From (Window Glazing, n.d.)

![Image](96405_images/image_000002_e0936df14c9b44914d154af1635a98ceb20af513f78244b04c27059e0dc8b562.png)

metadata.doc_title: EnergyStar Windows
metadata.measure_name: EnergyStar Windows

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

The appropriate choice of windows for a building depends on many factors. Some of the major energy-related factors include the climate, the orientation of the windows relative to the sun, and the architectural or landscape features surrounding the window. Non-energy-related factors such as material durability, aesthetics, and physical operation (opening and closing) are also important to consider.

metadata.doc_title: EnergyStar Windows
metadata.measure_name: EnergyStar Windows

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.2.1  ENERGY STAR Version 7.0 Residential Window Specification

Because of the wide variety of windows available, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) created the ENERGY STAR Program Requirements for Residential Windows, Doors, and Skylights to define energy-related performance characteristics for windows. Rather than specifying the materials, frame designs, fill gases, or coatings, the program specifies the performance metrics that a product must achieve. These performance metrics are:

- ' U-Factor : The heat transfer per time per area and per degree of temperature difference (Btu/h ft 2 ∙˚ F). The U-factor multiplied by the interior-exterior temperature difference and by the projected fenestration product area yields the total heat transfer through the fenestration product due to conduction, convection, and long-wave infra-red radiation. The lower the U-factor, the better the window insulates.
- 'Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC) : The ratio of the solar heat gain entering the space through the fenestration product to the incident solar radiation.
- 'Air Leakage : The volume of air flowing per unit time per unit area (cfm/ft 2 ) through a fenestration system due to air pressure or temperature difference between the outdoor and indoor environment.' (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2022).

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.2.2 Characteristics of Certified Products

As shown in Table 1, the certification requirements establish a range of performance values rather than a singular value for each climate zone. For this report, NLR performed an assessment to understand the range of performance characteristics available in the market as of the time of writing.

The EPA Product Finder is a database of certified products. As of the date of publication, there were more than 1,000 certified window product lines, with hundreds or thousands of individual products within each line (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, n.d.). Because of the limitations of the Product Finder, it was not possible to extract detailed information for every product in every line. Instead, a sample of products was reviewed. According to the websites of several of the largest window manufacturers in the U.S., double hung windows are the most common type of windows in the residential market. NLR's review of four lines of double hung windows covering 50,000 individual window configurations from four of the ten largest U.S. window manufacturers was performed using data available through the NFRC Directory Search linked from the EPA Product Finder (National Fenestration Rating Council, n.d.).

EnergyStar Windows — 1.2.3  Comparison of ENERGY STAR to Energy Code Requirements

In most places in the U.S., an energy code sets the minimum performance of new windows. For this upgrade, it is important that the modeled windows meet the energy code requirements for the locations they are installed.

To determine the minimum energy code performance by location, the methodology described in the 2024 NLR report Residential Facade Retrofits Modeling: Results and Documentation (Elaina Present, 2024) was followed. The code adoption status by state was updated as of July 2025, accessed from the International Code Council (ICC) website. For each county in the U.S., the ENERGY STAR and IECC climate zones were identified, and the required performance characteristics were assigned to each based on the IECC or state-specific code for the state where that county was located (International Code Council (ICC), 2025). For this exercise, no sub-state energy code requirements were considered.

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 1.2.5 Infiltration Impacts of Upgraded Windows

As described in most window manufacturer literature, and as indicated by the presence of an air leakage requirement in the ENERGY STAR V7 performance characteristics, air leakage through and around windows plays a role in their energy performance. Unfortunately, literature quantifying this impact using measured data is limited. A 2003 paper (Ian Ridley, 2003) developed a simple model of the reduction that could be expected from replacing windows in the UK and concluded: 'A review of existing data suggests that replacing old leaky windows with modern sealed windows will reduce the background infiltration rate by the order of 0.1 air changes per hour (ach) to 0.3 ach. The actual value being dependent on the number of windows being replaced, the volume of the house and the leakiness of the old windows.' The values given in the paper are at natural pressure. Using the calculations from that paper, this equates to a reduction of 2-6 air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50), which is a common way to describe infiltration levels.

metadata.measure_name: EnergyStar Windows

are at natural pressure. Using the calculations from that paper, this equates to a reduction of 2-6 air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50), which is a common way to describe infiltration levels.

In the ResStock baseline models, infiltration is specified as whole-dwelling ACH50. This input is dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. The mean infiltration rate is generally higher in smaller, older homes in warmer climates. The mean infiltration rate ranges from around 20 ACH50 in older homes to 10 ACH50 in newer homes. There is no explicit relationship between infiltration and window type. However, there is an explicit relationship between window type and dwelling vintage. The resulting correlation is that older homes tend to have both lower-performance windows and higher infiltration. text:
EnergyStar Windows — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, et al., 2025). These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sampled dwelling unit has an assigned option for each characteristic. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio and EnergyPlus through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here (NREL, 2025). Assumptions about the window modeling that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are handled by the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 3.3  Limitations and Concerns

There are two key limitations and concerns for this modeling. First, because the requirements for certification allow a range of performance characteristics, this modeling approach inherently cannot reflect the performance of all possible certified products. As described in the results, the choices of performance characteristics even show negative savings for a tiny segment of the stock. In reality, it is likely possible to identify certified products that achieve positive savings for this segment. It is also possible to select certified products that achieve better or worse performance compared to what was modeled.

The second concern is the use of the simplified window glazing model in OS-HPXML. A detailed investigation of the tradeoffs in that modeling simplification was beyond the scope of this effort because changing OS-HPXML was also beyond the scope. However, this simplification may have ramifications on the results.

EnergyStar Windows — 4.1.1 Single Dwelling Annual

Based on the applicability logic, the windows in all four individual dwellings were upgraded. In addition to the updated window performance characteristics, all four dwellings received a 30% infiltration reduction because they all started with single pane windows.

Looking at the results on an annual basis, the end uses and fuel types that changed significantly because of the upgrade were HVAC-related heating and cooling energy for dwellings with HVAC systems. This is expected, because upgrading the windows changes the overall heat transfer through the building envelope. Dwelling 1, located in Hawai'i, had no HVAC, which is common in Hawai'i. In this dwelling, the only impact of upgrading the windows was a tiny (1%) reduction in electricity consumption by the refrigerator, presumably because of slightly decreased indoor temperatures during parts of the year. The water heater was not impacted because it is outside of the living space in a separately conditioned mechanical space.

As expected, heating energy is reduced most significantly during the cold nighttime hours, and cooling energy is reduced most significantly during the hot afternoon hours.

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 4.2  Stock Energy Impacts

Replacing existing windows with those that meet the ENERGY STAR V7 criteria is estimated to create 7% (0.25 TWh) annual stock site energy savings for residential buildings nationally (see Figure 6). This includes 12% site electricity heating savings (1.3E11 kWh), 12% site natural gas heating savings (3.2E10 kWh), 10% site electricity cooling savings (4.0E10 kWh), and 11% site fan and pump energy savings (7.11E9 kWh). Heating, cooling, and fan energy savings can be partially attributed to the decreased thermal conductance (U-value) of the replacement windows, which generally reduces heating and cooling loads. This reduces the energy requirement of the heating and cooling system, but can also decrease the amount of time HVAC fans and pumps need to run, which explains the energy savings in that category. Similarly, a lower SHGC reduces solar gains to the building, which can also reduce cooling load, but it some cases may increase heating load due to reduced heat gain when the building is actively heating. Because this upgrade is applicable to all dwelling units, the whole-stock impact and applicable segment impact results are identical.

Figure 6. Comparison of annual site energy consumption between the ResStock baseline and the ENERGY STAR V7 Windows upgrade scenario. Energy consumption is categorized by both fuel type and end use.

V7 Windows upgrade scenario. Energy consumption is categorized by both fuel type and end use.

![Image](96405_images/image_000007_868897185000e3f28d9ff03d43f6a1499b4d1f5f7055cddaee4676db0c72ddd0.png)

Diving into the results in more detail, we first segment the savings by the type of window present in the baseline building. Looking at natural gas savings in homes with natural gas heating in Figure 7, we see that higher savings are found in dwellings upgrading from lower-performing single pane windows, while lower savings are found in dwellings that already have higher performance windows. Another notable output is that in some dwellings, upgrading the windows increases natural gas consumption. This is only seen in homes in warmer climates where overall heating energy is low. In these cases, the new windows let in less solar heat than the originals, increasing the need for heating energy. Only 1.7% of the building stock saw increases in total energy consumption. In Figure 8, we see a similar trend for electricity savings in homes with electric heating. In Figure 9, we see a similar trend for electricity used for cooling. In this last case, there are negative savings in the north-central climate, likely because the new windows trap more internal gains inside the home. Note that ENERGY STAR rating encompasses a range of performance values. With more nuanced product selection, it is likely possible to identify an ENERGY STAR window that does not have negative savings in a particular climate.

This upgrade changes both window properties and infiltration rates. In buildings with the same baseline window type, we would expect to see higher savings in buildings that started with a higher infiltration rate. Figure 10 shows savings in natural gas heating energy for natural gas heated homes, which start with single, clear, metal windows. In practice, the trend is visible but is not as strong as our intuition might suggest because of the confounding factors that are not controlled for, e.g. building size, weather differences, glazed area, orientation, etc. This figure also indicates that the bulk of the energy savings from this upgrade do not come from the infiltration reduction, because dwellings with infiltration rates ranging from 50 ACH50 down to 4 ACH50 show little difference in average savings.

This highlights the importance of making decisions for individual buildings based on savings results for their peer group. For applications like utility rebate programs where a prescriptive savings number is applied, it also highlights the importance of understanding whether the population of participants is likely to reflect the total population or be a subset. If it is expected to be a subset, savings for this subset should be analyzed.

Figure 12 shows a comparison of modeled utility bills with this measure applied. Stock-wide total bill savings are 7%, with a reduction of 5% in electricity bills and 7% in natural gas bills. This is similar to the magnitude of the overall stock level site energy savings. Propane and fuel oil bills also decrease, but these make up a small fraction of the total building stock utility bills.

Figure 12. Comparison of projected annual utility bills between the ResStock baseline and the ENERGY STAR V7 Windows upgrade scenario. Utility bills are categorized by fuel type.

text:
EnergyStar Windows — 4.4  Electrical Panel Impacts

An electric panel constraint occurs when a unit's electrical service panel (the breaker box) does not have enough capacity (amps) or space (breaker slots) to support new electrical equipment or increased electrical load from existing equipment. Upgrading windows does not add additional electric equipment to the dwelling. Depending on the existing HVAC equipment, it generally reduces either equipment runtime or equipment power draw. Therefore, this upgrade is broadly applicable nationwide without concerns related to electrical panel capacity (National Fenestration Rating Council (NFRC), n.d.).

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to energy efficiency retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles (https://www.nlr.gov/buildings/end-use-load-profiles.html) project.

Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — Executive Summary

Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles (https://www.nlr.gov/buildings/end-use-load-profiles.html) project.

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure-cold climate heat pump upgrade.

The cold climate heat pump upgrade demonstrated 30% total site energy savings (3,535 TBtu) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 7). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 53.7% stock total heating savings (3,173.8 TBtu)
- 10.1% stock total cooling savings (132.7 TBtu).

Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — Measure Summary

| Measure Title                 | Typical Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1  Technology Summary

Cold climate heat pumps are air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) that are designed to work efficiently at cold temperatures. This section will give an overview of ASHP technology and include details about the specific features of the cold climate ASHP included in this measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

ASHPs provide space heating and cooling in buildings. According to the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, only ~16.5% of dwellings in the contiguous United States have ASHP systems, with most ASHPs residing in warmer climate regions like the southern United States (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2022).

ASHPs transfer heat from outdoor air to indoor air during heating operation and from indoor to outdoor during cooling operation. During heating, an ASHP's compressor powers a vapor compression cycle that sends heat to the conditioned space of the dwelling. Unlike fossil fuel combustion or electric resistance heating, ASHPs can heat dwellings at an efficiency level over 100%. For example, average heating coefficients of performance (COPs)-the ratio of heating delivered divided by energy consumed-vary from ~2.0 in colder climates to ~3.0 in hotter climates for the ducted ENERGY STAR ®  air-to-air heat pump upgrade (Praprost, et al. 2026). For reference, an electric resistance heater heats at a COP of 1.0.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

in colder climates to ~3.0 in hotter climates for the ducted ENERGY STAR ®  air-to-air heat pump upgrade (Praprost, et al. 2026). For reference, an electric resistance heater heats at a COP of 1.0.

When an ASHP's compressor cannot meet the heating load of a dwelling, its backup heating system will turn on, if one exists, and aid in meeting the load. Backup heating systems can be either integrated into the ASHP or separate. Integrated backup heating systems use electric resistance heating or ducted fossil fuel furnaces. Separate backup heating systems can use either fossil fuel or electricity to help meet the load and can include a wide range of heating technologies.

The intent of this ASHP measure upgrade is to reflect the specifications of a typical cold climate air-source heat pump (termed 'ccASHP' by the Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships [NEEP]) based on the median metrics for ccASHPs in the NEEP cold climate ASHP database (Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships, Inc. 2023). NEEP requires heat pumps to have a variable-speed compressor to be noted as a ccASHP. More information on the cold climate designation can be found in NEEP's product list documentation. Section 1.2. describes this selection process in more detail (Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships, Inc. 2023).

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

This ASHP option reflects an installation of a ducted ASHP into a building that already has existing ductwork for either heating or cooling. This entails the ASHP indoor coil and blower being installed with the dwelling's existing air distribution system and an outdoor unit coil, fan, and compressor unit being installed outside.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.1  Compressor Speed

This ASHP option has a variable-speed compressor, because virtually all cold climate ASHPs on the market include variable-speed compressors. Variable-speed compressors allow the system to optimize energy consumption by ramping the compressor speed up or down depending on the indoor and outdoor conditions. Compared to a single-stage or two-stage options, this ASHP can more efficiently operate at extreme conditions because of the multiple speeds available to the compressor.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.2  Efficiency Ratings: HSPF2 and SEER2

This ASHP option has efficiency ratings based on the Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio 2 (SEER2) rating for cooling and the Heating Seasonal Performance Factor 2 (HSPF2) for heating. These ratings are calculated by taking the ratio of the cooling or heating output (Btu) of the system over the electricity consumed (Wh) over the respective heating or cooling season. SEER2 and HSPF2 were introduced in 2023 to replace the energy efficiency metrics of SEER and HSPF. The new metrics are measured with an increased external static pressure by up to five times to reflect the field conditions more accurately (Department of Energy 2025). HSPF2 can be calculated for several different regions to reflect the distribution of heating load hours at different outdoor air temperatures in different climates (Department of Energy 2025). Ratings for energy conservation standards use Region IV, so it is most common. However, Region V HSPF2s are often provided for cold climate ASHPs in addition to Region IV. These regions are as defined by the AHRI 210/240 Performance Rating of Unitary Air-condition and Air-source Heat Pump Equipment documents (AHRI 2024).

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.2  Efficiency Ratings: HSPF2 and SEER2

for cold climate ASHPs in addition to Region IV. These regions are as defined by the AHRI 210/240 Performance Rating of Unitary Air-condition and Air-source Heat Pump Equipment documents (AHRI 2024).

This measure upgrade's ASHP has a SEER2 of 17.5 and an HSPF2 (Region IV) of 8.5. These efficiency ratings were chosen to reflect median typical cold climate ASHPs on the NEEP database. These values are not representative of the ASHP's efficiencies at all temperatures, but an average of the efficiency over the respective cooling and heating season. The instantaneous efficiency of the cold climate ASHP will vary according to outdoor and indoor conditions.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.3  Sizing Methodology

This heat pump measure upgrade is sized to 'max load'. Sizing to max load involves sizing the ASHP to the maximum calculated load between the cooling and heating loads. This methodology considers the capacity degradation of the ASHP so that it is sized large enough to meet both the heating and cooling loads at design conditions. For example, a dwelling in a cold climate will have its ASHP rated capacity at 47°F be larger than its load at design conditions, since its capacity retention will not be 100% at the design temperature of the heating load.

Max load is chosen for this ASHP option because it has a variable-speed compressor that more effectively meets the heating load at low ambient temperatures. This effectiveness helps reduce the total size of the ASHP in cold climates from being unrealistically large. Additionally, the multiple speeds available for this ASHP allow it to avoid elevated indoor humidity due to short cycling issues that single-stage compressors incur.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.3  Sizing Methodology

from being unrealistically large. Additionally, the multiple speeds available for this ASHP allow it to avoid elevated indoor humidity due to short cycling issues that single-stage compressors incur.

Because this ASHP option is sized to max load, applicable dwellings in cold climates will receive ASHPs that are relatively larger than an existing fossil fuel system. Large ASHP sizing can increase the cost of the ASHP installation and require multiple mounted indoor units in the dwelling and possibly multiple outdoor units. However, because of this sizing and the variablespeed compressor, its backup system utilization will be much lower, leading to lower operational energy use.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.4 Capacity Retention

As outdoor temperature drops below the rated capacity temperature of 47°F, the available capacity of the ASHP decreases. The capacity that is retained by an ASHP below this temperature can be defined by its capacity retention fraction. At 5°F, this ASHP option's capacity retention fraction at the compressor's highest speed is 0.665. This capacity retention factor specifies the fraction of the ASHP's rated capacity available at 5°F. In the case of this ASHP, its rated capacity at 47°F will be reduced by 33.5% at its lowest and highest compressor speeds, respectively.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.5  Backup System

This ASHP option has an integrated electric resistance backup system. This backup system will turn on when the ASHP's compressor cannot meet the heating load of the dwelling unit. Below -15°F, the compressor will be locked out from providing heat, and only the backup system will be used if it remains below -15°F. This compressor lockout temperature is set at -15°F because of the variable-speed compressor's ability to effectively cover heating loads at low ambient temperatures. These two systems can operate coincidentally because the backup heating coil is in sequence with the ASHP heating coil. The airflow can initially be heated by the ASHP coil and then subsequently boosted by the backup heating coil. The backup system is sized according to the 'emergency' choice in OpenStudio ® -HPXML, which means the backup capacity will be sized to meet the ACCA Manual J heating design load. During operation in the EnergyPlus ® model, the software assumes a fully modulating backup coil that will perfectly meet the remaining heating load not met by the ASHP.

Because the backup system is electric resistance heat, there is a significant efficiency drop when it is utilized, as the COP of electric resistance heat is 1.0. This drop leads to higher energy consumption and higher instantaneous power demand by the dwelling unit's heating system.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.6 Cooling Levels

Dwelling units that are not 100% cooled by their existing AC system (e.g., room AC providing cooling for just one room of a home) will be 100% cooled by this measure upgrade. This will increase cooling energy consumption of those dwelling units that were not already 100% cooled. The cooling level increase for all applicable dwelling units is implemented because ASHPs in this measure upgrade will be sized as large as the duct system allows to attempt to cool the entire dwelling unit. Although this increases energy use associated with cooling, it also increases health and comfort of the home.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.7 Electrical Requirement

This subsection summarizes the electrical information of the typical cold climate heat pump upgrade. Electrical information is used in ResStock to assess whether the home's electrical panel would become space-constrained or over-capacity due to this upgrade. Section 3.3 describes the electrical panel constraint modeling in more details.

The power rating of a ducted heat pump system is the sum of the power rating of the compressor, the air handler, and any electric backup allowed to operate simultaneously, which are summarized in Table 1. The heat pump compressor power rating is estimated based on its design heating capacity using a regression equation derived from product labels. The air handler power rating is estimated from the design airflow rate and OS-HPXML assumption of fan power. The electric resistance backup power rating is directly converted from its heating capacity at an efficiency of 100%. For more information on the modeling assumptions, see the ResStock Technical Reference Documentation (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Ducted heat pumps require at least one 208/240V circuit, each of which is protected by a doublepole breaker. The specific number of circuits depend on whether the heat pump has backup heating (dual-fuel or electric) and how its indoor and outdoor units are configured along with the backup. Table 2 summarizes the wiring configuration for ducted heat pumps assumed in ResStock. For example, a dual-fuel heat pump is assumed to have a 120V air handler on one circuit and another 240V circuit for the compressor. For heat pump with electric backup, the air handler is commonly 240V to allow for the strip heat to be on the same circuit. This is also the assumption in ResStock. The maximum overcurrent protection allowed per circuit is assumed to be up to 50A. Therefore, more circuits may be required for larger heat pump systems, which correspond to the use of multiple compressors and/or heat kits in actual installed systems.

While a heat pump upgrade replaces both heating and cooling, it may take more circuits and breaker spaces to install than removing the incumbent HVAC systems is able to free up. The heat pump upgrade may also add more connected load to the panel, especially when the backup is sized for emergency use. The power rating of heat pump systems is driven by their heating configuration and the presence of electric resistance backup. Therefore, homes in colder climates are more likely to face a capacity constraint when upgrading to a heat pump since a backup is often required to supplement the heat pump performance and they are more likely to have fuel heating previously.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 1.2.8  Measure Upgrade Specification Process

The intent of this ASHP measure upgrade is to reflect the specifications of a typical cold climate ASHP based on the median cold climate ASHP found on the NEEP database (Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships, Inc. 2023). The NEEP database specifies an ASHP as cold climate if its HSPF2 ≥ 7.7 and SEER2 ≥ 14.3, it is variable speed, and its COP at 5°F ≥ 1.75 at maximum capacity. In an analysis of all ducted ASHP systems on NEEP, the plurality of systems have an HSPF2 between 8.5 and 9.0. Figure 1 shows the histogram of this analysis (Winkler, et al. 2026).

Figure 1. Histogram of NEEP ASHP analysis

These results are shown in Figure 2. These details are used as inputs into the ResStock model using the HVAC Detailed Performance Archetype option. Refer to Section 3 for more information on how this measure upgrade is modeled.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 2  Applicability

The cold climate ASHP measure upgrade applies to all dwelling units with the following:

- Dwelling units with ducts that meet the following criteria:
- o Have a non-shared HVAC system unless there is evidence of an existing ASHP or central AC condenser (i.e., the existing dwelling unit has space for a condenser; this is a consideration for multifamily dwelling units only)
- o Have a heating fuel that is not classified as 'Wood,' 'None,' or 'Other Fuel.'

Note that this upgrade explicitly is not applied to buildings without heating in the baseline. With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 78.0% of the existing building stock.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 2  Applicability

that this upgrade explicitly is not applied to buildings without heating in the baseline. With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 78.0% of the existing building stock.

Applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics that determine the available options and options' details. Specifically, the 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' characteristic in ResStock is used to apply this ASHP option. 'HVAC Has Ducts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling. 'Heating Fuel' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling. 'HVAC Cooling Type' describes the type of cooling system the dwelling possesses. 'HVAC Shared Efficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable. More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Documentation. The exact logic used in the ResStock project YML file for this dataset is available in the appendix. The remainder of this section provides discussion for why certain apply logic decisions were made.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 2.1  Treatment of Multifamily Dwellings With Shared HVAC Systems

Multifamily dwellings with ducts and shared HVAC systems will only receive this upgrade if the existing dwelling already has space for an outdoor unit. This is checked by looking at the HVAC cooling type and the HVAC shared system type. If the HVAC cooling type for a ducted dwelling with a shared HVAC system is 'Ducted Heat Pump' or 'Non-Ducted Heat Pump,' the measure upgrade will apply. If the HVAC cooling type for a ducted dwelling with a shared HVAC System is 'Central AC,' the measure upgrade will apply if the shared HVAC system is not a Fan Coil Cooling unit. All other ducted dwellings with shared HVAC systems that do not meet the above criteria will not receive the measure upgrade. This logic is developed to reflect the ease of install of a ducted ASHP system, which requires an outdoor space to install the condenser unit.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 2.2  Cooling-Level Increase for All Applicable Dwellings

Dwellings that are not 100% cooled by their existing AC system (e.g., room AC providing cooling for just one room of a home) will be 100% cooled by this measure upgrade. This could increase cooling energy consumption of those dwellings that were not already 100% cooled. There are rare circumstances where partially cooled dwellings in hot climates receive a heat pump that is not sized large enough to cover the cooling load. This is because the ducts, previously only used for heating, are not large enough to accommodate an adequate size of the heat pump to cool the entire dwelling.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 2.3  Exclusion of 'Other Fuel,' 'None,' and 'Wood' Heating Fuels

Dwellings with 'Other Fuel,' 'None,' or 'Wood' heating fuels do not receive this measure upgrade, because retrofits to these dwellings can lead to confusing results (e.g., false negative savings compared to baseline or installing heating in regions that do not need it). 'Other Fuel' includes fuels that are not currently represented in ResStock, so there is not an accurate baseline heating energy consumption to compare to. Additionally, there is not a large impact at scale because dwellings with 'Other Fuel,' 'None,' or 'Wood' heating fuels comprise approximately 2.6% of the total residential building stock.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3  Modeling Approach

This section will overview how the upgrade measure is functionally modeled via ResStock into OpenStudio-HPXML. Section 3.1 will briefly cover how OpenStudio-HPXML is used by ResStock to model the dwellings generated by ResStock's sampling. Section 3.2 will cover how inputs from ResStock and default values calculated by OpenStudio-HPXML create the typical cold climate heat pump measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, et al. 2025). These distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each dwelling model in the stock has an assigned representative option for each characteristic. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio and EnergyPlus through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the measure upgrades in a ResStock dataset release that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

was created can be found here. Assumptions about the measure upgrades in a ResStock dataset release that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

In the case of heating/cooling upgrades in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1, these assumptions are all HVAC related. This documentation covers the calculations directly related to the heat pump, but HVAC controls (e.g., setpoints, cycling) and HVAC distribution (e.g., airflow systems) are out of its scope. For information on how OpenStudio-HPXML handles controls in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1 see here, and for how it handles distribution see here. The following subsections will go through the ResStock inputs and the defaults calculated by BuildResidentialHPXML for the heat pump upgrade discussed in this documentation. Most defaults highlighted from the BuildResidentialHPXML measure stem from the apply\_hvac(), apply\_hvac\_sizing(), and apply\_detailed\_performance\_data() methods found in OpenStudioHPXML's hpxml\_defaults.rb file. Note: the defaults.rb file calls methods from various Ruby files within the directory it resides. See these Ruby files here.

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3.3  Electrical Panels

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025. As new electric loads are added into the home during an improvement project, the electrical panel may not have enough capacity or space to accommodate these new circuits. Thus, the panel may become constrained, requiring an electrical upgrade that may include upsizing the service entrance. Panel constraints can also be mitigated in other ways without the panel or service being upsized, by using load shedding devices, circuit sharing devices, or a smart panel to allow more loads to be connected; low-power, combination, or smart appliances to reduce electric loads at the source; slim tandem breakers or subpanels for more space; and more (Armstrong, et al. 2022). The panel constraint estimate from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

metadata.doc_title: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3.3  Electrical Panels

from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

Panel capacity and space constraints are modeled using a service load and a breaker space calculation, respectively. The load calculation is based on 2023 National Electrical Code's loadbased method in Section 220 (National Fire Protection Association 2023), which guides how the load diversity should be estimated and summed to estimate the total load connected to the panel. When this total load converted to ampacity exceeds the service rating of the panel, the panel is considered capacity-constrained in ResStock. Similarly, the panel is considered spaceconstrained when the total occupied breaker space counted from the bottom-up exceeds the rated space count of the panel. The panel's capacity and space ratings are probabilistically sampled based on other housing characteristics such as heating fuel and the presence of certain appliances. Users are encouraged to reevaluate these constraint metrics according to other considerations, such as a margin of safety to account for uncertainty in the modeling process. For more details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025).

text:
Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump — 3.4  Modeling Limitations

Ducted heat pump units run their indoor fan during defrost. This would create a 'cold blow' that would be objectionable to some homeowners. To avoid this, the backup heat is brought on to temper the air and avoid discomfort. This results in backup heating usage even at mild temperatures. This backup heating is not presently modeled in EnergyPlus. The cooling delivered during defrost is offset by additional heat pump heating if the building load does not exceed the heat pump capacity after defrost degradation penalties. This limitation causes lower estimates for backup heating (COP = 1.0) in simulations because the heat pump compressor (COP > 1.0) is being modeled to offset the defrost cooling.

Additionally, some dwellings that receive this heat pump will not have a duct system that is sized large enough for the heat pump's capacity. ResStock resizes ducts in the dwelling to accommodate the new heat pump upgrade.

The functions of flow fraction are 1 because the blower is assumed to have constant flow

It is estimated that 44.8% of dwellings upgrading to the typical cold climate heat pump face either a breaker space or a capacity constraint (or both) while 55.2% have no constraints. All post-upgrade constraint statistics include a minute fraction of homes that are already capacity-constrained in the baseline. Prior to the upgrade, 2.3% of the existing panels are estimated to already be over-capacity, which is possible as the capacity constraint is estimated based on code. In contrast, no existing panel is space-constrained, which makes sense as it is physically impossible to connect more loads than there is space. Capacity constraints in the existing stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it is important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on. During the cold climate ASHP upgrade, any homes already constrained before the upgrade will likely need to address their capacity issue to be permitted by code to connect a new load to the panel, whether the upgrade is making the constraint worse or not. Thus, the post-upgrade constraint statistics can be attributed entirely to the upgrade. Users are encouraged to alternatively analyze the constra

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to energy efficiency retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (https://www.nlr.gov/buildings/end-use-load-profiles.html).

The Dual Fuel Heat Pump System Upgrade demonstrated 9.3% total site energy savings (1,097 TBtu) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 5). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 5% stock total cooling savings (65.7 TBtu).

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1  Technology Summary

The dual fuel heating system in this measure upgrade consists of an air-source heat pump (ASHP) and a natural gas furnace. In this configuration the natural gas furnace heats the dwelling during the coldest outdoor temperatures of the year, while the ASHP cools the dwelling during the cooling season and heats it at mild outdoor temperatures during the heating season. This section provides an overview of the technology used in this measure upgrade and includes details about specific features of the dual fuel systems.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

A dual fuel heating system combines two technologies: an ASHP and a natural gas furnace. These systems operate together using the same indoor air handler (fan blower) and ductwork to distribute conditioned air throughout the home. The system is designed to alternate between the ASHP and the furnace depending on outdoor temperature.

In this configuration, the ASHP coil is typically installed in line with the furnace, positioned so that air flows through it after passing through the furnace's heat exchanger. During mild to moderately cold weather, the ASHP serves as the primary heating source, transferring heat from the outdoor air into the home using a refrigerant and a compressor.

As outdoor temperatures fall, the heating capacity of the ASHP decreases. At a specific outdoor temperature, known as the switchover temperature or balance point, the system stops the ASHP and starts the natural gas furnace. From this temperature and below, the furnace provides all heating to the home and operates independently when the ASHP is inactive.

The switchover temperature can be set manually or managed by a thermostat that monitors outdoor conditions and determines which system should be active. This arrangement allows for coordinated operation of the two systems without overlap in heating delivery.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

This type of system is commonly used in regions with a wide range of outdoor temperatures and where natural gas is available. More detailed information about the individual ASHP and furnace components is provided below.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.1.1  Air-Source Heat Pumps

ASHPs provide space heating and cooling in buildings. According to the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, only ~16.5% of dwellings in the contiguous United States have ASHP systems as their sole source, with most ASHPs located in warmer regions like the southern United States (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2022).

ASHPs transfer heat from outdoor air to indoor air during heating operation and from indoor to outdoor during cooling operation. During heating, an ASHP's compressor powers a vapor compression cycle that delivers heat to the conditioned space of the dwelling. Unlike fossil fuel combustion or electric resistance heating, ASHPs can heat dwellings with efficiency levels above 100%. For example, average heating coefficients of performance (COPs)-the ratio of heating delivered to energy consumed-range from ~2.0 in colder climates to ~3.0 in hotter climates for ducted air-to-air heat pump upgrades (Praprost, et al. 2026). For reference, an electric resistance heater operates at a COP of 1.0.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.1.2  Gas Furnaces

Natural gas furnaces are used to heat indoor environments. For a conventional ducted furnace, natural gas is ignited in the burner, and the flame heats a metal heat exchanger. A blower fan then moves supply air over the heat exchanger. The exhaust combustion products are vented through a flue in the dwelling to the outdoors. The supply air is distributed through the duct system of the dwelling to heat the indoor space.

In a dual fuel heating system like the one modeled in this measure upgrade, the ASHP cooling/heating coil is placed in line with the furnace, using the furnace's blower fan. This setup prevents both systems from operating simultaneously. For this dual fuel heat pump, a switchover temperature is set at which the ASHP heating mode stops and the natural gas heating system takes over. Some dual fuel systems have a switchover 'band,' a range of temperatures where both the heat pump and furnace can serve the load, but that is not the case in this measure. More information on the switchover temperature is available in Section 1.2.1.5. In this measure upgrade, the backup heating system is either a 92% AFUE natural gas furnace or a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace, depending on the climate zone region.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

This ASHP option involves retrofitting an existing heating and cooling system with a ducted ASHP and a natural gas furnace into a building that already has existing ductwork for heating or cooling. The ASHP coil, gas furnace, and blower are installed with the dwelling's existing air distribution system, while the outdoor coil and compressor unit are installed outside.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1  ASHP System

This ASHP option involves retrofitting a ducted ASHP into a building that already has existing ductwork for either heating or cooling. The ASHP coil is installed with the dwelling's existing air distribution system and an outdoor coil and compressor unit are installed outside.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.1  Compressor Speed

This ASHP option has a single-stage compressor. Single-stage compressors are the most affordable ducted version of baseline efficiency ASHPs that this measure upgrade intends to represent. Single-stage compressors operate at one speed across all operating conditions. Typically, single-stage ASHPs retain less heating capacity at cold temperatures than variablespeed ASHPs because the compressor cannot increase speed in colder temperatures.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.2  Efficiency Ratings: SEER2 and HSPF2

This ASHP option has efficiency ratings based on the Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio 2 (SEER2) for cooling and the Heating Seasonal Performance Factor 2 (HSPF2) for heating. These ratings are calculated by dividing the system's cooling or heating output (Btu) by the electricity consumed (Wh) over the respective cooling or heating season. SEER2 and HSPF2 became mandatory in 2023,  replacing the energy efficiency metrics of SEER and HSPF. The new metrics are measured with external static pressure increased by up to five times to more accurately reflect field conditions and with an updated building load line for HSPF (Department of Energy 2025).

This measure upgrade's ASHPs have a SEER2 of 15.2 and an HSPF2 of 7.8. These efficiency ratings were selected to reflect the minimum requirements for an ASHP to earn an ENERGY STAR ®  rating. These values represent an average efficiency over a typical cooling or heating season, respectively. The instantaneous efficiency of the ASHP will vary according to outdoor and indoor conditions.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.3  Sizing Methodology

This ducted ASHP is sized according to the load calculations in ACCA Manual J (Air Conditioning Contractors of America 2016) and system selection in ACCA Manual S (Air Conditioning Contractors of America 2014). ACCA Manual J provides the procedure for calculating the design heating and cooling loads of the building, while ACCA Manual S guides the selection of residential HVAC systems size. ACCA Manual S directs that ASHPs be sized to the dwelling's calculated cooling load with allowable oversizing limits. Oversizing limits are recommended, especially for single-stage equipment, because an ASHP sized to the heating load could be considerably larger than what the cooling load requires. This large difference in required size can lead to indoor humidity problems in some climate zones because short cycling reduces the ASHP's ability to dehumidify the space. ACCA Manual S seeks to avoid humidityrelated comfort problems with its guidance on oversizing. These oversizing limits depend on the climate of the dwelling and the type of compressor. The oversizing limits for single-stage (reflective of this measure's compressor), two-stage, and variable-speed ASHPs are 15%, 20%, and 30%, respectively, and are implemented only for dwellings with mild winters or humid climates. For dwellings in dry climates with less mild winters, an extra 15,000 Btu/h capacity can be added.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.3  Sizing Methodology

and 30%, respectively, and are implemented only for dwellings with mild winters or humid climates. For dwellings in dry climates with less mild winters, an extra 15,000 Btu/h capacity can be added.

Because this ASHP option is single-stage, the oversizing allowance for dwellings with mild winters or humid climates is 15%. ACCA Manual S considers a dwelling in a humid climate if the cooling load sensible heat ratio is less than 0.95. It considers a dwelling to have a mild winter if the amount of Heating-Degree-Days-65°F (HDD65F) compared to the amount of CoolingDegree-Days-50°F (CDD50F) is less than double (i.e., HDD65F/CDD50F <2.0). For dwellings that do not meet either of those requirements (i.e., dwellings with cold winters and dry climates), the ASHP's size is increased by the abovementioned 15,000 Btu/h (1.25 tons of refrigeration).

Because this ASHP option is sized using ACCA Manual S, dwellings in cold climates will receive ASHPs that are likely undersized for their respective heating load since ACCA Manual S sizes based on cooling load. That makes ACCA Manual S sizing a good choice for a singlespeed ASHP with a fossil fuel furnace as its backup, as in this measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.3  Sizing Methodology

load since ACCA Manual S sizes based on cooling load. That makes ACCA Manual S sizing a good choice for a singlespeed ASHP with a fossil fuel furnace as its backup, as in this measure upgrade.

Additionally, this sizing methodology is best practice when sizing a single-stage ASHP to avoid humidity issues from short cycling. Because this ASHP only has one compressor speed, if it were sized to the entire heating load it is likely that in heating-dominant dwellings it would cycle too quickly when in cooling mode and not remove enough moisture from the indoor air, causing discomfort for occupants, as stated above.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.4  Capacity Retention

As outdoor temperatures drop below the rated capacity temperature of 47°F, the available capacity of the ASHP decreases. The capacity retained by an ASHP below this temperature is defined by its capacity retention fraction. This ASHP option's capacity retention fraction is 0.5 at 5°F. This capacity retention factor specifies the fraction of the ASHP's rated capacity available at 5°F. For this ducted ASHP option, its capacity at 47°F-equal to the ACCA Manual J cooling load with ACCA Manual S oversizing allowances added-will be reduced by half at 5°F.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.5  Backup System and Switchover Temperature

This modeled ASHP option uses a natural gas furnace as its backup system. Fossil fuel furnaces and ASHP dual fuel systems cannot provide heating at the same time. Therefore, a switchover temperature must be defined for the ASHP system to switch over to the fossil fuel furnace to fully meet the heating load. To operate this system economically, the switchover temperature is typically set between 25°F and 45°F (Air Source Heat Pump Collaborative 2023). The ideal switchover temperature depends on the efficiencies of the ASHP and furnace systems as well as the prices of electricity and fossil fuel. Lennox recommends a switchover temperature of around 35°F for its products (Lennox 2016). For this measure upgrade, the switchover temperature is also set at 35°F.

metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.6  Duct Considerations

With this dual fuel system measure upgrade, there are some circumstances where the ducts in the dwelling are resized when the upgrade option is applied. This occurs if the existing ducts are not large enough to accommodate the ACCA Manual S-sized ASHP being installed. Because ACCA Manual S sized systems are smaller than systems sized for the full heating load of the dwelling, there is less likelihood that duct systems will be resized in this particular measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.7  Cooling Levels

This measure upgrade is intended to replace existing heating systems, but all dwellings that receive this dual fuel option will also receive whole-home cooling from the ASHP, regardless of whether the dwelling had cooling in the baseline. This will increase cooling energy consumption in dwellings that were not already fully cooled, but it will also provide greater comfort and safety in the simulated homes.

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.1.8  Electrical Requirements

This section summarizes the electrical information for the dual fuel heat pump upgrade. Electrical information in ResStock is used to assess whether the home's electrical panel would become space-constrained or over-capacity due to this upgrade. Section 3.3 describes the electrical panel constraint modeling in more detail.

The power rating of a ducted heat pump system is the sum of the power ratings of the compressor, the air handler, and any electric backup allowed to operate simultaneously, as summarized in Table 1. The heat pump compressor power rating is estimated based on its design heating capacity using a regression equation derived from product labels. The air handler power rating is estimated from the design airflow rate and the OS-HPXML assumption of fan power. The electric resistance backup power rating is directly converted from its heating capacity at an efficiency of 100%. For more information on the modeling assumptions, see the Technical Reference Document (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Ducted heat pumps require at least one 208/240V circuit, each protected by a double-pole breaker. The specific number of circuits depend on whether the heat pump has backup heating (dual fuel or electric) and how the indoor and outdoor units, along with the backup, are configured. Table 2 summarizes the wiring configurations for ducted heat pumps assumed in ResStock. For example, a dual fuel heat pump is assumed to have a 120V air handler on one circuit and a separate 240V circuit for the compressor. For heat pumps with electric backup, the air handler is commonly 240V to allow the strip heat to be on the same circuit; this is also the assumption in ResStock. The maximum overcurrent protection allowed per circuit is assumed to be up to 50A. Therefore, more circuits may be required for larger heat pump systems, which correspond to the use of multiple compressors and/or heat kits in practice.

While a heat pump upgrade replaces both heating and cooling, it may require more circuits and breaker spaces to install than are freed up by removing the existing HVAC systems. The heat pump upgrade may also add more connected load to the panel, especially when the backup is sized for emergency use. The power rating of heat pump systems is determined by their heating configuration and the presence of electric resistance backup. Therefore, homes in colder climates are more likely to face a capacity constraint when upgrading to a heat pump since a backup is often required to supplement the heat pump performance and these homes are more likely to have previously used fuel heating.

For natural gas systems, the load calculation generally does not include any electrical load from non-electric equipment or appliances. However, because heating and cooling loads in ResStock are determined based on individual HVAC components, gas furnaces are assigned a small service rating based on the air handler power, which is determined by the design air flow rate. Additionally, the air handler is typically on a 120V circuit, which uses a single-pole breaker. Upgrading to a natural gas furnace does not add any constraint to the electrical panel or service; instead, it frees up panel capacity and space for homes that previously used electric heating.

metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.2  Natural Gas Furnace Systems

The natural gas system included in this measure upgrade consists of a conventional ducted natural gas furnace that shares a blower fan and air handler with the ASHP described in the above section. The following subsections describe the technical aspects of the natural gas furnace system.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.2.1  Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

AFUE is the total annual fuel-generated heat output divided by the total annual fuel input (on a scale of 0% to 100%) over a 12-month period. ANSI/ASHRAE 103-2022 provides a procedure for determining the AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, using a test cycle designed to simulate typical heating conditions throughout the year-including seasons (ASHRAE 2022).

A higher AFUE rating indicates greater efficiency in converting fuel into usable heat. Energy lost through exhaust gases, radiation, and other components reduces the furnace's efficiency.

In this dual fuel heating system measure upgrade, a higher efficiency furnace with 95% AFUE is used in colder climates (IECC climate zones 5, 6, and 7) while a slightly lower efficiency furnace with 92% AFUE is used in warmer climates (IECC climate zones 1, 2, 3, and 4).

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.2.2  System Types

Natural gas furnaces can be either condensing or non-condensing (sometimes called conventional). Non-condensing furnaces have a single heat exchanger or set of heat exchangers designed to transfer only sensible heat from the flue gas to the supply air. This design ensures that the flue gas does not condense in the vent pipe and retains enough heat and buoyancy to vent without a fan providing positive pressure. As a result, non-condensing furnaces use non-airtight metal vent pipes and typically have efficiencies between 80 to 82% AFUE (North NJ HVAC 2025).

Condensing furnaces, in contrast, include an additional heat exchanger designed to recover latent heat from the exhaust gases. This process lowers the temperature of the flue gas to a point where it can no longer be vented without a fan providing positive pressure. The lower temperatures and positive pressure required for venting the flue gas also necessitate different vent materials and airtight vent construction. Condensing furnaces must use venting materials approved by the manufacturer, but most allow the use of low-cost polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe for venting. The additional heat transfer in condensing furnaces enables them to achieve AFUEs between 90% and 98 (North NJ HVAC 2025)%. Because they generate flue gas condensate, condensing furnaces require a condensate drain line.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 1.2.2.2  System Types

transfer in condensing furnaces enables them to achieve AFUEs between 90% and 98 (North NJ HVAC 2025)%. Because they generate flue gas condensate, condensing furnaces require a condensate drain line.

A non-condensing furnace typically has a lower upfront cost due to fewer components, but incurs higher operating costs because of lower efficiency. The furnace types modeled in this measure upgrade are condensing furnaces because of their high AFUE ratings.
