text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2  Applicability

The Dual Fuel Heat Pump System measure upgrade applies to all dwellings with the following:

- Dwellings with ducts that meet the following criteria:
- o Have a non-shared HVAC system
- o Have at least one appliance or an HVAC system fueled by natural gas
- o Have a heating fuel that is not classified as 'Wood,' 'None,' or 'Other Fuel'
- Dwellings in IECC climate zones 1-4 will receive a dual fuel system with a 92% AFUE natural gas furnace
- Dwellings in IECC climate zones 5-7 will receive a dual fuel system with a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace.

Note that this upgrade explicitly is not applied to buildings without heating in the baseline. With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 50.8% of the existing residential building stock.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2  Applicability

upgrade explicitly is not applied to buildings without heating in the baseline. With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 50.8% of the existing residential building stock.

Applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics that determine the available options and options' details. Specifically, the 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' characteristic in ResStock is used to apply this dual fuel heating system option. 'HVAC Has Ducts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling. 'Heating Fuel' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling. 'HVAC Shared Efficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable. More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Documentation (Reyna, et al. 2025). The exact logic used in the ResStock project YML file for this dataset is available in the GitHub release of the dataset. The remainder of this section provides discussion for why certain apply logic decisions were made.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2.1  Treatment of Dwellings With Shared HVAC Systems

Because there are no reported dwellings in the building stock that have only shared cooling and a personal fuel furnace that also have evidence of an outdoor space for a condensing unit (required for the ducted ASHP portion of the dual fuel system), no dwellings with shared systems will be applied with this measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.section: 2.1  Treatment of Dwellings With Shared HVAC Systems
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2.2  Dwellings With a Natural Gas Line Hookup

For this measure upgrade, only dwellings with an existing natural gas appliance will be able to support the dual fuel heat pumps. Installing a natural gas furnace into a dwelling without an existing natural gas line would incur more costs than a typical retrofit and may be prohibited based on the availability of natural gas in the dwelling's location There must be at least one existing appliance or HVAC system that uses natural gas for the measure upgrade to apply in the ResStock modeling.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.section: 2.2  Dwellings With a Natural Gas Line Hookup
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2.3  Cooling Level Increase for All Applicable Dwellings

Dwellings that are not 100% cooled by their existing AC system (e.g., room AC providing cooling for just one room of a home) will be 100% cooled by this measure upgrade. This will increase cooling energy consumption of those dwellings that were not already 100% cooled. The cooling level increase for all applicable dwellings is implemented because ASHPs in this measure upgrade will be sized to cool the entire dwelling regardless of sizing methodology used. Although this increases energy use associated with cooling, it also increases health and comfort of the home.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 2.4  Exclusion of 'Other Fuel,' 'None,' and 'Wood' Heating Fuels

Dwellings with 'Other Fuel,' 'None,' or 'Wood' heating fuels do not receive this measure upgrade because retrofits to these dwellings can lead to confusing results (e.g., false negative savings compared to baseline or installing heating in regions that do not need it) and the number of dwellings this affects is relatively small. 'Other Fuel' includes specific fuels that are not currently represented in ResStock, so there is not an accurate baseline heating energy consumption to compare to. Additionally, there is not a large impact at scale since dwellings with primary 'Other Fuel', 'None' or 'Wood' heating fuels comprise approximately 2.6% of the total residential building stock.

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3  Modeling Approach

This section will overview how the upgrade measure is functionally modeled via ResStock into OpenStudio-HPXML. Section 3.1 will briefly cover how OpenStudio-HPXML is used by ResStock to model the dwellings generated by ResStock's sampling. Section 3.2 will cover how inputs from ResStock and default values calculated by OpenStudio-HPXML create the Dual Fuel Heating System measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, et al. 2025). These distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each dwelling model in the stock has an assigned representative option for each characteristic. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the measure upgrades in a ResStock dataset release that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

In the case of heating/cooling upgrades in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1, these assumptions are all HVAC-related. This documentation covers the calculations directly related to the dual fuel heat pump, but HVAC controls (e.g., setpoints, cycling) and HVAC distribution (e.g., airflow systems) are out of its scope. For information on how OpenStudio-HPXML handles controls in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1 see here and for how it handles distribution see here. The following subsections will go through the ResStock inputs and the defaults calculated by BuildResidentialHPXML for the heat pump upgrade discussed in this documentation. Most defaults highlighted from the BuildResidentialHPXML measure stem from the apply\_hvac(), apply\_hvac\_sizing(), and apply\_detailed\_performance\_data() methods found in OpenStudioHPXML's hpxml\_defaults.rb file. Note: the defaults.rb file calls methods from various Ruby files within the directory it resides. See these Ruby files here.

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3.3  Electrical Panels

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025. As new electric loads are added into the home during an improvement project, the electrical panel may not have enough capacity or space headroom to accommodate these new circuits. Thus, the panel may become constrained, requiring an electrical upgrade that may include upsizing the service entrance. Panel constraints can also be mitigated in other ways without the panel or service being upsized, by using load shedding devices, circuit sharing devices, or a smart panel to allow more loads to be connected; low-power, combination, or smart appliances to reduce electric loads at the source; slim tandem breakers or subpanels for more space; and more (Armstrong, et al. 2022). The panel constraint estimate from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

metadata.doc_title: Dual Fuel Heat Pump
metadata.measure_name: Dual Fuel Heat Pump

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3.3  Electrical Panels

from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

Panel capacity and space constraints are modeled using a service load and a breaker space calculation, respectively. The load calculation is based on 2023 National Electrical Code's loadbased method in Section 220 (National Fire Protection Association 2023), which guides how the load diversity should be estimated and summed to estimate the total load connected to the panel. When this total load converted to ampacity exceeds the service rating of the panel, the panel is considered capacity-constrained in ResStock. Similarly, the panel is considered spaceconstrained when the total occupied breaker space counted from the bottom-up exceeds the rated space count of the panel. The panel's capacity and space ratings are probabilistically sampled based on other housing characteristics such as heating fuel and the presence of certain appliances. Users are encouraged to reevaluate these constraint metrics according to other considerations, such as a margin of safety to account for uncertainty in the modeling process. For more details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 3.4  Modeling Limitations

At the time of these simulations and dataset release, the heat pump fan airflow rate is used during backup heating mode; this is a bug in the EnergyPlus software. Typically, the airflow rate during backup heating mode would be a lower airflow rate because of the furnace's higher supply air temperature.

Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 4.1.1 Single Dwelling Annual Results

Table 7 presents the modeled annual energy consumption savings for key outputs for both individual dwelling test models. Both dwellings show expected savings, except for an increase in heating fans and pumps energy for Dwelling 2 and cooling fans and pump energy for Dwelling 1. The heat pump airflow rate is higher than typical furnace airflow rates, so the cooling and heating fans will not experience significant savings, if any. At the time of these simulations and dataset release, the heat pump fan airflow rate was used during backup heating mode due to a bug in the EnergyPlus software. This bug contributes to the low savings for heating fans. The EnergyPlus development team has been notified about the bug and no resolution has occurred at the time of this publication.

The N/A values for 'Electricity-Heating (incl. backup)' are due to from the absence of electric heating in the dwellings in the baseline. The nonzero electric heating in the upgrade results in an infinite increase in this category's energy consumption for both dwellings. For Dwelling 1, the increase in electric heating is reflected in the 'Utility Bills-Electricity' category. However, since Dwelling 2 requires far fewer heating hours than Dwelling 1, its savings for 'Utility Bills-Electricity' is only slightly negative.

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 4.4  Electrical Panel Constraints

Figure 11 shows the distribution of modeled panel constraints overall (see 'all' column) and by baseline heating fuel. It is estimated that 8.0% of dwellings upgrading to the typical cold climate heat pump face either a breaker space or a capacity constraint (or both), while 98.0% have no constraints. Most dwellings that face a panel constraint are those that do not have electricity as their baseline heating fuel (i.e., fossil fuel heated dwellings).

text:
Dual Fuel Heat Pump — 4.4  Electrical Panel Constraints

(or both), while 98.0% have no constraints. Most dwellings that face a panel constraint are those that do not have electricity as their baseline heating fuel (i.e., fossil fuel heated dwellings).

All post-upgrade constraint statistics include a minute fraction of homes that are already capacity-constrained in the baseline. Prior to the upgrade, 2.3% of the existing panels are estimated to already be over-capacity, which is possible as the capacity constraint is estimated based on code. In contrast, no existing panel is space-constrained, which makes sense as it is physically impossible to connect more loads than there is space. Capacity constraints in the existing stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it is important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on. During the Dual Fuel Heat Pump upgrade, any homes already constrained before the upgrade will likely need to address their capacity issue in order to be permitted by code to connect a new load to the panel, whether the upgrade is making the constraint worse or not. Thus, the post-upgrade constraint statistics can be attributed entirely to the upgrade. Users are encouraged to alternatively analyze

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly marketready) upgrades. ' Measures ' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al, 2022).

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1 Technology Summary

This work examines the technical potential for replacing existing heating systems with natural gas furnaces in homes with air ducts across the U.S. residential building stock. Natural gas furnaces are a type of heating system that combust natural gas to produce hot air. Natural gas furnaces distribute this heat through ducts systems to warm indoor spaces, and compose 47.7% of space heating technologies in the United States. The purpose of this upgrade is to provide a comparison point for futures where residential households adopt natural gas furnaces, in order to estimate potential energy and bill changes.

In cases where the heating system also provides air conditioning, like a heat pump, the air conditioning is removed from the dwelling unit.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

Natural gas furnaces are used to heat indoor environments. The natural gas is ignited in the burner, and the flame heats a metal heat exchanger that the exhaust gas flows through. For forced-air systems, the majority of furnaces, a blower fan moves air over the heat exchangers, which warms the air. Forced-air natural gas furnaces use ducts to distribute heat, while combustion exhaust is vented outside.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.2  Efficiency and System Types

Efficiency rated by annual fuel utilization efficiency (AFUE), capacity, and system types are key features of natural gas furnaces. Other technical upgrades are important to the function and performance of natural gas furnaces as well.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.2.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

AFUE is the standard rated efficiency for how efficiently a furnace converts fuel into heat at rated conditions. The higher the AFUE rating, the more efficient the system is at converting fuel into usable heat. Energy lost through exhaust gases, radiation, and other components decreases efficiency.

AFUE is the total annual heat output divided by the total annual fuel input -on a scale of 0% to 100%. Note that unlike SEER2 and HSPF2, 1  AFUE does not include the electricity used by the air handler blower, combustion blower, ignition system, or controls. ANSI/ASHRAE 103-2022 provides a procedure for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022) .

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.2.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022) .

'Residential furnaces manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16) must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 430.32,' (DOE 2025). 80% AFUE furnaces are the minimum for nonweatherized gas furnaces (i.e., natural gas and propane) manufactured from 2015 through Dec. 18, 2028. After Dec. 18, 2028, the minimum furnace is 95% AFUE. If an investigator would like to understand equipment standard changes over time, a useful approach could blend data from this study with data from the Propane and Fuel Oil Furnaces upgrade (Stenger, Liu, White, et al. 2025) and Reference Space Heating and Cooling (circa 2025) (Stenger, Liu, Wilson, et al. 2025), both of which model 95% AFUE for propane and heating and cooling minimum, respectively. In this study, we model a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace.

1 SEER stands for seasonal energy efficiency ratio, and HSPF stands for heating seasonal performance factor.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.2.2  System Types

Natural gas furnaces can be condensing or noncondensing (sometimes called conventional). Condensing furnaces have high-efficiency units that have a second heat exchanger used to recover latent heat from flue gases and can reach an AFUE between 90% and 99%, according to the Air-Conditioning, Heating and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) (AHRI 2025). A secondary heat exchanger condenses hot exhaust gases -extracting more remaining heat -resulting in a condensate and requiring a condensate drain line as well as a condensate pump if a floor drain is not available nearby. Condensing furnaces exhaust at lower temperatures of around 100° -150°F and mostly vent horizontally through polyvinyl chloride (PVC) ductwork as opposed to a metal vertical vent commonly used for noncondensing furnaces. Noncondensing furnaces often have an AFUE up to 80% and do not have a secondary heat exchanger, yielding exhaust that leaves at high temperatures -up to 350°F. Since noncondensing furnaces have steel vertical vents, it is important to avoid any condensation of the flue gas in the vent because the condensate is slightly acidic and can corrode the vent over time. A noncondensing furnace often has a lower upfront cost (because of fewer components), but higher operating costs (because of lower efficiencies). In this study, we model condensing furnaces as an upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 1.2.3 Other Technical Specifications

A prerequisite for natural gas furnaces is the access to natural gas distribution. In this upgrade, we assume that natural gas is available to homes regardless of prior heating fuel, geography, or other physical infrastructures.

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 2 Applicability

This upgrade applies only to dwellings with existing ducted systems. The choice to apply this upgrade to homes without current access to natural gas was made to evaluate the theoretical impacts of switching to this fuel. Whether or not installing new gas distribution to supply existing homes is financially or technically feasible is outside the scope of this document.

However, this upgrade could be used as part of an analysis into the financial viability of installing new gas distribution and the benefits-costs to households. The upgrade replaces the existing heating system with a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace. If a dwelling unit that has a heating system that also provides air conditioning, like a heat pump, the air conditioning is removed as part of the upgrade. No changes to infiltration are assumed as part of the flue removal or installation process.

Approximately 74.3% of the residential building stock meets the conditions for this upgrade. Details on the application logic are in Table 1.

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 3 Modeling Approach

This section outlines how a universal natural gas furnace upgrade is modeled in ResStock using the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. In this scenario, every dwelling unit with a ducted heating system is assigned a natural gas furnace, regardless of its original heating system. ResStock uses probabilistic sampling logic based on national housing stock data to assign each dwelling unit a set of baseline building characteristics, including existing heating fuel, system type, and duct configuration. For this upgrade, the workflow overrides the existing heating system and fuel type with a centrally defined natural gas furnace characterized by a specified AFUE. The furnace is modeled as a forced-air system with ducts, and the energy performance is governed by its AFUE rating, which reflects seasonal fuel-to-heat conversion efficiency. The model assumes consistent operation patterns across households and scales furnace capacity based on heating load requirements determined by building envelope characteristics and climate zone. While equipment brand and installation quality are not modeled explicitly, the total heating energy demand and fuel consumption are recalculated to reflect the standardized furnace and fuel use. This upgrade represents a scenario where dwellings with ducted systems could convert to natural gas furnaces, allowing for assessment of energy and infrastructure implications

The probability distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through the use of an HPXML file (HPXML 2025). For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the airsource heat pump (ASHP) upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML upgrade.

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 3.1  Natural Gas Furnace

In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OpenStudio-HPXML parameters. Upgrades, such as switching all ducted homes to natural gas furnaces, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how a universal natural gas furnace upgrade is implemented in the ResStock workflow.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 3.1.1  ResStock Inputs

This scenario assumes every household with existing ductwork receives a natural gas furnace, regardless of its original fuel type. The upgrade logic identifies all ducted homes and overrides their baseline heating system with a natural gas forced-air furnace of a defined AFUE, typically representing a modern, high-efficiency unit. The change is reflected in the OpenStudio-HPXML model via updates to fuel type, heating system type, and efficiency parameters. Heating capacity is sized based on Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) Manual J (ACCA 2016) and Manual S (ACCA 2014) calculations for the respective climate zone and building envelope. The model presumes standard furnace operation and does not include installation-specific variation, instead relying on the AFUE to govern thermal performance. This upgrade scenario enables simulation of the broad-scale impact of transitioning ducted homes to a single fossil fuel heating pathway, including effects on energy use and utility bills.

![Image](96634_images/image_000004_2c3b121e9c2ef0367fa54f730d30f013447b6cc26b593c0ce3e2d6ed6880d74c.png)

The application of the upgrade shown in Figure 3 represents a significant amount of savings in a dwelling heated with a 60% AFUE fuel furnace. Before the upgrade, the dwelling consumed 122.8 MBtu and dropped to 93.8 MBtu after the upgrade, where the majority of energy savings are sourced from natural gas heating.

metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.2  Aggregated Building Time Series

Colorado is selected as a case study to analyze the aggregated time-series data. Out of all national dwelling units, 1.7% are in Colorado. Figure 4 presents the aggregated average daily baseline energy consumption in Colorado, with February 20 identified as the day with the highest energy use. To further explore this peak, Figure 5 examines the aggregated average power on February 20 in Colorado, comparing conditions before and after the upgrade.

Figure 4. Aggregated daily average energy consumption of baseline in Colorado

![Image](96634_images/image_000005_2f942984f8e823946083ad7afdd8eb82c8845623b41b889dcf9f600f6740bdf6.png)

Figure 5 shows that the upgrade scenario consistently results in lower power demand throughout the day compared to the baseline.

Figure 5. Aggregated average power data in Colorado on peak day

![Image](96634_images/image_000006_fcc83a9461cbf269da6e1392c33758c97c6f33007914c00b5740457e8115a1d2.png)

metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 model building simulations (i.e., models), 408,800 models are applicable for the natural gas fuel furnace upgrade (74.3%), representing the 139,647,020 dwellings from American Community Survey's 2021, 5 -year estimate of U.S. households (not including territories).

For the applicable models, the total baseline consumption is 2.85 trillion kWh per year, and after the natural gas furnace upgrade, the total consumption is 2.67 trillion kWh per year, a 6.3% savings.

Figure 6. Annual total site energy consumption by fuel type

![Image](96634_images/image_000007_64d1e0add196fd28011977ea29d0d6243c7dca0de53fdae88cc7a2293ab6350d.png)

For the U.S. housing stock, total site energy consumption changes across heating fuels after a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace upgrade, with an increase of 0.38 trillion kWh from natural gas energy consumption and a decrease of 0.33 trillion kWh from electricity, as shown in Figure 6. Gaining more clarity on fuel type changes, Figure 7 shows the energy savings by heating type and fuel end use.

Figure 7. Annual energy consumption by HVAC heating type and fuel end use

![Image](96634_images/image_000008_4b9a06b1e2a72258941d2544723a9e62992b7a3a903356379f814ed027821d99.png)

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

and fuel end use.

Figure 7. Annual energy consumption by HVAC heating type and fuel end use

![Image](96634_images/image_000008_4b9a06b1e2a72258941d2544723a9e62992b7a3a903356379f814ed027821d99.png)

Figure 7 demonstrates a mixed effect for energy savings, where heating for natural gas increases (i.e., negative energy savings) by 157 billion kWh in ducted heat pumps, 185 billion kWh in ducted heating, and 38 billion kWh in non-ducted heating.

The modeling approach also removes cooling for dwellings heated with ducted heat pumps -as shown by the 87.5 billion kWh in energy savings from electricity for cooling. The distribution of annual energy savings per dwelling are shown in Figure 8.

Figure 8. Distribution of annual energy savings per dwelling by HVAC heating efficiency

![Image](96634_images/image_000009_4efe82ee84d13fb9c941435315e74fef712915c2a481212f228817efdffa0ecd.png)

Upgrading fuel furnace efficiency when lower than 95% AFUE yields energy savings, where dwellings with 60% AFUE fuel furnaces can save up to 30,800 kWh annually (i.e., upper fence of box plot), as shown in Figure 8. In contrast, ASHPs show a mixed effect for energy savings, where more efficient ASHPs -like ASHP, SEER 15, 7.7 HSPF -have a median of 1,178 kWh energy savings and as much as a 9,289 kWh increase in energy (i.e., lower fence of box plot).

metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

for energy savings, where more efficient ASHPs -like ASHP, SEER 15, 7.7 HSPF -have a median of 1,178 kWh energy savings and as much as a 9,289 kWh increase in energy (i.e., lower fence of box plot).

In other words, energy use can increase among dwellings with ASHPs, even with the removal of cooling as a service, after the transition from ASHP to natural gas furnace. In addition, boilers and wall/floor furnaces demonstrate a range of mixed effects on annual energy savings per dwelling. To better understand average changes, Figure 9 shows average energy savings by HVAC heating efficiency, end use, and fuel type.

Figure 9. Average annual energy savings per dwelling by HVAC heating efficiency and fuel end use

![Image](96634_images/image_000010_05cf11f9dd431519ce502f19da7b13dfe5814c0aacd3ac9091f006adefcd999b.png)

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

9. Average annual energy savings per dwelling by HVAC heating efficiency and fuel end use

![Image](96634_images/image_000010_05cf11f9dd431519ce502f19da7b13dfe5814c0aacd3ac9091f006adefcd999b.png)

As shown in Figure 9, natural gas heating results in negative energy savings (i.e., energy consumption increases). Interestingly, boilers, wall/floor furnaces, ASHPs, and electric baseboard heating demonstrate the mixed effect of energy savings after the upgrade -on average, 90% AFUE fuel boilers (1,934 kWh), 100% efficiency electric baseboard (1,633 kWh), 100% AFUE electric boiler (1,142 kWh), and 100% AFUE electric wall furnaces (1,572 kWh) show an average annual increase in energy consumption per dwelling. This average increase can be caused by a decrease in energy efficiency and fuel switching to a less efficient site energy (i.e., from electric to natural gas).

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.4  Stock Bill Impacts

As previously mentioned, stock bill impacts will be shown considering the reduction in cooling when dwelling upgrade to a natural gas furnace from ASHP. Figure 10 shows the average annual bill savings per dwelling by HVAC heating efficiency and bill savings energy source.

Figure 10. Average annual bill savings by HVAC heating efficiency and bill savings source

![Image](96634_images/image_000011_2f335617f989cf24767aec2c7496f85cbbddf6d9101dd6924f94068a0b9bf02a.png)

On average, upgrading a less efficient fuel furnace to a 95% AFUE gas furnace results in bill savings.

Table 5 shows the first quartile (Q1), median, and third quartile (Q3) for annual bill savings per dwelling by HVAC heating efficiency. While ASHPs show annual bill savings depending on the efficiency of the system, these cases have all cooling removed because the ASHP is replaced by a gas furnace, but no air conditioner.

The amount of unmet cooling drastically increases in the upgrade case, as it is assumed that there is not an air conditioner installed along with the gas furnace. As a result, occupants are losing comfort benefits while gaining some utility bill savings.

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.5  Electric Panel Impacts

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna et al, 2025).

Upgrading to a 95% AFUE natural gas furnace generally has no impact on the electrical panel, as no new electrical loads or circuits are being added. Most homes receiving this measure are replacing an existing fuel furnace. However, for the small fraction of homes previously heated by electrically (e.g., by an electric resistance furnace or a ducted heat pump), this measure can free up panel capacity and breaker space by removing those circuits and loads from the panel.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE

text:
Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE — 4.5  Electric Panel Impacts

heated by electrically (e.g., by an electric resistance furnace or a ducted heat pump), this measure can free up panel capacity and breaker space by removing those circuits and loads from the panel.

Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them. 2.3% of the existing panels are estimated to already exceed capacity based on code. Pre-existing capacity constraints are an artifact of the panel modeling process, in which panel service ratings are estimated from selected housing variables rather than detailed inventory data. While anecdotal evidence suggests these constraints can occur in practice -manifesting as flickering lights or tripping breakers -the lack of empirical data prevents us from confirming their prevalence.

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures . ' Measures ' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al 2022).

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 1 Technology Summary

This work examines the technical potential for replacing existing fuel oil and propane furnaces across the U.S. residential building stock -but only in homes where these types of systems are already installed. Though less widespread than natural gas systems, oil and propane furnaces remain common in areas without pipeline gas service, particularly in older and colder climate dwellings. Oil is most common in older or rural buildings in New England and the mid-Atlantic.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

Fuel-fired furnaces -including propane and fuel oil -are used to heat indoor environments. Fuel ignites in the burner, and the flame heats a metal heat exchanger. A blower fan moves air over the heat exchangers, which warms the air. Most furnaces use ducts to distribute heat, while combustion exhaust is vented outside. In comparison, gravity furnaces do exist but are older and not as common; as such in this study, we only model forced air furnaces.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 1.2  Efficiency and System Types

Efficiency, measured by annual fuel utilization efficiency (AFUE) is a key feature of furnaces heated by fuel oil or propane. In this measure upgrade, we include propane in the form of liquified petroleum gas and fuel oil -typically number 2 heating oil.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 1.2.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

AFUE is the standard rated efficiency for how efficiently a furnace converts fuel into heat at rated conditions. The higher the AFUE rating, the more efficient the system is at converting fuel into usable heat. Energy lost through exhaust gases, radiation, and other components decreases efficiency.

AFUE is the total annual heat output divided by the total annual fuel input -on a scale of 0% to 100%. Note that AFUE does not include the electricity used by the air handler blower, combustion blower, ignition system, or controls. ANSI/ASHRAE 103-2022 provides a procedure for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022) .

metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022) .

'Residential furnaces manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16) must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 430.32' (DOE 2025). 80% AFUE furnaces are the minimum for nonweatherized gas furnaces (i.e., natural gas and propane) manufactured from 2015 through Dec. 18, 2028. After Dec. 18, 2028, the minimum furnace is 95% AFUE. If an investigator would like to understand equipment standard changes over time, a useful approach could blend data from this study with data from the space heating and cooling (circa 2025) upgrade (Stenger, Liu, Wilson, et al. 2025) as well as the natural gas furnace upgrade (Stenger, Liu, White, et al. 2025), which model fuel oil, propane, and natural gas furnaces.

(circa 2025) upgrade (Stenger, Liu, Wilson, et al. 2025) as well as the natural gas furnace upgrade (Stenger, Liu, White, et al. 2025), which model fuel oil, propane, and natural gas furnaces.

Dwellings upgraded from lower efficiency furnaces often have atmospheric vents. After the upgrade, these will side vent rather than having an atmospheric vent, meaning some dwellings with propane furnace could changes in their infiltration (HPXML 2025). In this study, we model a 95% AFUE furnace consuming propane. For dwellings heated with fuel oil, we model an 88% AFUE furnace as a higher-efficiency furnace (AHRI 2025).

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 3 Modeling Approach

This section outlines how propane and fuel oil furnace upgrades are modeled in ResStock using the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. ResStock assigns each dwelling unit a set of building characteristics, including heating system type, efficiency, and fuel source, based on probabilistic sampling logic informed by national housing stock data. Furnaces are modeled as forced-air heating systems that distribute heat through ductwork. The primary variable representing an upgrade is AFUE, which characterizes how efficiently the furnace converts fuel to usable heat over a heating season. Ducts remain unchanged when heating systems are upgraded. ResStock models fuel type (e.g., propane or natural gas) explicitly, influencing energy use calculations. The model assumes consistent operation patterns across households, and scales furnace capacity based on heating load requirements determined by building envelope characteristics and climate zone. While equipment brand and installation quality are not modeled explicitly, the total heating energy demand and fuel consumption are recalculated to reflect the standardized furnace and fuel use.

Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 3 Modeling Approach

While equipment brand and installation quality are not modeled explicitly, the total heating energy demand and fuel consumption are recalculated to reflect the standardized furnace and fuel use.

These probability distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the oil and propane furnace upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 3.1  Propane and Fuel Oil Furnaces

In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OpenStudio-HPXML parameters. Measure upgrades, such as converting or replacing furnaces with higher-efficiency propane or fuel oil systems, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how propane and fuel oil furnace upgrades are implemented in the ResStock workflow.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 3.1.1  ResStock Inputs

Propane and fuel oil furnaces are modeled as forced-air heating systems serving homes with central ducts. Each upgrade replaces the existing heating system with a furnace that uses either propane or fuel oil, with efficiency defined by a target AFUE level: 88% AFUE for fuel oil heated dwellings and 95% AFUE for propane heated dwellings. These furnaces are modeled assuming that the efficiency is constant at the AFUE and that heating is always available if there is a demand for it. This measure assumes the furnaces are always installed correctly, although models exist in OpenStudio-HPXML to account for issues with installation that may degrade performance. The furnaces supply air at a constant temperature to the ducts. Duct losses are then calculated based on the supply temperature, airflow rate, and duct characteristics using a custom routine in EnergyPlus.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

For propane furnaces, the AFUE used here requires a condensing furnace, modeled with a side vent. Lower efficiency equipment often uses a vertical atmospheric vent, as it vents at a higher temperature and can rely on buoyancy. In OpenStudio-HPXML, the type of vent affects the infiltration in the home, as atmospheric vents can increase infiltration. This means this upgrade can also decrease infiltration in these homes if they don't have another atmospheric vent for the water heater; see references for more details on when atmospheric flues are modeled (HPXML 2025).

In OpenStudio-HPXML, each central furnace is represented under:

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 model building simulations (i.e., models), 31,876 models are applicable for the propane and fuel oil furnace upgrade (5.8%), representing the 139,647,020 dwellings from American Community Survey's 2021, 5 -year estimate of U.S. households (not including territories). For the 31,876 applicable units, 13,200 use fuel oil and 18,676 use propane. For the applicable models, the total baseline consumption is 302 billion kWh per year, and after the propane and fuel oil furnace upgrade, the total consumption is 278 billion kWh per year, a 7.9% savings.

Figure 6 shows that energy savings from the propane and fuel oil furnace upgrade mostly come from heating-related end uses.

Figure 6. Annual energy consumption by fuel end use and heating fuel

![Image](96635_images/image_000007_d49e1338055fcda4dd186927efbd6f68c27987d7d73ceb8d4927ffc8171294b8.png)

In dwellings heated with fuel oil, energy used for heating from fuel oil reduced 9.3%, from 98.2 billion kWh to 89.1 billion kWh after the upgrade. In dwellings heated with propane, energy used for heating from propane reduced 13.1%, from 101.4 billion kWh to 88.1 billion kWh after the upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

billion kWh to 89.1 billion kWh after the upgrade. In dwellings heated with propane, energy used for heating from propane reduced 13.1%, from 101.4 billion kWh to 88.1 billion kWh after the upgrade.

100% of energy savings for dwellings heated with fuel oil is sourced from fuel oil heating end uses. While 93% of average annual energy savings in dwellings heated with propane come from propane heating, cooling fans pumps using electricity composes 3%, heating fans pumps using electricity compose 3%, and cooling using electricity compose 1% of annual average energy savings, as shown in Figure 7. As mentioned in the Modeling Approach section, installation of the propane furnace can improve infiltration, which explains these energy savings. Because of this slight improvement in performance in propane furnace households, an annual average of 8.8 hours of unmet cooling hours are saved.

Figure 7. Average annual energy savings by heating fuel

![Image](96635_images/image_000008_4cb8fbcbb8acd5cbcaac182c7ea030523002f77f772e6f253528d2a76c5782b7.png)

To gain a better understanding of the range for energy savings, Figure 8 shows the distribution of annual energy savings by HVAC heating efficiency.

Figure 8. Annual energy savings by HVAC heating efficiency

![Image](96635_images/image_000009_6729dc009d95d940c09cd9f9109878adf8eaadc491c6904fdd1b4f689108e95c.png)

metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

by HVAC heating efficiency.

Figure 8. Annual energy savings by HVAC heating efficiency

![Image](96635_images/image_000009_6729dc009d95d940c09cd9f9109878adf8eaadc491c6904fdd1b4f689108e95c.png)

In Figure 8, the less efficient furnaces -60% AFUE fuel furnaces -show a wider range and higher median of energy saving (8,182 kWh) than higher-efficiency furnaces like 92.5% AFUE furnaces (411 kWh). By totals, opportunities for energy savings are greatest in the Middle Atlantic, East North Central, and New England Census Divisions, as shown in Figure 9.

Figure 9. Total annual energy savings by census division and fuel totals savings

![Image](96635_images/image_000010_50dfbf7205ee7ad3ad5bd1913d3db19a12e8a64d234768643cbbdf7b71c87b1e.png)

After the upgrade, the Middle Atlantic region could save up to 5.33 billion kWh, the East North Central region could save up to 5.27 billion kWh, and the New England area could save up to 4.45 billion kWh.

metadata.doc_title: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
metadata.measure_name: Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE

text:
Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE — 4.4  Stock Utility Bill Impacts

After the upgrade, the housing stock shows a reduction in energy bill costs, as shown in Figure 10, where dwellings heated with fuel oil show a 4.7% average percentage savings and dwellings heated with propane show a 7.4% average percentage savings.

Figure 10. Annual energy bills by heating fuel in baseline and upgrade

![Image](96635_images/image_000011_9fedc8e6adb6928cb9fe82c08f15554c7205b022d9afba0c6c3a96463f131a0d.png)

Figure 11 shows the average annual bill savings by HVAC heating efficiency and the energy source of the bill.

Figure 11. Average annual bill savings by HVAC heating efficiency

![Image](96635_images/image_000012_0fa7f9e75eda956a4a11774c15d688f309d989b45bb5ce4522413917e7419103.png)

Aligning with increasing energy performance shown in the previous section, lower efficiency furnaces show the greatest average annual bill savings after the upgrade. Dwellings receiving the upgrade and heated with fuel oil yield an average annual bill savings of $248, and dwellings heated with propane yield $293. Improving furnaces ' efficiency saves on both energy and bills.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures . ' Measure ' is another name for an upgrade or retrofit that can be applied to a building.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — Upgrade Summary

------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Measure Definition | This upgrade replaces space heating and cooling equipment in homes with existing ductwork with units that meet minimum efficiency standards reflective of circa-2025 requirements. It includes: • Replacement of ducted fuel furnaces with a minimum of 80% - 83% AFUE (92.5% AFUE for like-for-like replacements at higher efficiency). • Replacement of air-source heat pumps with equipment rated at 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2. • Replacement of central air conditioners (ACs) with units rated at 14.3 SEER2 in the South region and 13.4 SEER2 in the North region, with higher efficiency replacements (e.g., SEER2 15) applied where applicable. • Replacement of ducted electric resistance furnaces with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency. In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for air conditioning but not heating, the non-ducted heating systems are also replaced: • Replacement of fuel boilers with a minimum of 80% - 83% AFUE (90% AFUE for like-for-like replacements at higher efficiency). • Replacement of non-ducted electric resistance heating systems (boiler, baseboard, wall furnace) with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency. In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for heating but not central air conditioning, the non-ducted air co

metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — Upgrade Summary

furnace) with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency. In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for heating but not central air conditioning, the non-ducted air co

nditioning systems are also replaced: • Replacement of room ACs with models meeting an EER of 12.0. |
| Applicability      | This upgrade applies to all dwelling units that have existing ductwork and a heating fuel that is natural gas, electricity, fuel oil, or propane. For consistency with other upgrades, it excludes any homes that do not have existing ductwork, do not use heating, or that heat with wood. It applies to about 5% of homes that have non-ducted heating (electric resistance baseboard, boilers, or wall/floor furnaces) but have ducts used for air conditioning. This includes a small number (<1%) of multifamily dwelling units that have a whole-building shared heating system but that have individual ducted air conditioning systems serving each unit. It covers a wide range of heating technologies (furnaces, boilers, electric resistance) and cooling technologies (central AC, heat pumps, room ACs). With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 75.2% of the existing dwelling units.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1 Technology Summary

This work evaluates a reference case where existing space heating and air conditioning equipment in homes with existing ductwork is upgraded to the minimum efficiency available (circa 2025) ⎯ or like-for-like replacements for above-minimum equipment -across the U.S. residential building stock. The purpose of this reference case is to provide a comparison point for other measures and packages that simulate heating and cooling equipment replacements at the end of the equipment 's useful life (also called 'at wear out'). This enables estimates of incremental energy savings and incremental upfront cost of measures compared to an assumed alternative.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

Fuel-fired furnaces -including propane, fuel oil, and natural gas -are used to heat indoor environments. Fuel ignites in the burner, and the flame heats a metal heat exchanger. A blower fan moves air over the heat exchangers, which warms the air. Most furnaces use ducts to distribute heat, while combustion exhaust is vented outside. In comparison, gravity furnaces do exist but are older and not as common; as such in this study, we only model forced air furnaces.

Fuel-fired wall or floor furnaces are directly installed within walls or floors to serve one or a few rooms. They burn natural gas, propane, or fuel oil in a combustion chamber, transferring heat through a heat exchanger. Heated air rises by convection into occupied spaces, and combustion byproducts should be vented outside the dwelling. Unlike central furnaces, they typically do not use ducts and instead provide localized heating.

Electric furnaces use resistance heating elements rather than combustion to produce heat. When an electric current passes through the elements, they generate heat, which is transferred to air moving across them. A blower fan distributes this heated air through ducts.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

to produce heat. When an electric current passes through the elements, they generate heat, which is transferred to air moving across them. A blower fan distributes this heated air through ducts.

Fuel boilers heat water instead of air. Natural gas, propane, or fuel oil is burned in a combustion chamber to heat water. The hot water (or steam in some systems) is then circulated through pipes to radiators, baseboard heaters, or radiant floor systems. Boilers can provide both space heating and domestic hot water. Combustion gases are vented outside the building.

Central air conditioners typically use the same duct network as the heating system. They remove heat from buildings by operating a vapor-compression cycle: an outdoor unit compresses and condenses refrigerant, which then absorbs heat from indoor air as it passes over an evaporator coil. A blower fan circulates the cooled air through the ducts, and the absorbed heat is expelled outdoors; system efficiency is measured by the seasonal energy efficiency ratio, version 2 (SEER2), with higher ratings indicating more efficient cooling.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

the ducts, and the absorbed heat is expelled outdoors; system efficiency is measured by the seasonal energy efficiency ratio, version 2 (SEER2), with higher ratings indicating more efficient cooling.

Room air conditioners are self-contained cooling units designed to cool a single room or small area. They are typically mounted in windows or through walls and operate using a vaporcompression cycle: they draw in warm indoor air, cool it by passing it over the evaporator coil, return it to the room, and expel heat outside. Room air conditioners are rated by their combined energy efficiency ratio (CEER).

Air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) provide both heating and cooling using a reversible vaporcompression cycle. In cooling mode, they operate like a central air conditioner, transferring heat from indoors to outdoors, but in heating mode, the cycle reverses and they extract heat from outdoor air and deliver it indoors. Even at cold temperatures, heat pumps can capture usable energy from the outdoor air. Distribution is typically through the same duct network used for cooling, though ductless systems deliver conditioned air directly to rooms. Efficiency is rated using heating seasonal performance factor, version 2 (HSPF2) for heating and SEER2 for cooling.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.2  Sizing

HVAC sizing is automatic across all HVAC system types and sizes following the ACCA Manual J/S methodology. ACCA Manual J (ACCA, 2024) provides guidelines for calculating the design heating and cooling loads in a building, and ACCA Manual S (ACCA, 2014) provides a guide for selecting the size of residential HVAC systems to meet those loads. For a full description of sizing and system selection for ASHPs, reference the Dual Fuel Heat Pump System documentation (White et al. 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3  Efficiency

Efficiency is rated using annual fuel utilization efficiency (AFUE) for natural gas furnaces, SEER2 for air conditioning systems, HSPF2 for heat pumps, CEER for room air conditioners. Importantly, SEER2 and HSPF2 include fan energy but AFUE does not.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

AFUE is the standard rated efficiency for how efficiently a furnace converts fuel into heat at rated conditions. The higher the AFUE rating, the more efficient the system is at converting fuel into usable heat. Energy lost through exhaust gases, radiation, and other components decreases efficiency.

AFUE is the total annual heat output divided by the total annual fuel input -on a scale of 0% to 100%. Note that unlike SEER2 and HSPF2, AFUE does not include the electricity used by the air handler blower, combustion blower, ignition system, or controls. ANSI/ASHRAE 103-2022 provides a procedure for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022).

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.1 Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency

for determining AFUE of residential central furnaces and boilers, which is a test cycle structured to simulate ordinary heating conditions throughout the year -including seasons (ANSI/ASHRAE 2022).

' Residential furnaces manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16) must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 430.32 ' (DOE 2025b). 80% AFUE furnaces are the minimum for nonweatherized gas furnaces (i.e., natural gas and propane) manufactured from 2015 through Dec. 18, 2028. After Dec. 18, 2028, the minimum is 95% AFUE. If an investigator would like to understand equipment standard changes over time, a useful approach could blend data from this study with data from the Propane and Fuel Oil Furnaces upgrade (Stenger et al. 2026b) as well as the Natural Gas Furnaces upgrade (Stenger et al. 2026a), both of which model 95% AFUE for propane and natural gas furnaces, respectively. In this study, we model an 80% AFUE as minimum efficiency natural gas furnace when existing efficiency is rated lower than 80% AFUE, and a like-for-like replacement when the existing natural gas furnace is rated above 80% AFUE.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.2  Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio

CEER is the standard rated efficiency for room air conditioners under specific test conditions. It measures how effectively the unit converts electrical energy into cooling capacity; the higher the CEER rating, the more efficient the system.

CEER is defined as the ratio of the steady-state cooling capacity (i.e., Btu/hr) to the electrical power input (i.e., kW) under rated conditions (Code of Federal Regulations 2025). Because it is measured at a single set of conditions, energy efficiency ratio (EER) provides a snapshot of performance rather than a seasonal metric. For portable and room air conditioners, CEER accounts for standby and off-mode power consumption, but has different test procedures.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.3 Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, Version 2

SEER2 is a metric for representing the cooling efficiency of central air conditioners and heat pumps as they would perform over an entire cooling season. It is defined as the total cooling output (in British thermal units, Btu) during a typical cooling season divided by the total electrical energy input, including the blower fan energy (in watt-hours) consumed over that same period. Higher SEER2 values indicate more efficient systems, since they deliver more cooling per unit of electricity. Energy losses due to on-off cycling, blower waste heat, and refrigerant line heat transfer all reduce SEER2.

SEER2 is determined under standardized test conditions specified by ANSI/AHRI Standard 210/240-2024 (and DOE's Appendix M1), which simulates a range of outdoor temperatures and indoor loads to approximate real-world operation throughout the cooling season. Ratings typically range from about 13 SEER2 for older equipment up to 26 SEER2 for more advanced centrally ducted air-conditioner systems, and up to 35.1 SEER2 for non-ducted systems.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.3 Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, Version 2

cooling season. Ratings typically range from about 13 SEER2 for older equipment up to 26 SEER2 for more advanced centrally ducted air-conditioner systems, and up to 35.1 SEER2 for non-ducted systems.

In this study, dwellings with existing air-conditioning systems below the regional minimums are modeled with central air conditioners or heat pumps rated at 14.3 SEER2 in the South region and 13.4 SEER2 in the North region, and with central ASHPs rated at 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2. For dwellings whose current cooling equipment already meets or exceeds these thresholds, we simulate a like-for-like replacement at the higher efficiency.

The South region includes the following states: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawai ' i, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. The North region includes all states not listed in the South region.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
metadata.measure_name: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 1.3.4  Heating Seasonal Performance Factor, Version 2

HSPF2 is a rating representing the heating efficiency of heat pumps as they perform over an entire heating season. It is defined as the total heating output (in Btu) during a typical heating season divided by the total electrical energy input, including the energy consumed by the indoor blower fan (in watt-hours) and outdoor unit over that same period. Higher HSPF2 indicates more efficient systems, since they deliver more heating per unit of electricity. Factors such as on-off cycling, coil defrost cycles, and standby power consumption can reduce HSPF2.

HSPF2 is determined under standardized test conditions, which simulate a range of outdoor temperature and part-load conditions to approximate real-world performance throughout the heating season. Residential central air conditioning heat pumps manufactured and distributed in commerce, as defined by 42 U.S.C. 6291(16), must meet the energy conservation standards specified in the Code of Federal Regulations at 10 CFR 420.32(c)(5) (DOE 2025a).

In this study, dwellings with existing systems below the regional minimums are modeled with ducted heat pumps rated at 7.5 HSPF2. For dwellings whose current heating equipment already meets or exceeds these thresholds, we simulate a like-for-like replacement at the higher efficiency.

metadata.doc_title: Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 2 Applicability

This upgrade replaces space heating and cooling equipment in homes with existing ductwork with units that meet minimum efficiency standards reflective of circa-2025 requirements. It includes:

- Replacement of ducted fuel furnaces with a minimum of 80% -83% AFUE (92.5% AFUE for like-for-like replacements at higher efficiency).
- Replacement of air-source heat pumps with equipment rated at 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2.
- Replacement of central air conditioners (ACs) with units rated at 14.3 SEER2 in the South region and 13.4 SEER2 in the North region, with higher efficiency replacements (e.g., SEER2 15) applied where applicable.
- Replacement of ducted electric resistance furnaces with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency.

In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for air conditioning but not heating, the nonducted heating systems are also replaced:

- Replacement of fuel boilers with a minimum of 80% -83% AFUE (90% AFUE for likefor-like replacements at higher efficiency).
- Replacement of non-ducted electric resistance heating systems (boiler, baseboard, wall furnace) with baseline 100% efficiency electric options for costing consistency.

In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for heating but not central air conditioning, the non-ducted air conditioning systems are also replaced:

electric options for costing consistency.

In homes that have existing ductwork that is used for heating but not central air conditioning, the non-ducted air conditioning systems are also replaced:

- Replacement of room ACs with models meeting an EER of 12.0.

Where a dwelling 's existing cooling equipment already meets or exceeds these ratings, a like -for-like replacement at the higher efficiency is modeled instead. No changes to building infiltration or duct losses are assumed as part of the upgrades.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 3 Modeling Approach

This section outlines how the upgrade is modeled in ResStock using the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. In this scenario, dwellings meeting the applicability logic receive the upgrade. ResStock uses probabilistic sampling logic based on national housing stock data to assign each dwelling unit a set of baseline building characteristics, including existing heating fuel, system type, and duct configuration. Ducts remain unchanged when heating and cooling systems are upgraded, which can yield inefficiencies. The model assumes consistent operation patterns across households and scales furnace capacity based on heating load requirements determined by building envelope characteristics and climate zone. While equipment brand and installation quality are not modeled explicitly, the total heating energy demand and fuel consumption are recalculated to reflect the standardized furnace and fuel use. This scenario represents a reference case where all space heating and air conditioning equipment is upgraded to the minimum efficiency available (or like-for-like replacements for above-minimum equipment) across the U.S. residential building stock. The purpose of this reference case is to provide a comparison point for other measures and packages that simulate heating and cooling equipment replacements at the end of the equipment's useful life (also called 'at wear out'). This enables estimates of inc

point for other measures and packages that simulate heating and cooling equipment replacements at the end of the equipment's useful life (also called 'at wear out'). This enables estimates of inc

remental energy savings and incremental upfront cost of measures compared to an assumed alternative.

These probability distributions are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the ASHPs upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 model building simulation (i.e., models), 413,611 models are applicable for the reference space heating and air conditioning upgrade (75.2%). For the 413,611 models, the total baseline consumption is 2.87 trillion kWh annually, and after the upgrade is 2.80 trillion kWh, a 2% savings. Figure 6 shows the total site energy consumption between the baseline and upgrade.

Figure 6. Annual total site energy consumption for housing stock

![Image](96636_images/image_000007_364a491fc6506078058f88e1f374db2b5c739884bfc74818a0914c13e178f38e.png)

Figure 7. Annual energy consumption by HVAC heating type and fuel end use

![Image](96636_images/image_000008_c04c8c01ea88059b7267c2b82a1fdca1d3b42cde14a169f2080af53a3d168ada.png)

Cooling from electricity in ducted heating systems accounts for 42,000 GWh of energy reduction, the greatest energy reduction after the upgrade; in comparison, heating from natural gas in ducted heating systems was reduced by 6,000 GWh. Cooling fans and pumps (i.e., air handler fan energy) also yielded 6,400 GWh in energy savings, whereas heating fans and pumps yielded 1,300 GWh in energy savings. Energy savings from fans and pumps are primarily a result of more advanced motors and controls.

text:
Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025 — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

6,400 GWh in energy savings, whereas heating fans and pumps yielded 1,300 GWh in energy savings. Energy savings from fans and pumps are primarily a result of more advanced motors and controls.

Given that this is a reference case and relatively few HVAC systems are below minimum efficiency, only modest energy savings are expected: 4% for electricity-heated homes, 2% for natural gas, 3% for fuel oil, and 1% for propane.

Figure 8 shows average dwelling annual energy consumption by HVAC cooling efficiency, fuels, and end uses.

Figure 8. Average annual energy consumption per dwelling by HVAC cooling efficiency

![Image](96636_images/image_000009_709b301bf1a003d6cfeb91b8bba67e32331dc5a16fc3e7c04c86db8566c5ec6e.png)

On average, dwellings upgraded from an ' AC, SEER 8 ' cooling system to the minimum efficiency resulted in 2,900 kWh in energy savings, the largest average savings when segmented by HVAC cooling efficiency. In contrast, ' AC, SEER 15 ' shows 107 kWh in average perdwelling annual energy savings -all sourced from heating end uses and indicating efficiency gains in heating systems rather than cooling systems. Please note that the central AC cooling efficiencies are measured in SEER1 as the baseline condition. Conversion to SEER2 in the baseline condition may be a feature in future versions of ResStock outputs.

The upgrade can result in a total of $8.49 billion in energy bill savings when applied across the housing stock. Most savings would occur from electricity bills, as shown in Figure 12.

text:
Attic Floor Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna (2025) [1]. Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project [2].

text:
Attic Floor Insulation — Executive Summary

building stock model is available in Reyna (2025) [1]. Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project [2].

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: attic floor insulation for unfinished attics.

This upgrade demonstrated 2.2% total site energy savings (76 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 8). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 3.7% stock natural gas heating savings (42 TWh)
- 4.0% stock electricity heating savings (10 TWh)
- 2.4% stock electricity cooling savings (9.4 TWh).
