text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual

This section presents selected metrics before and after the gas tankless water heater upgrade and percent change. As expected, the total delivered hot water is higher in colder climates; this is because the mains water is colder, so more energy is needed to deliver the same amount of hot water. The amount of delivered hot water remains the same before and after the upgrade, indicating that both the baseline and the upgrade do not have any unmet water heating demand.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Water Heater
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Water Heater

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual

amount of hot water. The amount of delivered hot water remains the same before and after the upgrade, indicating that both the baseline and the upgrade do not have any unmet water heating demand.

The upgrade led to a significant reduction in water heating energy use across all locations. Water heater energy consumption was reduced by 60%, 64%, and 38% for the dwellings in Hawai'i, California, and Alaska, respectively. The percent reduction is lower for the Alaska dwelling sample than Hawai'i and California due to differences in their hot water demand. For Hawai'i and California, hot water demand is low, at 21.3 and 16 gal/day, respectively, due to the low occupant count. As a result, the overall efficiency of the baseline storage water heaters is very low, and more than half of the savings (i.e., 30%+) comes from eliminating the tank loss of the storage water heaters. On the other hand, the Alaska sample has a hot water demand that is three to four times higher than the other samples, at 55.5 gal/day. Consequently, the energy savings are primarily driven by the efficiency gain for the burner (~30%) as the tank-loss-related savings (8%) are overshadowed in comparison.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Water Heater
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Water Heater

Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual

samples, at 55.5 gal/day. Consequently, the energy savings are primarily driven by the efficiency gain for the burner (~30%) as the tank-loss-related savings (8%) are overshadowed in comparison.

The overall efficiency of the water heater is provided by the annual average efficiency, calculated as the ratio of the delivered hot water to the energy consumption for the hot water. As show in Table 7, the overall efficiency of the tankless water heater upgrade is 90% for all three samples, indicating that it does not vary by climate zone or hot water demand. This is because ResStock assumes a constant amount of cycling losses regardless of the amount and timing of hot water use. In practice, lower-use homes could have more cycling losses (Bohac, Schoenbauer, Hewett, Lobenstein, & Butcher, 2010); thus, the performance and energy savings potential of the gas tankless water heater upgrade could be overestimated, particularly for lowdemand households.

Figure 1 presents the breakdown of the modeled annual site energy consumption of the sample dwellings before and after the high-efficiency natural gas tankless water heater upgrade. The upgrade slightly increases the space heating energy consumption and reduces the cooling energy consumption by eliminating the tank loss of the baseline storage water heater from the conditioned space. This effect did not apply to the California sample because both its water heating and space heating are outside the apartment unit. In Hawai'i, space cooling energy decreased by 4%. In Alaska, space heating energy consumption increased by only 0.3% because the water heater is located in the unconditioned attached garage, which indirectly influences the thermal envelope.

The Alaska sample is the only dwelling with an atmospheric flue in the baseline to vent both the water heater and the boiler. Despite the high-efficiency water heater upgrade, it did not remove the vent for that sample because of the baseline low-efficiency boiler. The upgrade is assumed to remove the vent only when the existing space heating system has an efficiency at or exceeding

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time Series

Section 4.1.1 shows that for the dwelling samples, the high-efficiency natural gas tankless water heater upgrade primarily affects the water heater energy consumption, with no or small changes in other end uses. So, this section analyzes only the 15-minute time-series data of the water heater energy consumption for the three example units, as illustrated in Figure 2. The day Jan. 2, 2018, is selected as a representative day for this analysis.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Water Heater
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Water Heater

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time Series

15-minute time-series data of the water heater energy consumption for the three example units, as illustrated in Figure 2. The day Jan. 2, 2018, is selected as a representative day for this analysis.

In all three locations, upgrading to a high-efficiency natural gas tankless water heater reduces the hot water load profile compared to the baseline natural gas storage water heaters. Because the upgrade does not contain any tank loss, its profile represents the actual hot water draw pattern. On the other hand, the incumbent storage water heater periodically cycles on to offset the standby losses and to maintain the tank temperature, creating frequent and sharp peaks approximately 2 hours apart throughout the day. Actual gas storage water heaters might cycle on for a longer duration but less frequently due to a larger deadband on real products than what is assumed in the ResStock model, which still requires the same amount of gas annually to offset the standby losses. After the upgrade, energy use is substantially lower because there are no standby losses associated with keeping a tank of water hot. In Alaska, this day has much more hot water use than the other scenarios, and as a result, the baseline includes extended periods of high energy use, peaking at more than 7 kWh per 15 minutes between 8 a.m. and 12 p.m. The upgrade reduces the peak to 5.7 kWh per 15 minutes, representing a 20% reduction.

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.2.1  Annual Energy

By applying a high-efficiency tankless natural gas water heater to all homes eligible for such an upgrade-55.7% of the housing stock-the modeled overnight savings potential is estimated to be nearly 118 TWh in total site energy, with 60% of the savings from natural gas and 36% from electricity, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 4-Figure 8 present the measure impacts for the upgraded and occupied dwellings only, which represent 50% of the stock. Vacant units are excluded because they do not have occupant-driven consumption to illustrate realistic energy savings.

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Water Heater
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Water Heater

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.2.1  Annual Energy

for the upgraded and occupied dwellings only, which represent 50% of the stock. Vacant units are excluded because they do not have occupant-driven consumption to illustrate realistic energy savings.

Figure 4 compares the modeled energy end use breakdown of the average home before and after the water heater upgrade. The modeled average energy savings is 1,560 kWh per year, or 5.1% of the total site energy consumption. The savings primarily come from hot water energy reduction, with the electricity, propane, and fuel oil used for hot water reduced to zero due to the fuel switching and the natural gas for hot water reduced by 42% due to replacing the existing gas water heaters with more efficient models. This means that the overall savings from switching all the natural gas storage water heaters (76%) in the housing stock to higher-efficiency condensing gas tankless water heaters more than offsets the natural gas increase from converting the rest of the water heaters (24%)-which are electric resistance, propane, and fuel oil water heaters-to natural gas. This highlights the energy efficiency potential for gas tankless water heater adoption at scale, although the technology does not lead to energy savings for all the dwelling units, as shown in the next few figures.

On average, the gas water heater upgrade slightly decreased space cooling and space heating. Decreasing space heating can be attributed to the average being skewed by a handful of dwelling units with large space heating savings from the upgrade. The impact of the upgrade on space heating can be twofold and in opposite directions. First, space heating slightly increases when the upgrade removes the tank loss from the incumbent water heater located in a conditioned space or other spaces adjacent to the thermal envelope, such as a garage. Most dwellings have this impact, and it explains why most gas-heated dwellings have a net increase in space heating gas energy after the upgrade, as shown in Figure 5. Second, when the upgrade removes the atmospheric flue vent from the conditioned space, infiltration is reduced, and space heating and cooling decrease. This applies to dwellings whose water heater has an atmospheric flue vent in the conditioned space, but their heating system does not, either because it is high efficiency, with an AFUE of at least 89%, or it is located outside the conditioned space. In Figure 5, dwellings to the right of the y-axis have net gas heating savings because they have one such heating system.

Figure 6 compares the range of modeled energy savings by the baseline water heater fuel type. All fuel-based water heaters see energy savings from the upgrade that are primarily due to the efficiency gain. More than half of the electric (resistance) water heaters have a small net increase in total site energy consumption that is primarily due to an increase in space heating. Because the electric resistance water heaters are similar in overall efficiency (0.92-0.99 EF, depending on type) to the condensing gas tankless water heater upgrade (0.98 UEF), the impact of the upgrade is more dependent on the secondary effect on heating, ventilation, and air conditioning. Additionally, unlike with fuel water heaters, replacing electric water heaters does not change any existing flue vent for the heating system, so space heating will either increase or stay the same.

Across climate zones, absolute energy savings from the upgrade generally increase with colder climates, where the mains water temperature is lower, and therefore the overall water heating energy demand is higher when holding the hot water usage constant. But in relative terms, the energy savings do not significantly vary, with the median percent savings between 4% and 9%, as shown in Figure 7. This is because the modeled water heater efficiency stays constant at 90% regardless of hot water usage or temperature rise, as shown in Section 4.1.  When both the total energy and energy savings increase in a similar proportion with climate zone, the resultant percent change stays relatively the same.

Similarly, the variation in the median percent energy savings across the number of occupants in a household is not very substantial, as shown in Figure 8, because both the hot water use and the total energy consumption are correlated with household size. The range of relative savings is higher for smaller households because their total energy consumption can more significantly vary with the ownership of appliances in the smaller dwelling units. text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.2.2  Stock Aggregated Time-Series Impact

To illustrate the impact of the natural gas tankless water heater measure on the aggregated load profile, Figure 9 presents the modeled total residential stock electricity profile before and after the measure for Hawai'i, California, and Alaska during their respective peak days in 2018. The measure only slightly reduced the system electric peak across the three states because it replaces some electric resistance water heating with gas. For Hawai'i, the upgrade reduced the electric peak on Sept. 30, 2018, 16:30:00 local time, from 0.78 GW by 2.0%. For California, the upgrade reduced the electric peak on July 7, 2018, 17:00:00 local time, from 32.17 GW by 1.5%. For Alaska, the upgrade reduced the electric peak on Feb. 3, 2018, 19:45:00 local time, from 0.43 GW by 0.7%. This measure does not significantly impact the electric system load shape because on average only one in three homes with an electric resistance water heater has access to natural gas, and they are fuel switched in the measure, as shown in Table 3.

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.3  Stock Energy Utility Bill Impacts

The modeled overnight energy utility bill savings potential is $10 billion from the highefficiency natural gas tankless water heater upgrade, with 64% of the savings from electricity and 31% from natural gas, as shown in Figure 10. This is calculated using 2024 state-average utility rates and by applying the natural gas tankless water heater to all homes eligible for such an upgrade, which is estimated to be 55.7% of the housing stock. When downselected to occupied and upgraded dwellings (50% of the stock), the average utility cost savings from the upgrade is $136 per year, or 4.9% of the total annual average energy bills.

On average, 66% of the energy bill savings comes from electricity, which is attributed to only 36% of the total energy savings. In comparison, natural gas represents 29% of the bill savings but 60% of the energy reduction. Because natural gas is the cheapest energy source per unit of site energy in most places analyzed, bill savings are generally higher when switching from electric, propane, or fuel oil water heaters and lower when switching from natural gas water heaters, as shown in Figure 11 and Figure 11. Overall, less than 0.1% of the applicable dwelling units are estimated to see a net bill increase from the water heater upgrade, while 4.2% are expected to see a net increase in site energy consumption.

Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.4  Electrical Panel Constraints

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025).

metadata.doc_title: Natural Gas Water Heater
metadata.measure_name: Natural Gas Water Heater

text:
Natural Gas Water Heater — 4.4  Electrical Panel Constraints

has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al., 2025).

Switching to a gas water heater generally does not lead to an electrical panel constraint because it does not add new electric load or circuit to the electrical panel. Gas water heaters can be plugged into an existing 120V circuit (which is assumed to be a dedicated outlet if one is required by local amendments to the NEC). They are not considered an electrical load when sizing the electrical panel. Instead, this measure can reduce the total connected load and the number of dedicated circuits when the incumbent water heater being switched out is electric, thus freeing up capacity and breaker space. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect preexisting conditions, as this measure does not worsen them. 2.3% of the existing panels are estimated to already exceed capacity based on code. Pre-existing capacity constraints are an artifact of the panel modeling process, in which panel service ratings are estimated from selected housing variables rather than detailed inventory data. While anecdotal evidence suggests these constraints occur in practice - manifesting as flickering lights or tripping breakers - the lack of empirical data prevents us from confirming their prevalence.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna (2025) [1]. Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project [2].

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: advanced air sealing upgrade.

The advanced air sealing upgrade demonstrated 16% modeled total site energy savings (508 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (see Figure 8 for details). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 30% stock natural gas heating savings (318 TWh)
- 27% stock electricity heating savings (64 TWh)
- 9% stock electricity cooling savings (27 TWh).

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 1 Technology Summary

Air sealing is designed to reduce unwanted air leakage through a home's building envelope by sealing gaps and cracks. This helps prevent conditioned indoor air from escaping, and outdoor air, moisture, dust, and pollutants from entering. The result is lower energy use for heating and cooling equipment, and often improved indoor comfort, better indoor air quality, and building durability. This section provides an overview of common air sealing methods and references applicable building codes that set air leakage targets by climate zone. These specifications inform the air leakage rate included in this measure upgrade.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

Air sealing is a method used to reduce the amount of unwanted air that leaks in and out of a building through small gaps, cracks, and openings in the walls, floors, ceilings, and around windows and doors. These leaks allow outside air to enter the home and conditioned air to escape, which can lead to higher energy bills, drafts, uneven temperatures, indoor air quality concerns, and moisture issues [3], [4]. Studies show that air leakage can account for up to 30% of a home's heating and cooling costs [5]. By sealing these gaps, air sealing helps lower energy use, improves comfort by reducing drafts, supports better indoor air quality by keeping pollutants and allergens out, and protects the building's structure by reducing moisture intrusion [4]. Common air sealing techniques include: weatherstripping around doors and operable windows; caulking around stationary components such as window frames, baseboards, and wall penetrations; foam sealants or spray foam for larger gaps around plumbing penetrations, recessed lighting, and attic hatches; and airtight electrical boxes or gaskets around outlets and switches [3], [6]. In new construction, house wrap (a breathable material installed under exterior siding) is often used to limit air infiltration while allowing moisture to escape. In most climates, vapor retarders may be installed to manage indoor moisture and prevent condensation w

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

The 2024 International Energy Conservation Code (IECC) establishes maximum allowable air leakage rates for residential buildings, which are defined in terms of air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50). These infiltration rates vary across the U.S. climate zones. These limits reflect the need to balance air leakage reduction with adequate ventilation. Excessive air sealing in existing homes can reduce natural ventilation and contribute to indoor air quality and moisturerelated issues, particularly when mechanical ventilation is not present.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

Excessive air sealing in existing homes can reduce natural ventilation and contribute to indoor air quality and moisturerelated issues, particularly when mechanical ventilation is not present.

In some cases, air leakage is also expressed as CFM50 (cubic feet per minute at 50 pascals), which quantifies the total airflow through leaks, whereas ACH50 normalizes that leakage rate based on the volume of the home [8]. CFM50 is typically used in diagnostics and audits, while ACH50 is used for code compliance and comparisons between homes of different sizes. While the IECC sets air leakage standards for new construction, the U.S. Department of Energy's Weatherization Assistance Program does not use fixed ACH50 targets for compliance. Instead, the Weatherization Assistance Program utilizes blower-door diagnostics to identify leaks and set reduction goals based on pre-retrofit ACH50 levels. This approach helps avoid excessive air sealing in existing homes, where further reductions in air leakage may require consideration of mechanical ventilation to maintain adequate indoor air quality.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 2 Applicability

To identify which dwelling units qualify for advanced air sealing upgrades, the 2024 IECC air leakage thresholds for new construction (Table 2) are used to exclude units that already meet or exceed current standards. If an existing home's infiltration rate is below the IECC threshold, additional sealing using conventional techniques is unlikely t o yield significant improvements. Empirical results from

Table 3 are provided as case studies by climate zone. For example, data from a California study informs climate zone 3, while a Minnesota study informs zone 6. Because IECC zones reflect shared weather patterns and building practices, results from one state are assumed to represent conditions across the entire zone. Where no study exists for a specific zone, data from a nearby or similar zone are used. For example, Florida (zone 2) data is applied to zones 1 and 2. This zone-binning approach is consistent with IECC 2024's approach to climate zone binning.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 3 Modeling Approach

This section details how the upgrade measure is functionally modeled via ResStock into OpenStudio-HPXML. ResStock models residential air infiltration values expressed as ACH50. Each dwelling unit in the ResStock dataset is assigned an existing ACH50 value based on housing stock characteristics, informed by the Residential Diagnostics Database (ResDB). ResStock integrates this information using probabilistic sampling logic to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock. These infiltration rates are dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. In ResStock, the current infiltration values are based on single-family detached blower door tests in units of ACH50. For single-family detached homes, the ACH50 values reflect total leakage to the outdoors, and buffer zones such as unconditioned attics, crawlspaces, and garages. However, for multifamily and single-family attached units, ResStock models leakage as total unit air leakage, which includes airflow to both the exterior and adjacent units. To estimate only the leakage to the exterior, the model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exteriorfacing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs.

Advanced Air Sealing — 3 Modeling Approach

model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exteriorfacing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs.

In this work, b uildings with infiltration rates ≥6 ACH 50 are eligible for an upgrade to 5 ACH50. This threshold serves as a nationally consistent benchmark across the housing stock. In practice, some new construction households in climate zones (e.g., climate zones 3 -5) require tighter envelopes such as 3 ACH50 or better (Table 2), and many older or leakier homes may only feasibly reach ~5 ACH50 through air sealing (

Table 3). In practice, this infiltration level is typically achieved through blower-door-guided air sealing of attics, crawlspaces, rim joists, and other leakage pathways. Previous studies have shown that such practices can bring homes that start above 6 ACH50 down to or below the 5 ACH50 threshold [7] [13]. Therefore, 5 ACH50 provides a balanced and conservative target that represents a meaningful improvement for existing homes, while still allowing comparability across climate zones and building types.

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide [1]. Advanced air sealing does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the contiguous U.S. residential building stock. These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ® and EnergyPlus ® through the use of an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2024 Release 2 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the infiltration upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are taken care of in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — Default Inputs from OpenStudio-HPXML for Infiltration Upgrade

The ResStock inputs in the table above are sent to OS-HPXML. Any values that are not specified by ResStock are calculated using the defaults in the BuildResidentialHPXML OpenStudio measure based on building characteristics. These characteristics include the building ' s floor area, number of stories, vintage, ceiling height, duct locations, foundation type, and climate zone. Other characteristics include stack effect, indoor-outdoor temperature difference, wind speed, and more. In multifamily and attached buildings, OS-HPXML assumes that some air leakage occurs between units rather than solely to the outside. To account for this, the software adjusts total infiltration based on the portion of the building envelope that is exposed to the exterior. More details of the infiltration model and default values can be found in the Alberta Air Infiltration Model (AIM-2) [16].

Advanced Air Sealing — 4.1  Single Model Results

This section analyzes three example dwelling units that received advanced air sealing upgrades. Prior to the upgrades, each unit had air leakage rate of 50 ACH50 (Unit 1), 25 ACH50 (Unit 2), and 6 ACH50 (Unit 3). The upgrade reduced air leakage to 5 ACH50 for all units. The units are in Hawai ' i (climate zone 1A), Texas (climate zone 3A), and Alaska (climate zone 8AK). These represent a range of climate conditions. The floor area, heating setpoint, and cooling setpoint of these three dwelling units are different, so baseline performance across units is not comparable. This section focuses solely on the percentage energy reduction achieved by the advanced air sealing. The modeled annual energy consumption of the three example dwelling units before and after advanced air sealing upgrades are described below.

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 modeled units (i.e., the total number of units modeled in the ResStock 2025.1 dataset to represent the national building stock), 507,100 units are applicable for the advanced air sealing upgrade (92.2%). For the 507,100 applicable units, the total weighted baseline modeled site energy consumption is 3,140 TWh per year. After applying the air sealing upgrade, the total modeled site energy consumption was reduced to 2,632 TWh per year, a 16.2% reduction. Figure 8 shows that site energy savings from air sealing primarily come from heating and cooling related end uses, with 27.1% electricity heating savings (64.2 TWh), 29.9% natural gas heating savings (318 TWh), 7.8% electricity cooling savings (27.1 TWh), and 3.8% cooling fan and pump energy savings (2.18 GWh). Energy savings were observed only in heating and cooling, while other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged. This is because air sealing improves building performance by reducing air leakage. Thus, its impact is confined to systems that respond to indoor temperature fluctuations.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 4.3  Stock Energy Impacts

remained unchanged. This is because air sealing improves building performance by reducing air leakage. Thus, its impact is confined to systems that respond to indoor temperature fluctuations.

Site energy savings in space heating is greater than cooling. This is because the temperature difference (ΔT) between the indoor and outdoor environment is typically much smaller during the cooling season than during the heating season. This is one of the reasons why heating loads are often greater than cooling loads. For example, on a hot summer day, an indoor temperature of 72°F and an outdoor temperature of 95°F represents a ΔT of 23°F. On a cold winter day, an indoor temperature of 72°F and outdoor temperature of 25°F results in a ΔT of 47°F , approximately double the magnitude. Since the energy lost due to infiltration is directly proportional to ΔT, due to the HVAC systems conditioning the infiltrating outdoor air to the indoor setpoints, heating seasons experience higher infiltration-driven losses. This pattern aligns with typical climate conditions across the United States, where most regions have higher heating degree days than cooling degree days. Therefore, the dominant share of energy savings from advanced air sealing upgrades is expected to occur during the heating season, particularly in colder climates with leakier building envelopes and extended periods of high ΔT.

For the 507,100 applicable units, the average baseline site energy consumption is 24,386 kWh per unit per year. After the advanced air sealing upgrade, the stock average consumption is reduced to 20,440 kWh per unit per year, a 16.2% reduction (Figure 9). Similar to Section 4.2, only heating and cooling energy use decreased, while lighting, appliances, and other end uses were unaffected.

Figure 10 shows a general trend that baseline annual site energy consumption increases with higher initial infiltration rates. For instance, units with 40 ACH50 consume 14.3% more energy on average (26,929 kWh/unit/year) than those with 10 ACH50 (23,087 kWh/unit/year). As shown in Figure 11, upgrading all units to a target infiltration rate of 5 ACH50 results in the greatest energy savings for the leakiest units. For example, units starting at 40 ACH50 save 8,386 kWh/unit/year, while those at 10 ACH50 save 1,864 kWh/unit/year. This is expected, as units with higher air leakage have greater uncontrolled heat loss or gain, which increases HVAC runtime. Thus, reducing infiltration in these leakier homes improves thermal retention and reduces HVAC runtime more than in tighter units.

Figure 12 shows that across the 507,100 applicable dwelling units, older units tend to consume more site energy than newer construction. Where the units built before the 1970s typically consume over 25,000 kWh/unit/year on average, compared to around 22,000 kWh/unit/year or less for units built after the 1970s. There are a few exceptions to these trends. For instance, 1950s units have a slightly higher average baseline consumption (30,382 kWh/unit/year) than 1940s units (30,189 kWh/unit/year), which reflects variations in other building characteristics such as size, layout, or HVAC system performance. Nonetheless, older vintages consistently show the greatest absolute and relative energy savings from air sealing upgrades. As shown in Figure 13, upgrading all applicable units to a target infiltration rate of 5 ACH50 results in greater absolute energy savings for older buildings. For example, pre-1960s units save over 6,000 kWh/unit/year, while 2010s units only save 1,600 kWh/unit/year. These differences are primarily due to the higher baseline infiltration rate in older units, which offer more potential for improvement through air sealing.

The percentage savings continues to decline with newer vintages such as 15.8% for 1970s, 13.8% for 1980s, 11.2% for 1990s, 9.4% for 2000s, and 9.1% for 2010s units. These trends are driven by differences in baseline infiltration levels, as illustrated in Figure 1. Older units tend to have higher air leakage rates, which present greater opportunities for energy savings through air sealing. By improving the building enclosure, air sealing reduces uncontrolled air exchange and lowers HVAC energy demand, especially in older units.

Figure 18 shows that heating savings consistently exceed cooling savings across all zones. This is because heating tends to occur during periods with large temperature differences between indoor and outdoor air, which intensifies infiltration-driven losses. In contrast, cooling seasons are shorter, and indoor-outdoor temperature differences are smaller. Baseline infiltration also plays a key role in explaining energy savings patterns. As shown in Figure 2, many zones, such as 1A, 4C, and 5A, exhibit a wide range of initial infiltration levels, meaning some homes are leakier than others. Leakier homes benefit more from envelope tightening. This results in higher energy savings after air sealing. In contrast, tighter-construction zones like 2B and 3B have lower baseline infiltration rates and less room for improvement. This results in both lower energy consumption and more modest savings from air sealing upgrades.

Colorado is selected as a case study to analyze the aggregated time-series data. Out of all national dwelling units, 1.7% are located in Colorado. Figure 21 presents the aggregated average daily baseline energy consumption in Colorado, with February 20 identified as the day with the highest energy use. text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 5 Discussion

This study evaluates the energy impacts of an advanced air sealing upgrade that reduces infiltration to 5 ACH50 for eligible existing units (≥6 ACH50). Results show that modeled site energy savings scale with baseline infiltration level, building vintage, and climate zones. Units with higher initial leakage achieved the largest absolute energy savings. Units starting at 40 -50 ACH50 experienced the greatest reductions when tightened to 5 ACH50, while homes starting near 6 -10 ACH50 saw smaller savings. Leakier homes experience greater convective heat loss (winter) and sensible/latent heat gain (summer), so reducing infiltration has a larger marginal impact. Baseline energy trends (e.g., 40 ACH50 vs. 50 ACH50 groups) are likely driven by other correlated building characteristics such as floor area, vintage, HVAC type, and fuel mix rather than infiltration alone. However, the general relationship between leakage and savings holds across the stock.

metadata.doc_title: Advanced Air Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Advanced Air Sealing

text:
Advanced Air Sealing — 5 Discussion

building characteristics such as floor area, vintage, HVAC type, and fuel mix rather than infiltration alone. However, the general relationship between leakage and savings holds across the stock.

Site energy savings also increase with climate severity. Colder climate zones (e.g., 5A, 6A, 7A) show the highest absolute and percentage reductions because the number of heating degree days are greater than cooling degree days. Winter temperature difference is larger than summer difference and heating seasons are longer than cooling seasons. For example, a winter condition of 70°F indoors and 20°F outdoors yields a 50°F difference, while a summer condition of 75°F indoors and 95°F outdoors yields a 20°F difference. Because infiltration loads scale with temperature difference, heating savings are greater than cooling. In warm climates (e.g., 1A), annual consumption is predominately cooling, while heating is minimal or absent. Air sealing still reduces cooling loads, but percentage savings are smaller because temperature difference is modest and cooling seasons are less extreme than cold-climate heating seasons. Lastly, older homes show both higher baseline consumption and greater savings. Pre-1960 buildings show higher infiltration levels and therefore benefit more from tightening to 5 ACH50. Newer homes, especially post-2000 construction, begin closer to modern code performance and therefore show smaller savings.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (GHP). Single-stage GHPs reduce stock-level site energy consumption by 24% (Figure 18). Additional results provided below detail how savings changes for sections of the housing stock with different base heating fuel and in different climate zones, as well as the savings potential by state for both heating and cooling. Utility bills and electric panel impacts are also shown and discussed.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Accessing Results

This documentation covers the 'Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 Coefficient of Performance [COP], 18.6 Energy Efficiency Ratio [EER])' measure upgrade methodology and briefly discusses key results. All results can be accessed on the ResStock™ Open Energy Data Initiative 'End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock' data lake and on the Data Viewer at resstock.nlr.gov.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1.1 Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

Geothermal heat pumps (GHPs), 1 also known as ground-source heat pumps, provide space heating and cooling in buildings. What differentiates a GHP from other heat pump technologies is that GHPs use the naturally stable ground temperature and ability of the subsurface to store thermal energy to heat and cool a building. There are two main parts of a GHP: (1) the ground heat exchanger loop, sometimes referred to as the ground loop, which consists of a set of fluidfilled pipes buried underground that transfers heat between the ground and the heat pump, and (2) the heat pump system that distributes conditioned air (or water) to the building. During the winter, GHPs extract heat from the ground by circulating a working fluid in the ground heat exchanger. The thermal energy absorbed by the fluid is then used by the heat pump to transfer the absorbed heat to the building. During the summer, the system is reversed, using the ground as a heat sink to provide cooling to the building.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1.1 Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

the fluid is then used by the heat pump to transfer the absorbed heat to the building. During the summer, the system is reversed, using the ground as a heat sink to provide cooling to the building.

GHPs are classified by the configurations of their ground heat exchanger and heat pump. The heat pump can either be a water-to-air or a water-to-water (also called 'hydronic') system. There are four basic ground heat exchanger types: closed-loop horizontal, closed-loop vertical, closedloop surface water systems, and open-loop systems. 2 Closed-loop horizontal systems run the ground heat exchanger close to the surface in shallow trenches, which requires sufficient land available for horizontal loop installation. Closed-loop vertical systems run the ground heat exchanger in vertical boreholes and require less land area than horizontal systems. Closed-loop surface water systems use a nearby body of water as the heat exchanger in the ground heat exchanger. Open-loop systems allow the fluid in the ground heat exchanger to be exchanged with a well or body of water. In some instances, these open-loop systems require clean water and must meet local groundwater regulations. Another GHP configuration is a direct geo-exchange system, which uses the refrigerant lines of the heat pump as the working fluid in the ground heat exchanger rather than a water and antifreeze (usually propylene glycol) mixture.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1.1 Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

direct geo-exchange system, which uses the refrigerant lines of the heat pump as the working fluid in the ground heat exchanger rather than a water and antifreeze (usually propylene glycol) mixture.

By rejecting or absorbing thermal energy from the ground, GHPs have a relatively stable cooling and heating performance, as the ground temperature remains relatively constant throughout the year. In contrast, air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) draw thermal energy from the outdoor air. As the outdoor air temperature decreases, the ASHP has less ability to transfer heat from the air to the building. For ASHPs, this results in less efficient performance at extreme cold temperatures. To meet the heating demand when outdoor air temperatures are very low (Sergici, et al. 2023), less efficient backup electric resistance heat is generally used for ASHPs. In a situation with a large deployment of ASHPs in cold climates, the coldest hours of the year could result in large winter peak demand that utilities would have to manage (Murphy, Hagerty and Weiss 2020, Sergici, et al. 2023). GHPs could help reduce winter peak demand, as their performance is less affected by cold outdoor temperatures because they rely on stable subsurface ground temperatures. However, capital costs for GHPs are generally higher than ASHPs, in large part due to the cost associated with installing the ground heat exchanger. There are exceptions; for multifamily buildings the ground heat exchanger could be installed vertically under an existing parking lot (Lienau, Boyd and Rogers 1995). of these types can be found at https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/geothermal-heat-pumps

There are several GHP performance levels, including single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed systems.

- Single-stage GHPs operate at full capacity whenever they run, which can lead to energy inefficiencies under part-load conditions (when the system needs less than its maximum output).
- Two-stage GHPs improve upon this design by adding a second, lower-capacity stage. This allows the system to operate more efficiently during mild conditions while still having the capability to switch to full output when demand peaks.
- Variable-speed GHPs represent the most advanced option, using inverter-driven compressors and fans to continuously adjust their output in response to real-time heating and cooling needs. Unlike single-stage or two-stage systems that operate in discrete steps, variable-speed systems can modulate across a wide range of capacities. This precise control enhances energy efficiency, provides more stable indoor temperatures, reduces humidity swings, and minimizes noise from cycling.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1.2 Residential GHP Technology Review Summary

A review of GHPs in the U.S. building stock was performed as part of this work. A detailed discussion can be found in Appendix A. The review includes: (1) the number of GHP installations, where they were located, and the building types and when the homes were built; (2) the most common mechanical systems used in residential GHP installations; (3) the GHPs' heating and cooling performance; and (4) the common ground heat exchanger configurations and the frequency of installation. Key takeaways from the review are as follows:

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1.2 Residential GHP Technology Review Summary

installations; (3) the GHPs' heating and cooling performance; and (4) the common ground heat exchanger configurations and the frequency of installation. Key takeaways from the review are as follows:

- There are approximately 1.28 -2 million GHPs in the U.S. residential building stock (Gertler, Steeves and Wang 2025)
- Tennessee, North Carolina, Florida, Texas, and Alabama make up almost 40% of residential GHP installations. Almost 85% of GHPs are in the IECC 2012 (Burleyson, 2012) moist climate zones, 2A -5A. Climate zone 4A has the most GHP installations, with about 30% of total installations (U.S. EIA 2023).
- About 70% of GHP installations are in homes that were built since the 1980s and primarily are in single-family housing (U.S. EIA 2023).
- Approximately 75% of GHP installations are in new construction and 25% of GHP installations are in retrofit systems (U.S. EIA 2023).
- The most common ground heat exchanger configurations are vertical and closed-loop systems (Battocletti and Glassley 2013).
- Water-to-air heat pumps are the most common type of geothermal mechanical equipment used to deliver heating and cooling to residential buildings (Battocletti and Glassley 2013).

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.1 Applicability

The single-stage compressor, water-to-air vertical ground heat exchanger GHP upgrade measure applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to 71% of the existing residential building stock. Units that receive the GHP upgrade that do not have existing cooling systems make up 6.4%. These applicability rules are further described below.

Applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics that determine the available options and the options' details (Reyna, et al. 2025). Specifically, the 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' characteristic in ResStock is used to apply each respective heat pump option. 'HVAC Has Ducts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling. 'Heating Type' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling. 'HVAC Shared Efficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable. 'Geometry Building Type Height' describes the height and building type of the dwelling. More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna et al. 2025).

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.1.1 Exclusion of Dwellings Without Air Ducts

Dwellings without ducts are excluded from this upgrade measure because they would need to install a new ductwork system, which would increase the cost of the upgrade measure. The current modeling approach also does not have an option for a GHP hydronic (water-to-water) system (i.e., that would not require installation of a new duct system), which is roughly 22% of the stock.

High-rise (8+ stories) dwellings with shared HVAC are excluded from this upgrade measure because the outdoor units would have to be mounted directly outside the unit in the high-rise building, creating a uniquely complicated maintenance environment. 3 Due to the current unitbased multifamilty modeling approach in ResStock, these buildings are also complicated to accurately model the application of a GHP upgrade. Because these dwellings only comprise 1% of the total building stock, this housing segment was not upgraded.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.1.3 Cooling Level Increase for All Applicable Dwellings

Dwellings that are not 100% cooled by their existing AC system (e.g., room AC providing cooling for just one room of a home) will be 100% cooled by this measure upgrade. This will increase cooling energy consumption of those dwellings that were not already 100% cooled. The cooling level increase for all applicable dwellings is implemented because heat pumps in this measure upgrade will be sized to cool the entire dwelling.

Units that receive the GHP upgrade that do not have an existing cooling system make up 6.4% of the residential stock. Units with less than 100% (anywhere from 80% to 0%) of the floor area cooled make up about 33% of the stock. These units will see an increase in energy consumption because of the added service.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.1.4 Exclusion of 'Other Fuel' and 'None' Heating Fuels

Dwellings with 'Other Fuel' or 'None' heating fuels do not receive this measure upgrade because retrofits to these dwellings can lead to confusing results (e.g., false negative savings compared to baseline or installing heating in regions that do not need it) and the number of dwellings this affects is relatively small. 'Other Fuel' includes fuels like wood and coal, which are not currently represented in ResStock, so there is not an accurate baseline heating energy consumption to compare to. Additionally, there is not a large impact at scale since dwellings with 'Other Fuel' or 'None' heating fuels comprise approximately 2.9% of the total building stock. The 'Other Fuel' in ResStock is largely composed of solar heating systems. ResStock does not model solar heating systems.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.1.5 Exclusion of Low Thermal Conductivity Soils

We have chosen not to include low thermal conductivity soils in our GHP upgrade logic. In real systems, these soil conditions can significantly reduce the performance of ground heat exchangers and may require larger, more expensive loop fields to maintain system efficiency.

When we try to model these scenarios, we often run into simulation failures or unstable results. These issues make it difficult to trust the upgrade impacts, especially when scaling across a large number of homes. Additionally, soil thermal properties can vary a lot and may not be well represented in the data we have, which adds more uncertainty.

The result is that we are not applying these GHPs to units with a ground thermal conductivity of 0.5 Btu/hr-ft-F to 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-F which make up 7.6% of the total building stock based on (X. W. Liu 2016). This helps ensure the model results are reliable and representative of scenarios where GHPs are more likely to perform well in practice.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

OpenStudio-HPXML is a workflow, developed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), used for modeling residential buildings. This workflow uses the HPXML (Home Performance eXtensible Markup Language) standard for defining all the properties of a building that affect energy consumption, such as square footage, the type and efficiency of heating and cooling equipment, setpoints for heating and cooling, etc. NLR leads the development of this standard alongside a working group including a variety of industry stakeholders for determining what features are included in the standard, including updates to cover new technologies and additional inputs as appropriate. The OpenStudio-HPXML workflow uses a series of OpenStudio measures to translate an HPXML file into an EnergyPlus ®  input file to simulate the energy consumption of the building with the given inputs in a standard, repeatable way. The model outputs are time-series and annual energy consumption by end use and may also include outputs derived from energy consumption, such as utility bills. More information about the OpenStudioHPXML workflow can be found at the OpenStudio-HPXML documentation (NREL 2023).

OpenStudio-HPXML has had the ability to model GHPs for over 10 years, but the methods and assumptions it used have not been documented. More details of the approach that were maintained from the initial implementation through the current approach are contained in Appendix B.

methods and assumptions it used have not been documented. More details of the approach that were maintained from the initial implementation through the current approach are contained in Appendix B.

The GHP model implemented in OpenStudio-HPXML adds a GHP, the ground heat exchanger loop, and any associated distribution equipment (pumps and fans). Fixed sizes of equipment may be entered, but the most common use case is to 'autosize' both the ground heat exchanger and the heat pump. When autosizing, the design heating and cooling loads are calculated in accordance with Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) Manual J (ACCA 2016) and ACCA Manual S (ACCA 2014) using a routine included in OpenStudio-HPXML. ACCA Manual J is a design-day method for calculating residential building loads. The outdoor air temperature for heating and cooling is picked as the '99%' temperature, meaning only 1% of hours of the year are colder or hotter, respectively, than the design temperature. ACCA Manual S sizes the equipment based on the calculations in ACCA Manual J. Equipment that meets both heating and cooling loads, such as heat pumps, is sized based on the cooling load unless a system is installed for heating only (which is possible in the workflow but uncommon in practice). However, the ground heat exchanger is always sized based on the larger of the heating and cooling loads to ensure that sufficient length is installed to prevent substantial unmet loads in cooling-dominated climates. A high-level overview of the workflow, including the ground heat exchanger sizing routine, is shown

The length of the heat exchanger informs the number of boreholes, the depth of the boreholes, and the ground heat exchanger configuration. Finally, the g-functions are selected using a lookup table. G-functions are nondimensionalized ground temperature response functions that can be precalculated for specific ground heat exchanger geometries, and including a precalculated library within the workflow greatly reduces the simulation time required. The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the contiguous U.S. residential building stock. These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock uses the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio and EnergyPlus through the use of an HPXML file.

ResStock uses the single-unit workflow of OpenStudio-HPXML, which is designed to simulate individual residential dwelling units rather than entire buildings. In the case of multifamily or single-family attached units, this means that only a single representative unit is modeled, not the full structure or all attached units. This approach enables scalable and efficient modeling across a large housing stock, but it also affects system-level design outcomes, particularly for shared HVAC systems.

or all attached units. This approach enables scalable and efficient modeling across a large housing stock, but it also affects system-level design outcomes, particularly for shared HVAC systems.

Because each unit is treated independently in the simulation, the ground heat exchangers are sized to meet the thermal loads of that individual unit alone. This can result in smaller loop field requirements per simulation than would be observed in practice, where multiple units often share a common loop field in multifamily systems. Additionally, this simplification does not account for thermal interactions between units, shared infrastructure efficiencies, or diversity in load profiles that could impact system sizing and performance in a multi-unit building. As a result, while the ResStock framework provides valuable insights into unit-level energy use and retrofit impacts, care must be taken when interpreting or extending its GHP results to real-world multiunit or centralized system designs.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.2  Fan and Pump Assumptions

Assumptions made about the fan and pump size have an impact on the nominal efficiency of the GHP, which in turn impacts the overall energy consumption results. The EnergyPlus models require a gross COP, without any impact from the fan and pump, as an input because the fan and pump are modeled separately. Specification sheets for GHPs list the performance across a wide range of conditions, but these represent the net performance (including the impact of the heat from the fan and pump), not the gross (without the fan and pump). More information on converting net to gross can be found in (Cutler 2013). Since we are calculating the size of the GHP as part of the HVAC equipment sizing and explicitly modeling the fan and pump, we need to be able to go from the net to the gross capacity so that we do not include the impact of heat gains from these devices twice. These net-to-gross calculations need to be updated to correctly reflect the impact of both the fan heat and the pump. EnergyPlus models the fan and pump separately, so the proper model input for the coil object is the gross COP without any impact from the fan and pump.

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.3  Heat Pump Performance Curves

The curves previously used to represent the performance of the heat pump used when modeling GHP systems are based on a series of curves published in a master's thesis specifically for use in EnergyPlus (Tang 2005). However, these curves are based on an older product line, the ClimateMaster Genesis series (ClimateMaster 2023a). As this was an existing product when the thesis work was performed, these curves are based on technology that is now at least 20 years old, and the Genesis series is no longer available. To account for this, we regenerated curves for the GHP based on spec sheets for a newer product line available on the market today, the Tranquility TS series single-stage GHP (ClimateMaster 2023b), shown in Figure 2. These units are from the same U.S.-based manufacturer as was used for the previous curve derivation.

In the intervening years, the performance of this product has generally increased since the initial curves were generated, with higher performance at rated conditions as shown in Table 2. For GHPs, the curves are a function of incoming water temperature and indoor air temperature, while for an air-to-air heat pump they are a function of the indoor and outdoor air temperature. Other than difference in independent variables, the curves are identical in form. EnergyPlus also includes a single-stage version of the object, which uses curves of a different form. The variable-speed object allows inputs for one to ten different speeds. The single-stage version of the model uses only inputs for a single stage. Other models use different numbers of speeds, with details included in their measure documents.

To preserve this existing model while also adding the new model, users can choose which version of the GHP model they'd like to use. To generate the performance curves, the specification sheet for the 3-ton single-stage Tranquility TS GHP was used (see Figure 2). The 3-ton unit was selected because it is consistent with prior work, both in the thesis (Tang 2005) previously used to generate performance curves and the prior implementation in OpenStudio-HPXML. The product manual for this unit also includes correction factors for performance at different airflow rates, entering air temperatures (both wet bulb and dry bulb for cooling performance), and different concentrations of antifreeze. This allows the specification sheet to be expanded to additional points covering the full range of conditions that may occur during simulation. OpenStudio-HPXML assumes by default that a 20% mix of propylene glycol and water is used when simulating GHPs, so the antifreeze correction was applied to all curves. This is a conservative assumption that attempts to always keep the freezing point of the fluid below the ground temperatures likely to be seen in simulation, regardless of climate zone. This trades off performance for ensuring that the system will never fail due to hitting freezing conditions for the circulating fluid in a configuration with unexpectedly low ground temperatures.

Air temperature corrections account for less impactful differences in return air temperature that may occur due to difference in setpoint or ducting configuration and generally have less impact than the curves that depend on the incoming fluid temperature due to the narrower range of conditions seen. text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.4   Representing Cycling Within a Simulation Timestep

EnergyPlus allows users to enter a curve that impacts the efficiency of equipment at part load. This curve modifies the efficiency of the unit during times when the equipment only needs to run for a portion of the timestep and generally accounts for any losses that may occur due to cycling of equipment. 17 EnergyPlus uses the part load factor (which is related to the part load ratio by a user defined curve, with the specific curve used for GHPs shown in Figure 7) to determine the impact of cycling on HVAC equipment, with the efficiency directly proportional to the part load factor (which ranges from 0 -1).

A new approach to modeling cycling losses is being applied to GHPs in ResStock that differs significantly from the approach used for other residential HVAC systems such as air conditioners and ASHPs. Traditional air-to-air systems in EnergyPlus use a simplified method based on the coefficient of degradation (cd), typically derived from laboratory testing. A cd value of 0 indicates no degradation in performance due to cycling, and if the value is not known, EnergyPlus assumes a conservative default of 0.25, representing relatively high losses during part-load operation.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.section: 2.2.4   Representing Cycling Within a Simulation Timestep
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.4   Representing Cycling Within a Simulation Timestep

no degradation in performance due to cycling, and if the value is not known, EnergyPlus assumes a conservative default of 0.25, representing relatively high losses during part-load operation.

For GHPs, curves that relate the part load factor and part load ratio can therefore be used to have EnergyPlus account for any cycling losses that might occur for this equipment. For air-to-air equipment, a test to determine the coefficient of degradation (cd) is generally performed and reported. A cd value of 0 would represent no cycling losses, and if cd is not reported, a worst-case value of 0.25 is assumed. However, cd is generally not reported for water-to-air coils like those used for GHPs. Nevertheless, a European standard test, EN14825 (European Committee for Standardization (CEN) 2022) does capture the impact of cycling and allows for determining a way to model these impacts on the overall efficiency of the unit. They report a standby loss coefficient Cc. Unlike cd for air-to-air equipment, a value of 1.0 for Cc would represent no cycling losses, and a default worst-case value of 0.9 is used if it is not reported (Piechurski, Szulgowaska-Zgrzywa and Danielewicz 2018). The implication of using this new method is that GHPs may appear to suffer energy losses during cycling, especially in climates with highly unbalanced thermal loads (e.g., predominantly heating- or cooling-dominated regions) or with long swing seasons or mild climates. In these climates, part-load operation occurs more frequently, and the steeper part-load factor penalty results in a higher modeled energy use. Single-stage GHP systems are impacted more than twostage and variable-speed compressor systems.

For GHPs, additional curves can also be used to set the efficiency and capacity as a function of water flow rate and airflow rate. These curves allow performance to be corrected for airflow rates and water flow rates different from the nominal conditions. However, care must be taken that these relationships are not double-counting the impact of cycling, which is generally handled by the part load factor. While manufacturer spec sheets do report efficiency and capacity at different water and airflow rates, single-stage equipment generally operates at a single flow rate, where the exact flow rate used might vary based on the equipment size and application. Only three water flow rates are reported in the spec sheet for this unit, while a wider variety of airflow rates are reported. Curves for different water flow rates are not used, with the assumption that any cycling losses are fully captured by the part load factor and a purely single-stage pump would always be used with a single-stage GHP. Curves for airflow, however, are provided to allow for the possibility of a variable-speed fan with a single-stage system. Curves for airflow also allow for the model to account for faults that may impede airflow that can occur in real equipment over time or due to poor installation. Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.6  Ground Thermal Conductivity

With the new ability to specify the thermal conductivity of the ground, 20 better guidance is required to help users pick the right properties for their job site. However, substantial variability in ground conductivity exists by location, time of year, and depth due to differences in the local soil makeup and the presence or absence of groundwater. Many GHP manufacturers recommend performing a site-specific conductivity measurement when considering installing a GHP, with details on how to take this measurement often appearing in product manuals. The default assumption at the start of this project for ground thermal conductivity is to use a value of 1.0 Btu/h-ft-°F. However, there are resources available that can help users make an educated guess at the soil type for a location, absent a more thorough site analysis, such as (X. W. Liu 2016) or (U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) 2019). The USDA data provides conductivity by soil and moisture type. Liu (2016) provides climate zone 50 th percentile (median), 25 th percentile (lower quartile), and 75 th percentile (upper quartile) estimates based on a natural gas well dataset from Southern Methodist University (Southern Methodist University n.d.). While the Southern Methodist University natural gas well dataset is measurements of deep well data, it was the best identified dataset that provides distributions of measurements withi

The USDA dataset of soil thermal conductivities by climate zone is missing the conductivities for some climate zones, such as 7AK and 8AK. The Southern Methodist University data were combined with USDA data to get the most complete dataset possible. The USDA dataset was sorted by counties and aggregated to the respective IECC 2012 climate zones, then the upper quartile, lower quartile, and median values were computed for each of the missing climate zones. The resulting quartile values were repeated for some climate zones, as multiple sites had identical conductivity values across quartiles. For example, climate zone 1A had the same values of soil conductivity for the lower quartile, median, and the upper quartile. Climate zone 7AK had identical computed values for the lower quartile and median, and climate zone 8AK had identical computed values for the median and upper quartile. The latitudes and longitudes in the Southern Methodist University file were joined to the corresponding IECC 2012 climate zone. These data were then used to create distributions for ground conductivity by climate zone (Figure 12). Due to limitation of samples in climate zone 1A, the climate zone data were combined with samples from Florida in climate zone 2A. Discrete bins of ground conductivity values were created in ResStock. 21 These bins are [0.5-2.6] Btu/h-ft-°F with a step size of 0.3 Btu/h-ft-°F.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.2.7  Ground Heat Exchanger Sizing Methodology

Several software tools (Table 4) have emerged based on the need for a way to optimize ground heat exchanger design to minimize the size required to meet building loads and perform satisfactorily over the life span of the system. The general design approach involves the designer specifying ground thermal properties, number and arrangement of boreholes, the heat pump loads (building loads or the loads on the ground heat exchanger), and the in-borehole design of the ground heat exchanger. Design methodologies involve specifying ground heat exchanger size directly based on longer-term building loads estimation using peak design conditions (design days) or determining the ground heat exchanger size using finer time-series resolution (often from monthly or hourly building loads data). The iterative approach uses an initial ground heat exchanger size determination using borehole constraints and heat pump specifications guided by the building loads, then iteratively adjusts the ground heat exchanger size until it meets the userspecified design criteria for the maximum and minimum entering fluid temperatures.

Ground heat exchanger sizing design practices or methods are often categorized based on the time resolution into five levels from level zero to four (L0 to L4) (Spitler and Javed 2016). The level zero (L0) practice is to use rules of thumb relating ground heat exchanger length to building peak heating or cooling loads or installed equipment capacity. The L0 tools are applicable to only smaller systems and heating-only applications (J. D. Spitler 2016). However, peak heating and cooling loads are variable year to year and do not show a clear correlation with annual heating and cooling loads, resulting in highly variable entering fluid temperature values across different years. Because of this limitation, several other techniques have been developed by researchers over the years that involve 'pulses' of heating and cooling loads. Most borehole sizing methods using the pulse technique are derived from the following basic equation (Ahmadfard 2019):

During the HVAC sizing routine, no information about the monthly or hourly building loads is present. The result is that L2 through L4 approaches cannot be easily integrated into OpenStudio-HPXML. The integration of L2 to L4 approaches would require that the EnergyPlus model be simulated with an ideal load system to get an estimate of the time-series building loads. These loads would then need to get processed into the inputs necessary for the L2 to L4 approach. Then the ground heat exchanger L2 to L4 approach could be calculated. The impact of this level of integration would double the runtime of the OpenStudio-HPXML models as two annual simulations and file input/output would be required. The increase in runtime is the main reason OpenStudio-HPXML is staying with the Level 1 ground heat exchanger characterization algorithm.

Only the down-selected components of the JSON files with 10 or less boreholes are downloaded from the repository to be stored under the 'HPXMLtoOpenStudio/resources/g\_functions' module in the OpenStudio-HPXML repository (currently under development in the 'geothermal\_loop' branch at the time of writing of this report). This down-selection is done so that the live repository is not strained in terms of memory allocation for maintaining the gfunction library contents that are irrelevant at a residential dwelling unit scale. The user is given the degree of freedom to choose the specific type of configuration (U vs. L, etc.). The actual layout of boreholes within each configuration type is then chosen by OpenStudio-HPXML based on whichever layout has the minimum land area dimensions requirement at the ground level.

The documentation distributed together with the g-function library (Spitler, et al. 2021) describes the interpolation methodology that a design tool can use to iteratively adjust and choose a suitable depth for a correctly sized ground heat exchanger. Each layout within each configuration in the original g-function library provides g-functions for five different segments of depth for each borehole, for the depths of 24 m (79 ft), 48 m (157 ft), 96 m (315 ft), 192 m (630 ft) and 384 m (1,260 ft). In actual energy simulation using OpenStudio-HPXML (using the EnergyPlus simulation engine), the borehole configurations generated will have different borehole depths than one of the discrete bins provided in the OpenEI g-function library. Hence, interpolation is necessary between the values given in the g-function library for an OpenStudio-HPXML run.

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.3  Electric Panel Modeling

This section summarizes the electrical information for the ducted heat pump upgrade. Electrical information is used in ResStock to assess whether the dwelling unit's electrical panel would become space constrained or over capacity due to this upgrade.

The electric load assumption for all GHP upgrades is borrowed from another heat pump upgrade, the air-to-air heat pump without electric backup. This is a limitation of this work.

The power rating of a ducted heat pump system is the sum of the power rating of the compressor, the air handler, and any electric backup allowed to operate simultaneously, which are summarized in Table 7. The heat pump compressor power rating is estimated based on its design heating capacity using a regression equation derived from product labels. The air handler power rating is estimated from the design airflow rate and OS-HPXML assumption of fan power. The electric resistance backup power rating is directly converted from its heating capacity at an efficiency of 100%. For more information on the modeling assumptions, see the Technical Reference Document (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Table 7. Default Power Rating of Ducted Heat Pump System Components

Ducted heat pumps require at least one 208/240V circuit, each of which is protected by a doublepole breaker. The specific number of circuits depend on whether the heat pump has backup heating (dual-fuel or electric) and how its indoor and outdoor units are configured along with the backup. Table 8 summarizes the wiring configuration for ducted heat pumps assumed in ResStock 2025 Release 1. For example, a dual-fuel heat pump is assumed to have a 120V air handler on one circuit and another 240V circuit for the compressor. For a heat pump with an electric backup, the air handler is commonly 240V to allow for the strip heat to be on the same circuit. This is also the assumption in ResStock 2025 Release 1. The maximum overcurrent protection allowed per circuit is assumed to be up to 50A. Therefore, more circuits may be required for larger heat pump systems, which correspond to the use of multiple compressors and/or heat kits in real life.

Although upgrading to a heat pump replaces both the heating and cooling systems, it may require more electrical circuits and breaker space than what becomes available by removing the existing HVAC equipment. The heat pump upgrade may also add more connected load to the panel, especially when the backup is sized for emergency use. The power rating of heat pump systems is driven by their heating configuration and the presence of electric resistance backup. Therefore, homes in colder climates are more likely to face a capacity constraint when upgrading to a heat pump since a backup is often required to supplement the heat pump performance and they are more likely to have fuel heating previously.
