Electrical panel constraint modeling is added to ResStock 2025 Release 1 via OpenStudioHPXML measures in 2025. As new electric loads are added into the home during an improvement project, the electrical panel may not have enough capacity or space headroom to accommodate these new circuits. Thus, the panel may become constrained, requiring an electrical upgrade that may include upsizing the service entrance. Panel constraints can also be mitigated in other ways without the panel or service being upsized, by using load shedding devices, circuit sharing devices, or a smart panel to allow more loads to be connected; lowpower, combination, or smart appliances to reduce electric loads at the source; slim tandem breakers or subpanels for more space; and more. The panel constraint estimate from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.3  Electric Panel Modeling

from the upgrade measure allows for the costing of any potential electrical upgrade or mitigation, thus helping to capture the total cost of upgrade more holistically across the housing stock.

Panel capacity and space constraints are modeled using a service load and a breaker space calculation, respectively. The load calculation is based on 2023 National Electrical Code's loadbased method in Section 220, which guides how the load diversity should be estimated and summed to estimate the total load connected to the panel. When this total load converted to ampacity exceeds the service rating of the panel, the panel is considered capacity constrained in ResStock 2025 Release 1. Similarly, the panel is considered space constrained when the total occupied breaker space counted from the bottom-up exceeds the rated space count of the panel. The panel's capacity and space ratings are probabilistically sampled based on other housing characteristics such as heating fuel and the presence of certain appliances. Users are encouraged to reevaluate these constraint metrics according to other considerations, such as a margin of safety to account for uncertainty in the modeling process. For more details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025).

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.4 OpenStudio-HPXML Measure Inputs

This measure includes a water-to-air GHP with a single-stage compressor, variable-speed fan rated at a heating coefficient of performance (COP) of 3.8 and a rated cooling energy efficiency ratio (EER) of 18.6. The ground heat exchanger is a rectangular and vertically drilled single Utube design with enhanced grout and piping. This section will describe the inputs, sizing methodology, and modeling methodology for both the heat pump and the ground heat exchanger.

There are numerus ResStock arguments assigned in the HVAC Heating Efficiency characteristic. The arguments being specified (different than the default OpenStudio-HPXML defaults) that help distinguish these technologies from other heat pump upgrade measures are below.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.4.1  GHP Backup System

GHPs typically do not have integrated backup systems because they are designed to operate efficiently across a wide range of temperatures by leveraging the relatively constant ground temperature. The inherent stability and efficiency of GHPs eliminate the need for integrated backups in most installations. The GHP upgrade measures will not be modeled with integrated backup systems.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.4.2  GHP Sizing Methodology

The design heating and cooling loads are calculated in accordance with Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) Manual J (ACCA 2016), and the equipment size is selected based on ACCA Manual S (ACCA 2014) using a routine included in OpenStudio-HPXML. ACCA Manual J is a method for calculating residential building loads. The heating and cooling design temperatures are picked as the '99%' heating outdoor temperature and '1%' cooling outdoor temperature; that is, only 1% of hours in the year are colder or hotter, respectively, than the design temperature. ACCA Manual S uses these load calculations to select appropriately sized HVAC equipment, prioritizing cooling load to avoid issues like short cycling and poor humidity control. Using the dwelling unit's characteristics and location, the sizing strategy will be set to heat\_pump\_sizing\_methodology=MaxLoad . According to the OpenStudio-HPXML documentation:

MaxLoad : Autosized heat pumps have their nominal capacity sized based on the larger of heating/cooling design loads, while taking into account the heat pump's reduced capacity at the design temperature, such that no backup heating should be necessary.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.4.3 Grout and Pipe

For both the grout type and pipe type, HPXML provides inputs as 'standard' or 'thermally enhanced.' OpenStudio-HPXML uses grout conductivity of 0.75 Btu/h-ft-°F for standard grout (IGSPHA 2014) and 1.2 Btu/h-ft-°F 26 for thermally enhanced grout (Liu, et al. 2021). OpenStudio-HPXML uses pipe conductivity of 0.23 Btu/h-ft-°F for standard pipe and 0.4 Btu/hft-°F for thermally enhanced pipe (Liu, et al. 2021). Per conversations with industry, systems being installed today typically use thermally enhanced grout and pipes. The GHP measures use 'thermally enhanced' grout and pipe conductivities.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.4.4 Single-Stage GHP Heating and Cooling Efficiency

The compressor type significantly impacts the EER and COP of a GHP by affecting how efficiently the system transfers heat and matches the load. Two-stage and variable-speed compressors can fine-tune this process, reducing energy losses and improving heat exchange efficiency, especially under partial load conditions. Single-stage compressors use more energy through frequent on-off cycles. These extra cycles require more energy to start up and cause inefficient operation, either by overworking or underworking, leading to temperature fluctuations and unnecessary energy use.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.5 Limitations and Concerns

1. The ground heat exchanger design is based on a Level 1 method (described in Section 2.2.7), and other more detailed methods have been established. Given that this workflow explicitly targets residential buildings, and the approach is used to model multifamily buildings on a unit-by-unit basis (described in more detail below as an additional limitation and concern), ground heat exchangers are relatively small, and individual boreholes have relatively little interaction with each other. Level 1 methods are therefore more appropriate for the simpler geometries that occur in residential buildings. In addition, the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow is very explicitly designed with speed as a key priority. Annual hourly simulations of a dwelling unit are designed to take seconds rather than minutes, which enables other applications like BEopt™ and ResStock to run thousands to hundreds of thousands of simulations quickly to help analyze the optimal building design and the housing stock at a national scale. Implementing the more detailed approaches would require time-series loads, which would require running building models multiple times (once to get the loads, then again with the GHP installed), more than doubling the run time. Given these considerations, a Level 1 approach is considered appropriate for the goals of this particular workflow. Technical advisory group feedback has also indi

more than doubling the run time. Given these considerations, a Level 1 approach is considered appropriate for the goals of this particular workflow. Technical advisory group feedback has also indi

cated that a Level 1 approach is appropriate for many residential applications.
2. The g-function library is static. The library of g-functions is static and is not planned to be updated frequently. It is recommended that over time, the library be updated with the outputs of GHEDesigner as a future effort. This introduces some degree of maintenance burden if and when new approaches (or new, more accurate g-functions) are introduced. This can also introduce uncertainty over time about where certain inputs came from, as exemplified by the currently implemented g-functions that are poorly documented. To address this, thorough documentation (such as this document, but also in the OpenStudioHPXML documentation and the code itself) will clearly state the source of all empirical data, as well as any assumptions made within the workflow. The team also created a direct connection to an existing g-function library so that if the library is updated, new gfunctions can easily be downloaded and integrated into the workflow.
3. Large uncertainty exists in soil thermal property data. To account for this, documentation will point users to some of the best available resources with thermal properties of different soil types, as well as recent work that estimates the average soil conductivity as a function of climate zone (X. W. Liu 2016). This can help guide users to make more informed guesses o

n soil properties if desired. However, given the large amount of uncertainty that exists, we will not implement location-specific defaults to avoid giving the impression of a level of precision that does not exist.
4. OpenStudio-HPXML models multifamily buildings on a unit-by-unit basis, rather than modeling all units within a building simultaneously. There are several implications to this modeling assumption for GHPs. The ground heat exchanger for a single unit is much smaller than would be required for the entire building, which means different g-functions would be used for this approach, and less interaction between boreholes occurs in the current approach. This likely means that this approach

for the entire building, which means different g-functions would be used for this approach, and less interaction between boreholes occurs in the current approach. This likely means that this approach

- underestimates the total number of boreholes required for supporting the whole multifamily building. This may also underestimate the costs associated with installing a GHP, especially around the ground heat exchanger sizing. While costs may be estimated for the whole building and then attributed to individual units, the reduced number of boreholes will also lead to lower estimated installed costs. Given the complexity of dealing with the interactions (which are not a simple function of the overall size of the building, but depend on several other factors as well), this is documented as a known limitation and area of caution when understanding the results that come from modeling multifamily buildings and community-scale GHP installations. Note that large high rises (>8 stories) are excluded from having GHPs applied entirely because of this limitation.
5. GHP performance curves are based on a single unit. The approach to modeling the GHP used here is based on generating a performance map for a single unit, rather than trying to generate 'generic' curves that represent the performance of this technology as a product class. Some care has been taken in picking the unit used to specify the performance curves. The approach is to pick a product with rated performance that seems representative of the typical efficiency seen in this class of product relative to other ENERGY STAR-rat

text:

the performance curves. The approach is to pick a product with rated performance that seems representative of the typical efficiency seen in this class of product relative to other ENERGY STAR-rat

ed GHPs. The performance curves are also based on a product from a major U.S. based manufacturer of this technology with a long track record to try to ensure that performance is closer to representative, rather than picking the product with the highest efficiency on the market today or the newest product to hit the market. There is some inherent uncertainty in picking any single set of performance curves to represent an entire class of product, but the NLR residential team has had success with this approach representing multiple products of similar design (same refrigerant, similar condenser lengths, etc.) for other technologies like ASHPs and heat pump water heaters. Unit-specific product curves have been used to represent heat pump water heater performance in the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow, and validation efforts have shown that the curves do not vary substantially from manufacturer to manufacturer for other technologies. The performance curves used here are also for a single-stage GHP.
6. A new approach to cycling losses is being used for GHPs compared to other residential HVAC systems. This new approach is based on a European standard and has steeper penalties on energy use at very low part-load conditions compared to the approach used for air-to-air systems such as air conditioners and ASHPs. This could potentially lead to GHPs assuming more energy is wasted during cycling,

metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2.5 Limitations and Concerns

low part-load conditions compared to the approach used for air-to-air systems such as air conditioners and ASHPs. This could potentially lead to GHPs assuming more energy is wasted during cycling,

 particularly in climates where there are unbalanced loads (heavily heating- or cooling-dominated climates) or mild climates when comparing these options in different upgrade scenarios.
7. Calculations are performed for only a single year. OpenStudio-HPXML is a tool designed primarily for annual calculations, rather than calculations over multiple years. For GHPs, if the heating loads are substantially larger than the cooling loads, this may lead to a thermal imbalance (Saaly and Maghoul 2019). Over the course of multiple years of operation, extracting heat from the ground can lead to changes in the soil temperature. This leads to decreases in the outlet temperature from the ground heat exchanger and reduced efficiency of the GHP. The magnitude of this change depends on the size of the ground heat exchanger, the difference in heating and cooling loads, and how long the system has been operating. As ground temperature changes over the course of a period

much longer than the annual simulations performed here, it is difficult to account for this effect over the lifetime of the GHP. Additional work would be required to try to correct for this effect over the lifetime of the system.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 3  Results

This measure replaces the existing applicable HVAC equipment with a new GHP system. The measure requires an existing system to be in place, as some inputs from the existing system are recycled for use with the new system. Specifically, this measure implements a single-stage compressor, variable-speed fan water-to-air heat pump system with a vertical ground heat exchanger.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 3.1 Annual Stock Savings

Overall stock-level energy consumption for baseline and Single Stage GHP is shown in Figure 18 (full stock) and Figure 19. Single-stage GHPs reduce site energy consumption 24.3% at the stock level (Figure 18), and by 31.3% in dwellings applicable to the GHP upgrade (Figure 19). All results are site energy in TBtu regardless of fuel used. Results are filtered such that the baseline contains only buildings for which the GHP upgrade is applicable. Refer to Section 2.1 for the applicability criteria for GHPs. GHP upgrades were applicable to 71% of the homes included in the ResStock 2025 Release 1. 38 Heating energy decreases by 45% for these homes, but electricity used for space heating more than doubles when GHPs are installed due to the substantial amount of fuel switching away from natural gas (and to a lesser extent, fuel oil and propane). Cooling energy consumption decreases by 19%. Note that the baseline includes homes that do not have cooling or are partially conditioned by room air conditioners (but use ducted heating systems, so a GHP upgrade is still applicable), in which the GHP upgrade increases energy consumption for cooling. Less than 100% of the space is cooled for about 33% of the homes with cooling equipment. Figure 20 shows the energy consumption of baseline and GHP upgrade cases disaggregated by baseline heating fuel. Natural gas is used by the majority of the stock and therefore makes up the majority of the residential stock. Propane and fuel oil are the least common, primarily used in more rural areas without access to natural gas infrastructure. Fuel oil is generally used in the New England region and rarely used in other parts of the country. For homes with natural gas, installing a single-stage GHP reduces heating energy by 50% due to the higher efficiency of the GHP relative to the baseline equipment, primarily furnaces. Note that heating fan and pump energy do increase substantially, largely attributable to the pump energy use associated with the GHPs, but these increases have a minor impact relative to the overall savings of the more efficient equipment. Cooling energy savings are much less substantial due to the much smaller difference in the efficiency of equipment used in the baseline and upgrade cases across the stock and because some units do not have cooling in the baseline stock.

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 3.2 State Average Energy Savings and GHP Efficiency

Figure 22 shows the average cooling energy savings between the baseline and upgrade scenarios in different states in the contiguous United States. Note that savings can be negative, sometimes substantially, in cases where a substantial portion of the housing stock did not have cooling in the baseline. In the results below many units in Vermont, Maine, New Hampshire, Wyoming, and Montana do not have cooling or do not cool their entire floor area. The adoption of GHPs adds cooling and conditioning to the entire floor area, resulting in a cooling energy increase. Similarly, Washington and California see an increase in cooling load due to a large portion of the dwelling units being in the Marine IECC climate zone, where many homes do not have cooling or do not cool their entire floor area.

In states where cooling loads are substantial and the majority of the state has cooling in the baseline, such as most of the southeastern U.S., average cooling energy savings of 20% -30% are possible across the stock. For states with negative savings, there is a substantial comfort benefit to cooling the entire space. This benefit will become even more substantial with the projected rise in cooling degree days in the coming decades (EPA 2024).

Figure 24 shows the average cooling COP for the single-stage GHP. In this context, COP is the ratio between cooling load delivered and the electricity consumed by the cooling unit and the air handler fan to meet that cooling load. This is not to be confused with the rated COP of the system. The COP being reported is the state average simulated COP and does not include duct losses, which may be substantial. Cooling efficiency is highest in heating-dominated states, particularly in the upper Midwest, which have cooler ground temperatures in summer. However, these states also have the lowest cooling loads, so the overall savings are more modest in these locations. Cooling COPs range from 2.9 to 3.7 at the state level, with almost all states achieving a COP over 3. Note that individual buildings within each state may have higher or lower COPs than the state average due to differences in climate within a state and other factors.

Figure 25 shows the average heating COP for the single-stage GHP. The COP does not include duct losses, which may be substantial, particularly in existing homes where ducts are often located in unconditioned spaces and are not upgraded as part of the GHP measure. These losses can significantly degrade overall system performance relative to the rated equipment COP. The reported COPs focus solely on the efficiency of the equipment itself.

Observed heating COPs range between 2.0 and 2.4 across climate zones, with lower values in the coldest states. Colder regions not only experience lower ground temperatures (which reduce heat pump efficiency due to decreased entering water temperatures), but also tend to have higher annual heating loads, further stressing the system. Additionally, these COP values reflect simulated operation conditions that diverge from the idealized lab test settings under which manufacturers report rated COPs. In practice, GHPs often operate at part-load conditions where cycling is frequent, especially during shoulder seasons. This introduces cycling losses not captured in steady-state ratings.

Despite these inefficiencies, GHPs still deliver substantial energy savings over conventional combustion systems. Even high-efficiency condensing furnaces top out at annual fuel utilization efficiencies (AFUEs) around 0.96, and many existing systems-especially older, non-condensing furnaces-operate in the range of 0.6 to 0.8. text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 3.4  Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the single-stage GHP upgrade will have on electrical panels.

First, Figure 28 and Figure 29 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. Figure 28 shows in the first column, 'All', that about 35% of all dwelling units have 0 or only 1 breaker space available. Figure 29 shows in the first column that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock, but that the other 2.3% of electric panels already have an existing capacity constraint.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it's important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Appendix A: Review of Residential GHPs in the U.S. Building Stock

A review of GHPs in the U.S. residential building stock was performed as part of this work. The review covered how GHPs have been installed in the U.S. residential building stock. The outcome of the review helps target the modeling improvements and helps answer the following questions:

1. How many GHP systems exist in the residential building stock, where are they located, and in what type of buildings have the systems been installed?
2. What is the most common ground heat exchanger configuration?
3. How common are water-to-water, water-to-air, and direct geo-exchange systems?
4. How have ENERGY STAR GHPs improved in recent years and how many units have been shipped?

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Residential Building Stock Characterization of GHP Installations

Characterizing the GHP installations in the U.S. residential building stock helps identify segments of the stock that have GHPs and segments of the stock that have not been the focus of the GHP market. This characterization focuses on the number of GHP installations, where they are located, in what type of buildings, when the buildings were built, and some recent trends in GHP installations.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Residential GHPs Installations by Various Housing Characteristics

Characteristics about the housing units with GHPs also illuminate where the market has higher or lower penetrations. Figure A-4 illustrates that residential GHP installations in the U.S. are focused primarily in the single-family detached and mobile home housing stock. There are fewer GHP installations in multifamily apartment buildings with 5 or more units relative to the U.S. residential stock.

The RECS 2020 data shows that there are fewer GHP installations in the pre-1980s residential stock (Figure A-5). Residential building stock housing units built before 1980 makes up roughly 54% of the U.S. residential building stock. Approximately 1.9% of the housing units built after 1980 have GHP installations compared to 0.7% built before 1980. This indicates that newer homes are more likely to have GHPs installed. Approximately 75% of residential GHP installations are in new construction, while 25% are retrofits (Liu, et al. 2019).

Targeting only new construction to install GHPs would be limiting. According to the American Community Survey, the number of residential housing units has grown by about 0.7% each year over the last 10 years (U.S. Census 2021). There are a large number of homes in the existing U.S. residential building stock in which GHPs could be installed if the land area is available for installation of the ground heat exchanger.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Residential GHP Mechanical Equipment Types and Efficiencies

This section reviews (1) the typical mechanical equipment types and their market penetration in the U.S. residential building stock, (2) the equipment rated heating and cooling efficiencies along with historical ENERGY STAR specifications, and (3) ENERGY STAR certified unit shipments and market penetration. The discussion in this section helps prioritize what type of heat pump is modeled in the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow and what default efficiency values are reasonable based on when the equipment was installed.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — GHP Mechanical Distribution System Market Penetration

There are four major types of GHP systems based on heat transfer system design:

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.section: GHP Mechanical Distribution System Market Penetration
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1. Water-to-Air

In these types of GHP systems, the ground heat exchanger is composed of either an open- or closed-loop circuit containing water or a water-antifreeze solution. The heat transfers between the ground heat exchanger and the heat pump system, which operates on a vapor-compression refrigeration cycle. The use of refrigerant is limited to within the heat pump system itself. The heat transfer between the heat pump system and the interior of the building is achieved through forced air movement through heat exchangers transferring heat between the heat pump system and the indoor air through ducts.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2. Water-to-Water

In these types of GHP systems, the ground heat exchanger is the same as in water-to-air systems. However, the heat transfer to the indoor environment is done using a second hydronic loop. Heat is exchanged between the ground heat exchanger and the heat pump system operation on a vapor-compression refrigeration cycle. The hydronic loop absorbs heat from the heat pump system via heat exchanger(s) and circulates that heat to various parts of the building using one or more closed circuit hydronic (water) loops running through baseboard hydronic radiators or radiant floors. Water-to-water systems perform much better in space heating than space cooling in residential buildings, with some manufacturers not recommending using water-to-water heat pumps for residential cooling (Dandelion Energy 2023).

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 3. Combined Systems (Water-to-Air and Water-to-Water Hybrids)

These systems use a combination of water-to-air and water-to-water systems to exchange heat between the ground heat exchanger and the indoor environment.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 4. Direct Geo-Exchange

These systems use a refrigerant directly in the ground heat exchanger, instead of a waterantifreeze mix, to exchange heat between the heat pump system and the ground. The heat exchange on the building-interior side can either be a water-to-air, water-to-water, or combined system. These systems are less commonly used due to the risks of corrosion to the buried copper tubing carrying the refrigerant, which sits in direct contact with the soil, leading to potential system failure as well as the potential for environmental issues such as groundwater contamination. As a result, these systems are also more tightly regulated by local jurisdictions.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Presence of Residential GHP Equipment Types in the Residential Building Stock

A review of GHP deployments was performed in 2013 as part of a market analysis (Battocletti & Glassley, 2013). The study surveyed manufacturers, geothermal loop installers, and mechanical equipment installers. The survey of residential mechanical equipment installers resulted in the distribution of equipment types seen in Figure A-6. Water-to-air heat pumps made up the largest fraction of residential GHP mechanical equipment installations at 77%. If the combined systems are also included, as they have a water-to-air component, this fraction increases to 87%. Waterto-water and direct geo-exchange systems made up a lower fraction of installations at 8% and 5%, respectively.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Residential GHP Heating and Cooling Efficiencies

The efficiency of GHPs has improved over time. Combining historical federal equipment efficiency standards with historical unit shipment data provides insights into the efficiency of the GHP units in the residential building stock. The GeoVision report used an energy efficiency ratio (EER) of 18.2 and coefficient of performance (COP) of 4.0 at 100% load (heating or cooling) to represent typical GHPs installed in the U.S. in 2012 (U.S. DOE 2019).

ENERGY STAR sets voluntary efficiency criteria for GHPs. Figure A-7 and Figure A-8 illustrate the EER and COP criteria, respectively of the ENERGY STAR program for GHPs since 2001. From 2010-2012, there were significant increases to ENERGY STAR GHP performance criteria. Open-loop systems have higher performance criteria than closed-loop systems. Water-to-air systems have higher performance criteria than water-to-water heat pump systems.

Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Ground Heat Exchanger Configurations

There are two types of ground heat exchanger systems for GHPs: open- and closed-loop systems.

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 1. Open-Loop Systems

Open-loop systems use a well or a surface body water (like a local pond or lake) directly as heat exchange fluid that circulates through the GHP system. Feasibility of the use of open-loop systems, however, depends on location, local codes, and regulations (U.S. DOE. 2023).

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — 2. Closed-Loop Systems

Closed-loop GHP systems use a constant volume of a working fluid (usually a mixture of water and antifreeze) that circulates in a closed loop (piping that is joined end-to-end), absorbing heat in one segment and rejecting heat through another segment of the closed loop without any exchange of mass of the working fluid between the heat pump system and the surrounding environment as in an open-loop system. Based on how the ground heat exchanger are installed, there are four major types, two horizontal closed loop, one vertical closed loop, and one pond/lake closed loop (U.S. DOE. 2023).

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — a. Horizontal Closed Loop

Horizontal ground heat exchanger systems are deemed by U.S. DOE as generally the most costeffective closed-loop configuration for residential (particularly for new construction) installations where sufficient land is available (U.S. DOE. 2023), but are less commonly installed as many sites don't have the land area or are retrofits. The trenches for the horizontal loop systems are generally dug about 4 ft deep. The most common layouts use either:

- Two pipes, one buried at 6 ft and the other at 4 ft, or
- Two pipes placed side-by-side at 5 ft in the ground in a 2 ft wide trench.

The Slinky method of looping pipe allows the use of more pipe in a shorter trench, resulting in lower installation cost.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — b. Vertical Closed Loop

Vertical ground loop GHP systems are common for large commercial buildings and schools because the land area required is small compared to horizonal loop systems. The boreholes for vertical loop systems are typically approximately 4 inches in diameter and are drilled approximately 20 ft apart. The boreholes are 100 to 400 ft deep. Two pipes connected at the bottom with a U-bend to form a loop are inserted into the hole and grouted to improve performance. The vertical loops are connected with horizontal manifolds placed in trenches (U.S. DOE. 2023) (Self et al. 2013).

metadata.doc_title: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER)

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — c. Pond/Lake Closed Loop

If the installation site has adequate access to a body of water, such as a pond or lake, a surface water system may be the most suitable option. A supply line pipe is run underground from the building to the water and coiled into circles at least 8 ft under the surface to prevent freezing. There is no specific way or orientation of looping for this type of system, but the coils should only be placed in water source that meets minimum volume, depth, and quality requirements (U.S. DOE. 2023). Rivers are not ideal for this application due to their unpredictable behaviors, including flooding and droughts that can damage loop systems, as well as hazards due to moving debris (Omer 2008), (Ma 2004).

text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Ground Heat Exchanger Configurations in the U.S. Residential Stock

Across the data sources reviewed, there is general agreement that most of the U.S. residential ground heat exchanger configurations are closed-loop horizontal or closed-loop vertical systems. Horizontal and vertical closed-loop systems make up 84%-93% of the ground heat exchanger installations. Ground heat exchangers that use groundwater or surface water make up 4%-16%. The only source with reporting on direct geo-exchange systems, Battocletti and Glassley, reported that these systems made up about 3% of ground heat exchanger installations (Battocletti and Glassley 2013). There is some disagreement across data sources about the relative prevalence of horizontal and vertical ground heat exchanger systems. Liu et al. 2019 (Liu, et al. 2019) and Battocletti and Glassley (Battocletti and Glassley 2013) state that vertical ground loops are more common, while Lund and Boyd (Lund and Boyd 2016) state that horizontal ground loops are more common. The Lund and Boyd 2016 study focuses on residential systems only, while the other two studies combine residential and commercial. It is possible that the Battocletti and Glassley and Liu et al. sources predict a higher fraction of vertical ground loop configurations because they include commercial ground heat exchanger systems, which are typically vertical installations. With the total length required, the number of boreholes can then be calculated. To calculate the number of boreholes required, an initial guess of one borehole for every ton of required capacity is used before some geometry parameters are enforced. A maximum depth of 345 feet is also assumed, based on the maximum depth before a mining permit is required in certain states. If necessary, these constraints will add or remove a borehole, up to a maximum of 10 boreholes. Based on the number of boreholes, the configuration of the bore field is then determined. text:
Residential Single-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (3.8 COP, 18.6 EER) — Soil Properties

At the start of the project, the soil properties defaulted to a conductivity of 1.73 W/m-K, a density of 920 kg/m 3 , a specific heat capacity of 3.5 kJ/kg-K, and a thermal diffusivity of 5.37x10 -7 m 2 /s. Conductivity values have been updated as described above, with others still used in the existing workflow by default. The undisturbed deep ground temperature was originally modeled using the Kusuda/Achenbach model (T. A. Kusuda 1965) as implemented in EnergyPlus, although as noted the annual average dry-bulb temperature is used instead in some calculations (U.S. DOE 2022). The detailed description of the ground temperature model implemented in (Xing 2014) above is currently used in ResStock. Inputs for ground properties have been added to the HPXML schema, meaning users can now overwrite the default values if measured characteristics are available. However, our default assumptions have not changed.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in site energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This document focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER). This document builds on details established in the single-stage document (Maguire et al. 2025) to detail differences in the approach to modeling this higher efficiency and more commonly deployed, type of geothermal heat pump. Specific EnergyPlus ® objects and product specific curves used are highlighted along with showing the results of this measure compared to the baseline and single-speed geothermal heat pumps. Twospeed heat pumps are able to save even more site energy and on utility bills than single-speed products, albeit at the expense of a higher first cost.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — Relation to Other GHP Models

Unless otherwise noted in this document, it is assumed that certain components of the two-stage GHP model overlap with (i.e., are the same as) single-stage model components. The following summarizes these overlapping components:

- Technology summary : The two-stage GHP works using the same general principles as the single-stage GHP, except that it has a two-stage compressor along with improved rated heating and cooling efficiency values.
- Applicability : The two-stage GHP applies to the same set of dwelling units as the singlestage GHP.
- Modeling approach : The two-stage GHP follows the same basic modeling approach as the single-stage GHP, except that the heat pump performance curves are updated, and a pump power energy management system (EMS) program is used. The model of the ground heat exchanger is identical for any GHP.

See the single-stage report (Maguire et al. 2025) for more detailed information about components that do not change between single-stage and two-stage GHPs. It is recommended to read that report first to fully understand the background technology, summary, assumptions, and discussions that were completed as part of this work.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 1.1  Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

Geothermal heat pumps (GHPs) are highly efficient systems that provide space heating and cooling by using the relatively stable temperatures found below the Earth's surface. GHPs exchange heat with the ground, where temperatures remain more constant year-round. This enables GHPs to operate efficiently and reliably in a wide range of climates. GHP systems typically consist of three main components: a ground heat exchanger, a heat pump unit, and an air distribution system within the building.

There are several types of GHPs, including single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed systems.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 1.1  Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

a ground heat exchanger, a heat pump unit, and an air distribution system within the building.

There are several types of GHPs, including single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed systems.

- Single-stage GHPs operate at full capacity whenever they run, which can lead to energy inefficiencies under part-load conditions (when the system needs less than its maximum output).
- Two-stage GHPs improve upon this design by adding a second, lower-capacity stage. This allows the system to operate more efficiently during mild conditions while still having the capability to switch to full output when demand peaks.
- Variable-speed GHPs represent the most advanced option, using inverter-driven compressors and fans to continuously adjust their output in response to real-time heating and cooling needs. Unlike single-stage or two-stage systems that operate in discrete steps, variable-speed systems can modulate across a wide range of capacities. This precise control enhances energy efficiency, provides more stable indoor temperatures, reduces humidity swings, and minimizes noise from cycling.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 1.1  Introduction to Geothermal Heat Pumps

can modulate across a wide range of capacities. This precise control enhances energy efficiency, provides more stable indoor temperatures, reduces humidity swings, and minimizes noise from cycling.

Like single-stage systems, two-stage GHPs draw on the ground's thermal properties to deliver heating and cooling via a ground heat exchanger and an indoor heat pump. The difference lies in the system's ability to adjust its output. By operating in a low stage under mild conditions, a twostage GHP reduces energy use, improves comfort by maintaining more stable temperatures and humidity, and can result in quieter operation. When heating or cooling demand increases (such as during extreme weather) the system shifts to high stage for full-capacity operation.

Although two-stage GHPs typically come with higher initial capital costs than single-stage models, they are usually more energy efficient and can lead to lower lifetime operating costs (Trane 2023). Due to these advantages, two-stage systems have become the most commonly installed type of GHP in the residential market, capturing the largest share among GHP technologies according to the technical advisory group (U.S. EPA, 2025).

The modeled system assumes a vertical ground heat exchanger configuration, which is a common and space-efficient option for residential installations.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.1  Applicability

Using the same applicability criteria as the single-stage GHP, the two-stage compressor, waterto-air heat pump with a vertical ground heat exchanger upgrade measure applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to roughly 71% of the existing residential building stock. 6.4% of the residential units that receive the GHP upgrade lack existing space cooling systems in the baseline. Units that are excluded from this measure, as well as more details about GHP modeling and assumptions, are more fully described in the documentation for the single-stage GHP measure (Maguire et al. 2025).

that are excluded from this measure, as well as more details about GHP modeling and assumptions, are more fully described in the documentation for the single-stage GHP measure (Maguire et al. 2025).

Applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics that determine the available options and the options' details (Reyna, et al., 2025). Specifically, the 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' characteristic in ResStock is used to apply each respective heat pump option. 'HVAC Has Ducts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling. 'Heating Type' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling. 'HVAC Shared Efficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable. 'Geometry Building Type Height' describes the height and building type of the dwelling. More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Guide. 1

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

For the two-stage GHP, the same ResStock building energy model and OpenStudio-HPXML workflow is used as for the single-stage GHP (Maguire et al. 2025).

OpenStudio-HPXML's apply\_ground\_to\_air\_heat\_pump() 2  method in OpenStudio-HPXML is used to assign two-stage levels (and their corresponding performance curves) to water-to-air coil objects that support variable speeds:

- CoilCoolingWaterToAirHeatPumpVariableSpeedEquationFit
- CoilHeatingWaterToAirHeatPumpVariableSpeedEquationFit.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.1  Two-Stage GHP Heating and Cooling Efficiency

This measure includes a water-to-air GHP with a two-stage compressor rated at a heating coefficient of performance (COP) of 4.0 and a rated cooling energy efficiency ratio (EER) of 20.5. The ground heat exchanger shape and properties are the same as used for the single-stage GHP: rectangular and vertically drilled single U-tube design with thermally enhanced grout and piping. This section will describe the inputs and modeling methodology for the heat pump. Refer to the single-stage GHP model documentation (Maguire et al. 2025) for inputs and methodology not discussed in this document.

The ResStock arguments assigned in the 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' characteristic (different than the default OpenStudio-HPXML defaults) that help distinguish the two-stage GHP from the single-stage GHP are:

- Heat pump compressor type
- Heat pump heating efficiency
- Heat pump cooling efficiency.

For this measure, the compressor type is two-stage, as stated by the measure definition.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.2  Two-Stage GHP Performance Curves

GHPs are highly efficient systems that use the relatively constant temperature of the Earth to provide heating and cooling for buildings. Accurately modeling the performance of GHPs in building energy simulation tools like EnergyPlus ® is critical for evaluating system performance, energy consumption, and cost-effectiveness under different operating conditions.

Unlike single-stage equipment, two-stage and variable-speed GHPs can operate at multiple capacity levels, allowing them to better match building loads and improve part-load efficiency. To capture this behavior in EnergyPlus, the

Coil:Cooling:WaterToAirHeatPump:VariableSpeedEquationFit and

Coil:Heating:WaterToAirHeatPump:VariableSpeedEquationFit objects are used. These components rely on a suite of performance curves to simulate how the system responds to changes in water and air temperatures, as well as airflow and water flow rates. Despite 'VariableSpeed' in the name, this object is the best EnergyPlus model for two-stage equipment as well as fully variable-speed.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.2  Two-Stage GHP Performance Curves

and air temperatures, as well as airflow and water flow rates. Despite 'VariableSpeed' in the name, this object is the best EnergyPlus model for two-stage equipment as well as fully variable-speed.

Each curve provides a mathematical relationship between a key input (e.g., entering water temperature, airflow fraction) and the resulting system output, such as capacity or efficiency. These relationships are derived from manufacturer data, laboratory testing, or calibrated models and are essential for producing accurate, realistic simulations of two-stage GHP operation.

To fully represent system performance across both part-load and full-load conditions for heating and cooling, the following sets of performance curves are required:

- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of water and air temperature (biquadratic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of water and air temperature (biquadratic)
- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of airflow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of airflow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of water flow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of water flow fraction (quadratic or cubic).

- The capacity of the GHP as a function of water flow fraction (quadratic or cubic).

The EnergyPlus Auxiliary Program: HVAC Performance Curve Fit Tool was used to develop the biquadratic curves for capacity and efficiency as function of temperatures (Big Ladder 2024). The tool is designed for direct expansion coil performance curves, which depend on two air temperatures, but appropriate biquadratic curves can be generated using the same tool if water temperature is used instead of one air temperature. The approach used is consistent for all GHP measures in ResStock, with additional curves being developed for each stage for coils that can operate at multiple stages.

The two-stage GHP performance curves were developed based on data provided in the spec sheet for a 3-ton Tranquility 30 SE two-stage GHP manufactured by ClimateMaster (ClimateMaster 2025). This model is in the same product line as what was used for the single-stage GHP performance curves. The same overall approach described in the performance curve section of the single-stage GHP documentation for deriving performance curves is used for the two-stage GHP system, with some exceptions noted here. The two-stage GHP spec sheets provide data for performance at both part-load and full-load conditions, which means that two separate performance maps are required for the lower and higher stages. Nominal points are at the same temperatures as single-stage equipment (70°F/80°F entering water/air temperature for cooling and 70°F/70°F entering water/air temperature for heating), with the highest airflow and water flow rate (1,200 cfm and 9 gal/min, respectively) provided used for both part-load and full-load conditions as the nominal condition. Off-rated air and water flow rates are accounted for using the curves shown later in this report.

After generating coefficients with the spreadsheet tool from EnergyPlus, the original manufacturer catalog data were compared with the curve-fit data to ensure the correctness of the curve coefficients. These comparisons are documented in Appendix A.

Quadratic curves for the impact of airflow and water flow on efficiency and capacity can be generated by fitting directly to published data of a product at nominal conditions. As these curves are simpler and made up of fewer points, a simple quadratic regression can yield a good fit for each curve. While two-stage GHP systems typically operate at the nominal flow rate for each stage when in low- and high-stage operation, flow rates may be reduced due to equipment faults and degradation, which are modeled within OpenStudio-HPXML, and these curves can capture the impact of faults on the annual performance of affected systems.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.3  EnergyPlus Energy Management System Correction to Pump Power

The EnergyPlus models with the variable-speed water-to-air coil object for two-stage and variable-speed water-to-air GHP systems did not by default model the expected behavior of the pump for these GHP systems. To modify the default behavior to try to more accurately model the pump behavior, especially in cases where the GHP is in part-load conditions, a custom energy management system (EMS) script was developed and added to the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. EMS is a custom scripting language packaged with EnergyPlus that allows users to write short custom programs to modify the behavior of certain components of the model. In addition to developing the standard EnergyPlus GHP models, an EMS program was developed to overcome the limitations in current EnergyPlus capabilities to model the two-stage water-to-air GHP systems:

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.3  EnergyPlus Energy Management System Correction to Pump Power

addition to developing the standard EnergyPlus GHP models, an EMS program was developed to overcome the limitations in current EnergyPlus capabilities to model the two-stage water-to-air GHP systems:

1. There is an improper limit on the node water flow rate found in EnergyPlus. This limit will cause the pump water flow rates to be capped at the first-stage nominal flow rate, and the remaining water flow is bypassed. It will likely cause warnings/errors complaining about unrealistic water temperatures due to the reduced water flow rates, which largely impacts the accuracy and stability of simulation. This limitation was fixed by the ResStock team and will be included in future EnergyPlus releases from 25.1.0 onward. See the merged EnergyPlus pull request 3 for the full details of this change.
2. EnergyPlus models a constant water mass flow rate equal to the first-stage flow rate during part-load conditions, where the heat pump may only be running for part of the time step, and the average flow rate over the time step may be less than the minimum even with a two-stage pump. This affects the pump energy calculation, which is fixed by the EMS program described below. In addition, an EnergyPlus issue 4 was created to

[3  https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/pull/11005](https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/pull/11005)

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.2.3  EnergyPlus Energy Management System Correction to Pump Power

the EMS program described below. In addition, an EnergyPlus issue 4 was created to

[3  https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/pull/11005](https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/pull/11005)

[4  https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/issues/10936](https://github.com/NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus/issues/10936)

report this defect to the development team. Ideally the defect will be fixed in the future version of EnergyPlus, and then the EMS workaround can be eliminated or simplified.

In this case, an EMS program is used to recalculate the pump power in every time step. It involves two steps:

1. Calculate the correct pump power if part-load conditions exist. The internal EnergyPlus pump energy calculations do not handle the pump part-load ratio correctly in the use case. The pump part-load ratio at each time step is recalculated in the EMS program based on pump volume flow rates and heat pump coil speed levels/ratios. The part-load ratio is assumed to be equal to the fraction of pump full-load power.
2. Apply the calculated fraction to calculate and override the pump power consumption at each time step.

The part-load ratio is assumed to be equal to the fraction of pump full-load power.
2. Apply the calculated fraction to calculate and override the pump power consumption at each time step.

Even though EMS programs offer flexibility for users to override some aspects of EnergyPlus simulation and achieve the desired energy results, there are still some limitations to using EMS programs. The EMS program described above is included in OpenStudio-HPXML, but other EnergyPlus modelers would not have easy access to it and may not know about the limitations requiring its use. EMS also adds complexity to the models, may impact simulation runtime, and may cause one-time-step lag on reporting the energy consumption of components controlled via EMS. Therefore, if the EnergyPlus issue being reported can be fixed in the future versions, it will largely simplify the workflow and benefit more users of these EnergyPlus objects.

Combining all the efforts above, OpenStudio-HPXML is capable of modeling the desired pump operation and giving satisfying pump energy results for two-stage GHP systems.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 2.3  Limitations and Concerns

Some limitations unique to two-stage GHPs include:

1. The two-stage GHP uses EMS to account for energy consumption of the pump when modeled as operating below the lowest stage. A change to the EnergyPlus source code would be ideal and more widely accessible than the EMS-based approach used here, but source code changes can be complicated, time-consuming, and require expertise with the C++ based source code. Future runs will also use the bug fixed version of EnergyPlus, and the impact of the EMS workaround described here will need to be re-evaluated with the newer releases.
2. Desuperheater curves were not developed for two-stage equipment. Although data are available for desuperheater performance at both stages, adding a desuperheater to a GHP is relatively uncommon and assumed to not happen in ResStock when applying GHPs as an upgrade. This capability may be added to OpenStudio-HPXML in the future, which would make it available to be leveraged in ResStock for future runs.

Note that the limitations listed in the single-stage GHP measure documentation apply to all GHPs modeled in ResStock, particularly when it comes to modeling of the ground heat exchanger.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 3.1  Annual Stock Savings

Figure 25 shows the annual site energy consumption for homes with and without GHP upgrades. Homes with a single-stage GHP upgrade are also shown as a point of comparison for the twostage GHP upgrade. Note that the figures show two sets of dwellings: the top figure includes the entire housing stock, including homes that GHP upgrades do not apply to, in both the baseline and upgrade scenarios. All results are in site energy in TBtu regardless of fuel used. This captures the impact of the upgrades on all homes across the country, which may be of interest to certain stakeholders who care about the entire load post-upgrade. The bottom figure only shows dwellings that could receive a GHP as an upgrade for both the baseline and upgrade scenarios. This result makes it easier to determine the impact of the upgrades on the applicable stock by excluding buildings that do not receive an upgrade. Note that homes that a GHP upgrade does not apply to (most often due to a lack of ducts) make up about 25% of the building stock. Refer to the 'Applicability' section of the single-stage GHP measure documentation to see the full list of criteria that determines which dwellings can receive a GHP as an upgrade.

When two-stage GHPs are considered as an upgrade, this leads to a substantial amount of fuel switching for heating, even when considering the portion of homes where the upgrade does not apply, which leads to an increase in heating electricity consumption. This change is larger than the reduction in electricity consumption resulting from replacing existing cooling equipment with the more efficient two-stage GHP across the entire stock.

For dwellings that can receive a two-stage GHP as an upgrade, cooling electricity consumption is 35% less and heating electricity consumption is 168% larger than the baseline, which still substantially reduces the overall energy consumption of the residential stock when this upgrade is applied. A two-stage GHP also saves substantially more energy than the single-stage GHP considered here, with savings of 12% over the single-stage case when considering the portion of the stock that can receive a GHP and 8% when considering the entire stock.

Figure 26 shows the annual energy consumption of the portion of the housing stock that can receive a GHP upgrade split out by heating fuel type of the baseline buildings. The majority of the stock uses natural gas for heating. All segments reduce energy consumption for both heating and cooling when moving to a GHP upgrade. For homes that use natural gas for heating, twostage GHPs reduce energy use for heating by 76% and cooling by 40% compared to the baseline.

Figure 27 shows the annual energy consumption for the applicable portion of the stock for the baseline, single-stage GHP upgrade, and two-stage GHP upgrade separated by Building America climate zone. GHPs show substantial savings potential in cold climates, which also contain the largest number of dwellings, with two-stage GHPs using 32% less energy for heating than single-stage systems along with some additional cooling savings. Across all climate zones, GHPs may reduce electricity consumption during the cooling seasons but increase electricity consumption during the heating season while saving energy overall due to the higher efficiency of the equipment.

Figure 28 shows the cooling energy savings for homes receiving the upgrade over the baseline by state for the contiguous United States. Vermont has the least savings, largely due to the low amount of cooling equipment present there in the baseline. Negative savings, or an increase in cooling energy, happens in several colder climate zones, notably in northern New England, where cooling equipment in the baseline is less common. Note that fewer states have negative savings when using a two-stage GHP than when using a single-stage GHP due to the higher efficiency of the two-stage equipment.

Figure 29 shows the heating energy savings from installing a two-stage GHP compared to the baseline. In general, the Southeast exhibits smaller savings percentages than the rest of the contiguous United States. This is because many homes in this region already use electric heating systems (such as electric resistance or heat pumps) in the baseline scenario. In contrast, much of the rest of the country relies on combustion-based HVAC systems, which have inherent heat losses due to exhaust from combustion products. Georgia shows relatively higher heating savings as a percentage because the Atlanta area (where a large portion of the state's residential stock is located) primarily uses natural gas for heating. The range of cooling energy savings is narrower than the range of heating energy savings. This is partly because nearly every home already has some form of heating in the baseline.

Figure 30 shows the simulated heating COP by state for homes that receive a two-stage GHP upgrade. Efficiency is highest in the hottest climate zones, which have the warmest ground temperature during winter but also the lowest loads, so they may not save as much energy on an absolute basis. All states have a high average simulated heating COP, notably higher than the single-stage GHP case, with the minimum state average simulated COP of 2.7 in North Dakota. Figure 31 shows the average cooling COP in each state for homes that receive a two-stage GHP upgrade. This COP is highest in cold climate zones, with the highest values seen in Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, and Wyoming. Like with heating, the highest efficiency occurs in the states with the lowest overall load, and the two-stage GHP systems are consistently more efficient than single-stage GHPs. Cooling COP varies more than heating COP across states, but the lowest cooling COP is close to the highest COP seen during heating. Average COPs seen here are also higher than the average COP of air conditioners in the baseline case as shown by the savings seen in Figure 29, indicating that GHPs could lead to substantial savings for the overall stock for both heating and cooling.

Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 3.3  Annual Energy Bill Impact for Applicable Dwelling Units Only

Energy bills for applicable dwelling units only are shown in the following figures. On average, energy bills decreased 11% for the two-stage GHP. This is a greater percent savings than the single-stage GHP, which was a 3% energy bill decrease on average. The average energy bill for the two-stage GHP is shown in Figure 32. Electricity bills increased slightly, while natural gas, fuel oil, and propane bills all decreased. Electric bills increasing on average is to be expected because of switching from non-electric heating to electric heating, and then some units receiving cooling if they did not have air conditioning before the two-stage GHP.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) — 3.4  Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the two-stage GHP upgrade will have on electrical panels. The modeling assumptions and details about electric panels in ResStock can be found in the singlestage GHP documentation (Maguire et al. 2025).

First, Figure 36 and Figure 37 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. Figure 36 shows in the first column, 'All', that about 35% of all dwelling units have 0 or only 1 breaker space available. Figure 37 shows in the first column that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock, but that the other 2.3% of electric panels already have an existing capacity constraint.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it's important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly marketready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An ' end-use savings shape ' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Residential VariableSpeed Geothermal Heat Pump (GHP). This document provides the relevant new modeling information for variable-speed systems not previously covered in either the single-stage or twostage documents. Variable-speed GHPs represent the most efficient option available for this technology; they provide the highest site energy savings, with up to 46% for the applicable portion of the housing stock, compared to 31% for less efficient single-stage GHPs. Additional results shown here detail how the savings change for sections of the housing stock with different base heating fuels and in different climate zones, and they show the savings potential by state for both heating and cooling. Utility bills and electric panel impacts are also shown and discussed.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — Relation to Other GHP Models

Unless otherwise noted in this document, it is assumed that certain components of the variablespeed GHP model overlap with (i.e., are the same as) single- and two-stage model components. The following summarizes these overlapping components:

- Technology summary : The variable-speed GHP works using the same general principles as the two-stage GHP, except that it has a variable-speed compressor along with improved rated heating and cooling efficiency values.
- Applicability : The variable-speed GHP applies to the same set of dwelling units as the single- and two-stage GHPs.
- Modeling approach : The variable-speed GHP follows the same basic modeling approach as the two-stage GHP, except that the performance curves are updated, and a pump power energy management system (EMS) program is used. The model of the ground heat exchanger is identical for any GHP, and documentation is included in the single-stage GHP measure document.

See the single-stage (Maguire et al. 2025a) and two-stage (Maguire et al. 2025b) reports for more detailed information about components that do not change between single-stage and two-stage GHPs.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

GHPs are highly efficient systems that provide space heating and cooling by leveraging the relatively stable temperatures below the Earth's surface. By exchanging heat with the ground , where temperatures remain more constant year-round, GHPs can operate with greater efficiency and reliability across a wide range of climates. A typical GHP system includes three main components: a ground heat exchanger, a heat pump unit, and an air distribution system within the building.

There are several types of GHPs, including single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed systems:

metadata.doc_title: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 1.1  Introduction to Technology

a ground heat exchanger, a heat pump unit, and an air distribution system within the building.

There are several types of GHPs, including single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed systems:

- Single-stage GHPs operate at full capacity whenever they run, which can lead to energy inefficiencies under part-load conditions (when the system needs less than its maximum output).
- Two-stage GHPs improve upon this design by adding a second, lower-capacity stage. This allows the system to operate more efficiently during mild conditions while still having the capability to switch to full output when demand peaks.
- Variable-speed GHPs represent the most advanced option, using inverter-driven compressors and fans to continuously adjust their output in response to real-time heating and cooling needs. Unlike single-stage or two-stage systems that operate in discrete steps, variable-speed systems can modulate across a wide range of capacities. This precise control enhances energy efficiency, provides more stable indoor temperatures, reduces humidity swings, and minimizes noise from cycling.

can modulate across a wide range of capacities. This precise control enhances energy efficiency, provides more stable indoor temperatures, reduces humidity swings, and minimizes noise from cycling.

Although variable-speed GHPs typically have the highest upfront cost among GHP technologies, they deliver superior part-load efficiency and can achieve the lowest overall operating costs over time. As a result, they are often considered the premium choice for homeowners seeking maximum comfort and performance.

The intent of this GHP measure is to reflect the characteristics of a high-performance, variablespeed, water-to-air GHP, modeled after the most advanced products on the 2025 ENERGY STAR ®  Most Efficient 2025 GHP list. 1 The system assumes a vertical ground heat exchanger configuration, which is a common and space-efficient option for residential applications.

1  https://www.energystar.gov/most-efficient/me-certified-geothermal-heatpumps/results?is\_most\_efficient\_filter=Most%20Efficient

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.1  Applicability

Using the same applicability criteria as the single- and two-stage GHPs, the variable-speed compressor, water-to-air, vertical ground heat exchanger GHP upgrade measure applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height that is less than eight stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to roughly 71% of the existing building stock. The 6.4% of the residential units that receive the GHP upgrade lack existing space-cooling systems in the baseline. Units that are excluded from this measure, as well as more details about GHP modeling and assumptions, are more fully described in the documentation for the single-stage GHP document (Maguire et al. 2025a).

The applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics that determine the available options and the options' details (Reyna, et al. 2025). Specifically, the 'HVAC heating e fficiency' characteristic in ResStock is used to apply each respective heat pump option. 'HVAC has d ucts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling. 'Heating t ype' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling. 'HVAC shared e fficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable. 'Geometry building type h eight' describes the height and building type of the dwelling. More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Documentation . 2

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.2  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

For the variable-speed GHP, the same ResStock building energy model and OpenStudio ® -HPXML workflow are used as for the single- and two-stage GHPs.

OpenStudioHPXML's apply\_ground\_to\_air\_heat\_pump() 3 method is used to apply multiple sets of speeds (and their respective performance curves) to water-to-air coil objects that support various speed levels:

- CoilCoolingWaterToAirHeatPumpVariableSpeedEquationFit
- CoilHeatingWaterToAirHeatPumpVariableSpeedEquationFit.

New performance curves, representing variable-speed equipment, were developed and used to calculate the cooling/heating total capacity/energy input ratio (EIR) 4 as a function of temperature, as a function of airflow rate, and as a function of water flow rate. Updates were also made to an EnergyPlus ® EMS program controlling the flow rate of water though the heat pump and ground heat exchanger.

2  https://NatLabRockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/assets/trd/ResStockTechnicalReferenceGuide\_2025\_1.pdf

3  https://github.com/NatLabRockies/OpenStudio-

4 The EIR is defined as the inverse of the coefficient of performance (1/COP)
