text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.2.1  Variable-Speed GHP Heating and Cooling Efficiency

This measure includes a water-to-air GHP with a variable-speed compressor rated with a heating COP of 4.4 and a rated cooling EER of 30.9. The ground heat exchanger shape and properties are the same as used for the single- and two-stage GHPs: a rectangular and vertically drilled single U-tube design with thermally enhanced grout and piping. This section describes the inputs and modeling methodology for the heat pump. Some inputs, the sizing methodology, and the modeling methodology for the heat pump and the ground heat exchanger are the same as for the single- and two-stage GHPs. Refer to the section with the corresponding name in those documents for additional details.

Many ResStock arguments are assigned in the HVAC heating efficiency characteristic. The arguments being specified (different than the OpenStudio-HPXML defaults) that help distinguish these technologies from the single- and two-stage GHP are:

- Heat pump compressor type
- Heat pump heating efficiency
- Heat pump cooling efficiency.

For this measure, the compressor type is variable speed, as stated by the measure definition.

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.2.2  Variable-Speed GHP Heat Pump Performance Curves

To model variable-speed GHPs with

Coil:Cooling:WaterToAirHeatPump:VariableSpeedEquationFit and Coil:Heating:WaterToAirHeatPump:VariableSpeedEquationFit EnergyPlus objects, several different performance curves are required. At both part load and full load, for both heating and cooling, curves are required for:

- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of water and air temperature (biquadratic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of water and air temperature (biquadratic)
- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of airflow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of airflow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The efficiency of the GHP as a function of water flow fraction (quadratic or cubic)
- The capacity of the GHP as a function of water flow fraction (quadratic or cubic).

The EnergyPlus auxiliary program HVAC Performance Curve Fit Tool was used to develop the biquadratic curves for capacity and EIR as a function of air temperature and water temperature. 8 The tool is designed for direct expansion coil performance curves, but considering the similarity of the curve requirements between these two coils, it is reasonable to use the same tool for GHPs.

Curves here were generated based on data for a variable-speed WaterFurnace 7 Series 3-ton GHP unit (WaterFurnace SDW7-0018W 9 ). This unit comes from a major U.S. manufacturer and includes data in a format that is easy to translate into EnergyPlus inputs. Although this is a fully variable-speed unit, the specification sheet for this unit only includes the performance of the unit at full-load and part-load conditions, similar to what is shown for two-stage units. Although the model can handle additional speeds, specification sheets for products that included additional speeds did not have all the details necessary to translate into the required EnergyPlus inputs. Curves for the unit performance were derived in a similar manner as for the two-stage unit, and the overall equations for efficiency and capacity as a function of water and air temperature have the same form as what it used for the two-stage 10 and single-stage units. 11 As a result, only two sets of curves, for full and part load, are shown here. Unlike the two-stage coil, a part-load curve is not applied when the load is less than the part-load conditions because the equipment is assumed to be able to correctly modulate to very low part-load ratios, whereas a two-stage system might be cycling during low loads. The model interpolates when operating between full load and part load in a way that can account for the real

Because these curves are simpler and comprise fewer points, a simple quadratic regression can yield a good fit for each curve. Cubic fits could be used if they yield better results, but they would require additional data of a shape where the impact would be meaningfully affected. Variable-speed equipment also sees a wider range of water and airflow conditions during operation because it modulates to match the load, rather than cycling at low loads.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.2.3  Pump Mass Flow Rate EMS

As mentioned in the two-stage GHP document EMS section, EnergyPlus models with the variable-speed, water-to-air coil object for two-stage systems and variable-speed, water-to-air GHP systems have some deficiency in pump operations and pump energy calculations.

As described in the previous section when discussing the operation of variable-speed GHPs and how that relates to how the performance curves are used, the pump used for a GHP can also modulate across most conditions, with the only exception being that at continuously very low loads (less than 20 -30% of the full-load capacity), the equipment will cycle rather than being able to maintain continuous operation. But as mentioned in the two-stage GHP document, EnergyPlus currently models a constant water flow rate at time steps below the first specified speed in the two-stage and variable-speed GHP models. In addition to what is mentioned in the two-stage GHP document about the EnergyPlus pump power EMS program, a pump mass flow rate EMS program is therefore needed for variable-speed GHP models to account for the varying water flow rates below the first specified speed and to account for the impact on coil performance.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)
metadata.measure_name: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.2.3  Pump Mass Flow Rate EMS

flow rate EMS program is therefore needed for variable-speed GHP models to account for the varying water flow rates below the first specified speed and to account for the impact on coil performance.

EMS is an advanced feature in EnergyPlus to develop custom control and modeling routines. It allows users to write their own computer programs to override selected aspects of EnergyPlus modeling. In this case, the pump mass flow rate is overridden and recalculated in the EMS program for every time step when the heat pump is operating below the first specified speed. This program is combined with the program previously described in the two-stage GHP report that changes the pump power below the lowest specified speed to correctly model the pump behavior of variable-speed GHP units.

EnergyPlus-predicted heating and cooling loads are reported and used in the EMS program along with the system nominal capacities to calculate the fraction of full load for the GHPs. The pump mass flow rate is calculated based on the fraction of full load. Whenever the pump mass flow rate is below the first specified speed of a variable-speed GHP, it will be overridden to overcome the EnergyPlus limitation mentioned in the two-stage GHP document.

load. Whenever the pump mass flow rate is below the first specified speed of a variable-speed GHP, it will be overridden to overcome the EnergyPlus limitation mentioned in the two-stage GHP document.

Because the two-stage and variable-speed GHP models use the same EnergyPlus HVAC objects, they share the same basic model structure with different inputs and performance curves processed from their respective equipment manufacturer data. This means that the EnergyPlus node water flow rate limit bug fix described in the two-stage document will be applied to both types of GHP systems when EnergyPlus 25.1.0 or later is used for ResStock.

By combining all these efforts, OpenStudio-HPXML can model the desired GHP operations with the correct interactions between pumps and heat pump coils and give satisfying results for the variable-speed GHP systems.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 2.3  Limitations and Concerns

In addition to the limitations and concerns discussed in the prior single-stage and two-stage GHP documents, the following concerns are unique to variable-speed GHPs:

- EMS program flow rate calculation: The EMS program used for variable-speed GHPs calculates the pump mass flow rate based on the steady-state heat pump capacities. Although this approach is sufficient for most conditions, it could introduce minor differences in the mass flow estimates, which could slightly affect flow-rate-dependent capacity and efficiency curves.
- Limited compressor speed data: Only two speeds are explicitly modeled due to limitations in the manufacturer data for the variable-speed unit used here. Interpolation between these speeds, along with water flow and airflow-rate-dependent curves, is applied to represent performance across the full operating range.
- Part-load representation: Unlike single- or two-stage systems, no part-load ratio to partload fraction curve is applied for the variable-speed model. In EnergyPlus, the system is assumed to continuously modulate between 0 and 100% capacity, even at very low-load fractions. In reality, at extremely low-load conditions (for example, 5% of the maximum load), even variable-speed equipment might cycle on and off to meet the load seen during

Figure 25 shows the annual energy consumption of homes with baseline HVAC and three different GHP options (single stage, two stage, and variable speed) for comparison. For the overall housing stock (top) -including homes ineligible for GHP upgrades -variable-speed GHPs could save as much as 35% of the energy consumed by residential buildings, compared to 24% saved by single-stage GHPs. The variable-speed GHP systems represent a substantial efficiency improvement over existing air conditioners and air-source heat pumps used for cooling, such that the energy savings outweigh the addition of cooling in homes that do not have cooling in the baseline, leading to positive cooling energy savings nationwide. When only considering the portion of the housing stock in which GHPs can be installed (see Section 2 for the applicability criteria of this measure), variable-speed GHPs reduce the homes' energy consumption by 46%, compared to 31% for single-stage GHPs.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) — 3.4  Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the variable-speed GHP upgrade will have on electrical panels. The modeling assumptions and details about electric panels in ResStock can be found in the single-stage GHP documentation (Maguire et al. 2025a).

First, Figure 36 and Figure 37 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. The first column in Figure 36 , 'All,' shows that approximately 35% of all dwelling units have 0 or only 1 breaker space available. The first column in Figure 37 shows that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock, but the other 2.3% of electric panels already have an existing capacity constraint.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. But it is important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable; hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

text:
Light Air Sealing — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover the majority of high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

Light Air Sealing — Executive Summary

is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Light Air Sealing .

This upgrade demonstrated 6% modeled total site energy savings (166 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (see Figure 3 for details). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 11% stock natural gas heating savings (103 TWh)
- 10% stock electricity heating savings (21 TWh)
- 11% stock fuel oil heating savings (15 TWh)
- 11% stock propane heating savings (11 TWh).

text:
Light Air Sealing — 1  Technology Summary

Air sealing involves identifying and closing large and small gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the home's primary or secondary pressure boundaries, such as around windows, doors, attic hatches, and plumbing or wiring holes (U.S. Department of Energy 2025). These leaks, whether large or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air to escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the workload on the heating and cooling system. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Green Building Alliance 2025). For a comprehensive overview of air sealing and the technology in general, see ResStock Measure Documentation: Advanced Air Sealing (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026).

metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing

text:
Light Air Sealing — 1.1  Technical Measure Details

Only dwelling units that have an infiltration rate of 10 ACH50 or greater are assumed to be applicable for this 'Light Air Sealing' measure. That is because this ResStock measure does not add mechanical ventilation to dwelling units with a low infiltration rate. Whole-home mechanical ventilation should be considered when the infiltration rate is 5 ACH50 or less according to the 2015 International Residential Code (ICC Digital Codes 2024). This 10 ACH50 cutoff is due to natural ventilation requirements that homes generally receive at least 0.35 air changes per hour (ASHRAE 2016, International Code Council 2021). 1 A 25% reduction in infiltration of a 10 ACH50 dwelling will reduce its ACH50 value to 7.5 ACH50. The 'LBL factor' (developed by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) is a factor based on climate region and other characteristics, and is used to convert estimated air changes in a building by natural means without a fan to the air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50). Using an LBL factor of 20, the lowest allowable infiltration level without forcing natural ventilation into the house is 7 ACH50 (ENERGY STAR 2001).

1 At least 0.35 air changes per hour, but not less than 15 cubic feet of air per minute per person (International Code Council 2021). See ASHRAE 2016 for the specific requirements and equations for calculating required ventilation.

text:
Light Air Sealing — 3  Modeling Approach

Previous air sealing modeling in ResStock covers how residential air infiltration is modeled (Phoung, Lou and White 2026). ResStock models residential air infiltration values expressed as ACH50. Each dwelling unit in the ResStock dataset is assigned an existing ACH50 value based on housing stock characteristics, informed by the Residential Diagnostics Database (ResDB). ResStock integrates this information using probabilistic sampling logic to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock. These infiltration rates are dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. In ResStock, the current infiltration values are based on single-family detached blower door tests in units of ACH50. For single-family detached homes, the ACH50 values reflect total leakage to the outdoors, and buffer zones such as unconditioned attics, crawlspaces, and garages. However, for multifamily and single-family attached units, ResStock models leakage as total unit air leakage, which includes airflow to both the exterior and adjacent units. To estimate only the leakage to the exterior, the model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exteriorfacing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs. In this work, dwelling units with infiltration rates ≥ 10 ACH50 are eligible for a 25% reduction in infiltration rat

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025). This measure does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

text:
Light Air Sealing — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

ResStock relies heavily on the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow, and the general steps are as follows:

- -Step 1: Build probability distributions for housing characteristics in the energy model
- -Step 2: Apply custom ResStock model arguments to the energy model
- -Step 3: Fill in energy model assumptions using BuildResidentialHPXML
- -Step 4: Fill in appliance and occupant schedule assumptions using BuildResidentialScheduleFile
- -Step 5: Use the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to change the building energy model to a HPXML file and then model the dwelling unit

For in-depth information about the ResStock modeling workflow, including repository version tags, housing characteristic distribution examples, sampling descriptions, and model articulation, see the Version History and the Workflow sections of the Technical Reference Guide from the ResStock 2025 Release 1, which is unchanged for this ResStock 2025 Release 2 (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Light Air Sealing — 3.2  Air Sealing

In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OS-HPXML parameters using the options\_lookup.tsv file. Measure upgrades, such as infiltration, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how infiltration upgrades are implemented in the ResStock workflow.

In cases where infiltration details (ACH50) are not explicitly defined in ResStock, default values (Table 3) are assigned by OS-HPXML based on building characteristics.

text:
Light Air Sealing — Default Inputs from OpenStudio-HPXML for Infiltration Upgrade

The ResStock inputs in the table above are sent to OS-HPXML. Any values that are not specified by ResStock are calculated using the defaults in the BuildResidentialHPXML OpenStudio measure based on building characteristics. These characteristics include the building's floor area, number of stories, vintage, ceiling height, duct locations, foundation type, and climate zone. Other characteristics include stack effect, indoor-outdoor temperature difference, wind speed, and more. In multifamily and attached buildings, OS-HPXML assumes that some air leakage occurs between units rather than solely to the outside. To account for this, the software adjusts total infiltration based on the portion of the building envelope that is exposed to the exterior. More details of the infiltration model and default values can be found in the Alberta Air Infiltration Model (AIM-2) (Walker and Wilson 1990).

text:
Light Air Sealing — 4.4  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 dwelling models (i.e., the total number of units modeled in the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset to represent the national building stock), 426,800 models (77.6%) are applicable for the light air sealing upgrade. For the 426,800 applicable models, the total weighted baseline modeled site energy consumption is 2,664 TWh per year. After applying the light air sealing upgrade, the total modeled site consumption was reduced to 2,498 TWh per year, a 6.2% reduction. Figure 3 shows that energy savings from light air sealing primarily come from heating and cooling end uses, with 11% natural gas heating savings (104 TWh), 10% electricity heating savings (21 TWh), 11% fuel oil heating savings (15 TWh), 11% propane heating savings (11 TWh), and 3% electricity cooling savings (8 TWh). Other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged or very minimally impacted.

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing

text:
Light Air Sealing — 4.4  Stock Energy Impacts

heating savings (15 TWh), 11% propane heating savings (11 TWh), and 3% electricity cooling savings (8 TWh). Other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged or very minimally impacted.

Reasoning for these results was provided in previous air sealing work (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) and is restated here. Air sealing improves building performance by reducing air leakage. Thus, its impact is confined to systems that respond to indoor temperature fluctuations. The heating and cooling energy savings can be attributed to reduced air infiltration, which limits the amount of cold or hot outdoor air entering the building envelope during the heating or cooling season, respectively. This leads to lower heating and cooling loads, reduced runtime for space heating and cooling systems, and associated reductions in fan and pump operation.

As shown in Figure 10, greater average annual energy savings are generally achieved in colder climates, particularly zones 7A, 6A, and 5A. These cold climate zones start with higher average consumption and therefore have more opportunity for savings through air sealing. Figure 11 further confirms these trends, with the highest percent savings observed in 7A (9%), 6A (8%), and 5A (7%). This is primarily due to large heating loads in these climates and the greater temperature differentials that drive infiltration losses.

Climate zones with moisture classification A (moist) typically exhibit higher energy savings compared to climate zones with moisture classifications B (dry) or C (marine). In moist climates, infiltration air contains more humidity, requiring HVAC systems to expend additional energy to remove both sensible and latent heat. In contrast, dry climates have minimal latent loads, and marine climates generally experience more moderate temperatures, resulting in lower overall energy use associated with conditioning infiltration air. Therefore, improving infiltration will have greater effect in moist climates and demonstrate higher savings.

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. This results in a time-series profile broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model represents the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in (Reyna, et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are provided in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (National Laboratory of the Rockies 2025).

et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are provided in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (National Laboratory of the Rockies 2025).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape package: light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation upgrade.

The advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation upgrade achieved 14% modeled total site energy savings (461 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 3). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 18% stock natural gas savings (261 TWh)
- 9% stock electricity savings (141 TWh)
- 19% stock fuel oil savings (33 TWh)
- 18% stock propane savings (27 TWh).

metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1  Technology Summary

This upgrade package, which includes light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation, combines three key areas of a retrofit measure. As stated in previous reports about these topics, the goal of these upgrades is to reduce heat losses in winter and retain cool air in the conditioned space during summer. Air sealing alone does not eliminate the need for insulation (U.S. Department of Energy 2025). Insulation and air sealing work best together to improve comfort and energy efficiency. Therefore, they are often implemented as a package to address complementary aspects of a home's energy performance, and their combined effect is much greater than any single measure alone. Together, these upgrades help to lower energy bills, enhance indoor comfort, and improve indoor air quality year round (Lou, Phoung and Parker 2026).

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Light Air Sealing

The light air sealing methodology in this measure package is reused from an existing measure, and the background information is restated here (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026). Air sealing involves identifying and closing large and small gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the home's primary or secondary pressure boundaries, such as around windows, doors, attic hatches, and plumbing or wiring holes (U.S. Department of Energy 2025). These leaks, whether large or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the workload on the heating and cooling system. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Green Building Alliance 2025).

Refer to the light air sealing documentation for more information on this topic (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026).

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Attic Floor Insulation

The attic floor insulation methodology in this measure package is also reused from an existing measure, and the background information is restated here (Phoung, Lou and White 2026). Insulating the attic floor reduces heat transfer between the living space and the unconditioned attic. In colder climates, this keeps heat inside during winter. In warmer climates, it helps keep the living space cooler. The effectiveness of insulation is measured by its R-value; a higher R-value indicates better resistance to heat flow. Installing insulation in existing homes typically involves blowing loose-fill insulation over the attic floor, especially in unfinished attics. The optimal insulation level depends on the climate zone and the home's existing insulation. Refer to the attic insulation documentation for guidance on recommended R-values (as established by International Energy Conservation Code) and installation approaches (Phoung, Lou and White 2026).

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — Duct Sealing and Insulation

The duct insulation and sealing methodology in this measure package is similarly reused from an existing measure, and the background information is restated here (Lou and Liu 2026). Ducts distribute heated or cooled air throughout the house. In many homes, especially older ones, these ducts have leaks that allow conditioned air to escape into unconditioned or semi-conditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. As a result, the system must work harder and use more energy to maintain the desired temperature. Duct sealing addresses these leaks using mastic, metal tape, or an aerosol-based sealant, depending on the situation. Sealing ducts improves system efficiency, maintains more consistent room temperatures, and enhances indoor air quality by preventing dirty attic or crawlspace air from entering the ducts. Duct sealing can also reduce unintentional pressure imbalances, which may cause indoor air quality or combustion safety concerns. See the duct sealing documentation for more information on methods and materials (Lou and Liu 2026).

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

If this work were to be done as a retrofit, the correct order for implementing this upgrade package is: (1) light air sealing, (2) duct sealing and insulation, and (3) attic floor insulation. The building science behind this ordering has been previously described in another report (Lou, Phoung and Parker 2026), and the information is restated here. Sealing leaks before adding insulation ensures that the insulation performs as intended. It also makes leaks easier to identify and reduces the burden on field staff since they are not working around additional insulation. Once air sealing targets are met, it is essential to address the HVAC system by sealing any leaky ducts to prevent the loss of conditioned air, particularly in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. Attic floor insulation should be installed last. While highly effective, it must follow air and duct sealing to avoid covering up critical areas that require sealing and to ensure ducts running through the attic are properly sealed and insulated beforehand.

Therefore, we assume that upgrades will be implemented in the following sequence: light air sealing is applied first to applicable dwelling units, with the goal of achieving a 25% reduction in the infiltration rate measured by an ACH50 change.

After air sealing, HVAC ducts in applicable homes are sealed and insulated to achieve the following:

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 1.2  Technical Measure Details

with the goal of achieving a 25% reduction in the infiltration rate measured by an ACH50 change.

After air sealing, HVAC ducts in applicable homes are sealed and insulated to achieve the following:

- A maximum of 5% duct air leakage to the outside
- Duct insulation level of R-8.

Attic floor insulation is the upgraded in applicable dwelling units to the following levels:

- R-49 in climate zone 1
- R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

Note: when modeling these upgrades in ResStock, the order does not affect the outputs of the model. All upgrades are applied at the same time to the model file. More details about the modeling assumptions for these three measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026) (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) (Lou and Liu 2026).

metadata.doc_title: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation
metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 2  Applicability

The light air sealing upgrade is applied to dwelling units with infiltration rates greater than or equal to 10 ACH50.

The attic floor insulation upgrade is applied only to dwelling units with unfinished attics (vented and unvented attic types in ResStock). Specifically, the upgrade is applied when attic floor insulation is below R-49 in climate zone 1 and below R-60 in climate zones 2 through 8.

Duct sealing applies to dwelling units with duct leakage to the outside greater than 6% or duct insulation rated below R-6. Dwelling units with 0% leakage to the outside and uninsulated ducts are not applicable, as these configurations typically indicate that the ducts are located entirely within conditioned spaces (Lou and Liu 2026).

Further details on the applicability criteria and residential building stock saturation for each of these three measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026) (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) (Lou and Liu 2026).

Table 1 summarizes the stock saturation for the upgrade package that includes all three measures. This comprehensive package is applicable to approximately 92.5% of the U.S. housing stock. However, most dwelling units receive only one or some of these upgrades. Only 22.9% of dwelling units receive all three upgrades.

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 3  Modeling Approach

The modeling approach of the three individual measures can be found in the accompanying documentation (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026) (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) (Lou and Liu 2026).

Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025). This measure does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. However, electrical panel metrics are included as a standard output for this and all other envelope measures. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

This section first confirms the intended modeling approach for the upgrade by examining individual dwelling models, then presents the results if the upgrade were applied to the entire applicable building stock.

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1  Single Building Example

This section examines a modeled dwelling unit in Colorado (climate zone 5B) that underwent the envelope package upgrade, which includes light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation. The dwelling unit is in Denver County, and it has a Single-Family Attached geometry. It has a central air conditioning system that is SEER 13 and an 80% AFUE natural gas furnace. Table 3 presents the housing characteristics of the unit before and after the upgrade.

Table 3. Housing Characteristics of the Example Dwelling Unit Before and After the Envelope Package Upgrades (Light Air Sealing + Attic Insulation + Duct Sealing and Insulation)

| Housing Characteristics     | Before Envelope Package Upgrades    | After Envelope Package Upgrades   |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Infiltration                | 30 ACH50                            | 22.5 ACH50                        |
| Attic Insulation            | R-30                                | R-60                              |
| Duct Leakage and Insulation | 30% Leakage to Outside, Uninsulated | 5% Leakage to Outside, R-8        |

metadata.measure_name: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.1 Individual Building Annual Results

Table 4 shows the modeled annual energy consumption of the example dwelling unit before and after the upgrade.

Table 4. Individual Dwelling Unit Modeled Annual Results

|                                    |   Before |   After | Percent Decrease   |
|------------------------------------|----------|---------|--------------------|
| Site Energy for All Fuels [kWh]    |   34,457 |  24,165 | 29.9%              |
| Cooling Energy Consumption [kWh]   |    1,393 |   1,025 | 26.4%              |
| Heating Energy Consumption [kWh]   |   21,909 |  12,302 | 43.8%              |
| Cooling Hourly Peak Power [kBtu/h] |     21.0 |    20.7 | 1.4%               |
| Heating Hourly Peak Power [kBtu/h] |     59.5 |    34.4 | 42.2%              |

The dwelling unit shows a 29.9% annual site energy decrease, driven by the natural gas heating energy decrease of 43.8%. Cooling energy consumption decreases moderately as well at 26.4%. In terms of peak power impacts, the heating peak power decreases by 42.2% and the cooling peak power decreases by 1.4%.

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.1.2 Individual Building Time-Series Results

This section shows heating and cooling energy impact from two select days, January 3 as a representative winter day and July 11 for a representative summer day. These timeseries values are from the AMY 2018 dataset. Heating end uses include heating and heating fans/pumps. Cooling end uses include cooling and cooling fans/pumps.

Figure 1 shows the time-series heating energy consumption, which in this case comes from a natural gas furnace. This upgrade, shown in orange, consistently lowers the required heating energy throughout the whole day with the most significant impact during the early morning.

Figure 1. Modeled heating energy impact from the upgrade measure for one example dwelling unit model

![Image](99818_images/image_000002_4d7e81636b291ce740d47e604cf8809f3b81700045b6f6206a4c6bb5dc91da2f.png)

Figure 2 shows the time-series cooling energy consumption. This dwelling unit has a central air conditioning system. In general, the upgrade slightly lowers the required cooling energy consumption during the whole day. The sudden decrease in cooling energy around 12pm is due to thermostat changes. The largest impact is seen from the late afternoon into evening.

Figure 2. Modeled cooling energy impact from the upgrade measure for one example dwelling unit model

![Image](99818_images/image_000003_399736cc038f78c854548212a1ee2fe59abe2fe4f674cb357e6bfac7f2e62da8.png)

text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.2.1  Annual Energy Analysis

Figure 3 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the upgrade for all applicable dwelling units. The annual stock site energy savings from the package are 461 TWh, representing a 24% reduction. Most savings occurred in heating and cooling end uses. These include a 23% site energy reduction in electric heating fans and pumps, 23% site energy reduction in natural gas heating, 22% reduction in propane heating, 21% in electric heating, 21% in fuel oil heating, 18% reduction in cooling fans and pumps, and finally a 16% reduction in electricity for cooling.

Figure 3. Modeled annual site energy consumption for all applicable dwelling units

![Image](99818_images/image_000004_33e9629de1411eb0aa411ed5b81a43a6601ebece358f31b01763bb620121af3d.png)

Figure 4 shows the average annual site energy consumption per dwelling unit by end use before and after the envelope package for upgraded dwelling units. At least one measure in the package was applied to 92.5% of dwelling units. The average annual site energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 3,570 kWh, representing a 14% reduction.

Figure 4. Modeled average annual site energy consumption per upgraded dwelling unit

![Image](99818_images/image_000005_5c67dc53470d03a040991a1d59d537a3218decc7dd191cf35338b4845e0ef72a.png)

text:

4. Modeled average annual site energy consumption per upgraded dwelling unit

![Image](99818_images/image_000005_5c67dc53470d03a040991a1d59d537a3218decc7dd191cf35338b4845e0ef72a.png)

Figure 5 shows that older homes benefit most from the envelope package upgrades. On average, homes built before the 1960s achieve close to 16% annual energy savings, compared to less than 10% for homes built after the 2000s.

Figure 5. Modeled average annual site energy consumption saving percentage per upgraded dwelling unit, grouped by vintage

![Image](99818_images/image_000006_f4b1c423a98498dd7dfb915511b1ff1ddec902cc844117e16c6809db2bb194d2.png)

Figure 6 shows average site energy savings by baseline infiltration rate. Dwelling units with an infiltration rate of 10 ACH50 or above were eligible for all three measures of this package, whereas dwelling units with less than 10 ACH50 were not eligible for the light air sealing upgrade. Therefore, there are higher average site energy savings for infiltration rates 10 ACH50 and above.

Figure 6. Modeled average percent site energy savings per upgraded dwelling unit, grouped by baseline infiltration rate

![Image](99818_images/image_000007_e2baee4eaa779ed9d080b86a39b83a0091eb7542490304a061497591863c0640.png)

Attic insulation levels of R-49 and R-7 show site energy savings between 14% and 22%, respectively. text:
Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation — 4.3  Energy Utility Bill Impacts

This section shows modeled energy utility bill impacts as a result of this upgrade. Figure 9 shows a comparison of energy bill savings broken out by fuel for applicable dwelling units. Overall, most bill savings occur in electricity, with a total of $19.2B saved across the residential stock. Stock natural gas bill savings are $10.7B, while stock fuel oil and propane bill savings are dwelling units $3.0B and $2.6B, respectively.

Figure 9. Residential building stock modeled energy bill savings by fuel type

![Image](99818_images/image_000010_2ec6ff900dc5ed99d7712da4713df36c8a8fecb7d38d289c335007fb77bcdfcd.png)

Figure 10 shows the average annual energy bill percent savings broken out by fuel type. Average total bill savings are 10%, with an 8% reduction in electricity bills and a 15% reduction in natural gas bills. Fuel oil bills and propane bills see the largest percent reductions at 19% and 18%, respectively, however bills from these fuels make up a small portion of the total stock.

Figure 10. Modeled annual average energy bill impact by fuel

![Image](99818_images/image_000011_4e61da3669b0bfe92ffb114f9495ee1069571fff868bfdb02625477bc5ca7fa7.png)

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model represents the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al. 2022).

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — Executive Summary

is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al. 2022).

This document focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (GHP) (4.0 Coefficient of Performance [COP], 20.5 Energy Efficiency Ratio [EER]) With Light Envelope Improvements. This measure combines a two-stage GHP with light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation as a single package. Because this package is a combination of two other measures, this document focuses on the results associated with this combination of technologies, while individual measure documents for the two-stage GHP and light envelope improvements package provide methodology and results for these measures.

This upgrade package demonstrates 35% modeled total site energy savings (4.12 quadrillion Btu [quads]) for the U.S. residential building stock. These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 80% stock natural gas heating savings (3.14 quads)
- 42% stock cooling savings (0.55 quads)
- 70% stock fuel oil heating savings (0.40 quads)
- 80% stock propane heating savings (0.35 quads)
- 34% stock electricity heating increase (0.29 quads).

Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — Applicable

The GHP measure in this package applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with air ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

The light envelope measures in this package apply according to the following criteria:

- Light air sealing measure applies to dwellings with:
- o Infiltration rate of 10 ACH50 or more
- Attic insulation measure applies to dwellings with:
- o Unfinished attic & less than R-49 attic floor insulation & in climate zone 1
- o Unfinished attic & less than R-60 attic floor insulation & in climate zones 2 through 8
- Duct sealing and insulation measure applies to dwellings with:
- o More than 6% duct leakage to outside
- o Less than R-6 duct insulation.

The GHP must be applicable in order for the dwelling unit to also be eligible for the light envelope measures.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 1  Technology Summary

This measure combines a GHP measure and an envelope measure package into a single upgrade measure package. The first measure is a water-to-air GHP with a two-stage compressor rated at a COP of 4.0 and an EER of 20.5. More details on GHPs and how they are modeled in ResStock 2025 Release 1, including the details of modeling the ground heat exchanger, are included in the single-stage GHP measure document (Maguire, Fontanini, et al. 2026). The details of how twostage GHPs with this rated efficiency are modeled are included in the two-stage GHP measure document (Fontanini, et al. 2026). The details of the light envelope improvement measure package are included in the light air sealing, attic insulation, and duct sealing improvement measure document (Brossman and White 2026).

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.1  Applicability of Two-Stage GHP Measure

Using the same applicability criteria as the single-stage GHP and the stand-alone two-stage compressor, the water-to-air vertical ground heat exchanger GHP upgrade measure applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to roughly 71% of the existing building stock. 6.4% of the residential units that receive the GHP upgrade lack existing space cooling systems in the baseline and therefore receive a central cooling system via the GHP.

From the previous work on this GHP model, applicability of this measure upgrade is based on ResStock housing characteristics. These characteristics determine the available options and the options' details (Reyna, et al. 2025) (Fontanini, et al. 2026):

- 'HVAC Heating Efficiency' is used to apply each respective heat pump option.
- 'HVAC Has Ducts' describes the presence of ducts in the dwelling.
- 'Heating Type' describes the baseline heating fuel of the dwelling.
- 'HVAC Shared Efficiencies' describes the shared HVAC system of the dwelling, if applicable.
- 'Geometry Building Type Height' describes the height and building type of the dwelling.

More information on the ResStock housing characteristics can be found in the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025).

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.2  Applicability of Light Envelope Improvements Package

While envelope improvements are included for any home receiving a dual-stage GHP, the baseline conditions must warrant an improvement for each component of the upgrade to apply.

For the light air sealing upgrades to apply, the infiltration rate of the baseline home must be at least 10 air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50). The light air sealing upgrade is then applied to reach a 25% infiltration reduction. More details on air sealing applicability can be found in the light air sealing measure document (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026).

For duct sealing and insulation, the upgrade case installs R-6 duct insulation if existing ducts have an insulation level of R-4 or worse. Ducts are sealed to 5% leakage if there is more than 6% leakage in the baseline. These improvements can be installed independently of each other, or both may apply if both the leakage and insulation criteria are met. More details on duct sealing and insulation applicability can be found in the duct improvement measure document (Lou, Liu and Parker 2026).

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.2  Applicability of Light Envelope Improvements Package

apply if both the leakage and insulation criteria are met. More details on duct sealing and insulation applicability can be found in the duct improvement measure document (Lou, Liu and Parker 2026).

For attic insulation, this measure upgrades attic floor insulation in unfinished attics where the existing insulation is more than a difference of R-10 below the maximum level recommended by the IECC for each unit's climate zone. The post-retrofit Rvalue is set to reflect the maximum value recommended by code. For example, while the IECC recommends an R-value range of R49 to R-60 for climate zone 2, dwelling units in this zone are upgraded to R-60 to represent the upper bound of achievable performance. This approach ensures that the modeled retrofit captures both the energy savings potential of code-compliant upgrades and the levels typically achieved in field implementations. More details on attic insulation applicability can be found in the attic insulation measure document (Phoung, Lou and White 2026).

The ResStock 2025 Release 1 includes an additional, similar upgrade package to this document's upgrade package. The only difference in this upgrade package is that this document's air sealing is less intense. This document has a 25% infiltration reduction across homes with a baseline infiltration level of 10 ACH50 or more, while the similar upgrade package has prescriptive ACH50 values based on climate zone. For more information see the more advanced air sealing documentation (Phuong, Lou and White 2026) and the two-stage GHP with advanced envelope improvements (Maguire, Fontanini, et al. 2026).

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.3  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, et al. 2025). These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudioHPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the GHP upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are contained in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

For information on how OpenStudio-HPXML handles controls in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1 see here, and for how it handles HVAC distribution see here. Additional details on applying the two-stage GHP measure are included in the relevant section of that measure document.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.4  Two-Stage Water-to-Air Vertical Ground Heat Exchanger GHP Upgrade Details

This section about the GHP is covered in the two-stage GHP document, and is restated here (Fontanini, et al. 2026).

Details specific to the two-stage GHP that may interact with the light envelope improvements are included below. In many cases, the approach used here is the same as when two-stage GHP equipment is installed on its own, but relevant portions of that approach are reiterated here. Since envelope improvements can change the loads and size of equipment installed, this document focuses on the approach to sizing equipment.

metadata.section: 2.4  Two-Stage Water-to-Air Vertical Ground Heat Exchanger GHP Upgrade Details
metadata.measure_name: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.4.1  GHP Sizing Methodology

The two-stage GHP uses the same sizing methodology as the single-stage GHP (Maguire, Fontanini, et al. 2026). The design heating and cooling loads are calculated in accordance with Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) Manuals J (ACCA 2016), and the equipment size is selected based on ACCA Manual S (ACCA 2014) using a routine included in OpenStudio-HPXML. Note that because the GHP sizing routine includes accounting of the peak heating and cooling building loads, equipment sizes are decreased when envelope improvements are included. This means that for the combined package the equipment capacity, ground heat exchanger size, and associated cost for installing a GHP may be reduced compared to just installing a two-stage GHP.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements
metadata.measure_name: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — Why sizing around envelope improvements matters:

When the building envelope is improved (through measures such as added insulation, air sealing, or high-performance windows) the peak heating and cooling loads are reduced. This directly impacts the sizing calculation for the GHP, allowing for smaller-capacity equipment to meet the same comfort requirements and reducing the capital costs for the heat pump. Smaller systems also require less ground heat exchanger length, which further lowers installation costs and can improve system efficiency. By addressing the envelope before or during GHP sizing, the project avoids oversizing, reduces upfront and operating costs, and maximizes the long-term performance of the system.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.4.2 Ground Heat Exchanger

The two-stage GHP uses the same type of ground heat exchanger as the stand-alone two-stage GHP measure. Both use thermally enhanced grout and pipe materials to improve heat transfer, and the loop is installed in a vertical, rectangular configuration.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — Why the ground heat exchanger matters when adding envelope improvements:

The ground heat exchanger is one of the largest cost components of a GHP system because drilling and installing the vertical loops is labor- and equipment-intensive. When the building envelope is improved, the heating and cooling loads are reduced, which means the GHP can be smaller. A smaller GHP requires less heat exchange with the ground, allowing for shorter ground heat exchangers. This reduction in drilling length can significantly cut installation costs and make the overall system more affordable. Better insulation and air sealing can not only shrink the equipment size, but also shrink the number of vertical feet of drilling.

Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing

Each individual component of this measure is documented separately (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026) (Lou, Liu and Parker 2026) and documented as a package (Brossman and White 2026).

The rest of this section is restated here from previous work done on the GHP and envelope measure (Maguire, Fontanini, et al. 2026) (Brossman and White, ResStock Measure Documentation: Light Air Sealing, Attic Floor Insulation, and Duct Sealing and Insulation

2026). The goal of this package is to capture efficiency measures that can be applied to existing buildings. This is similar to what might be done as part of weatherization upgrades to a home, where the easiest and most beneficial improvements are made.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing

measures that can be applied to existing buildings. This is similar to what might be done as part of weatherization upgrades to a home, where the easiest and most beneficial improvements are made.

This upgrade package integrates three coordinated energy efficiency measures: light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation, to address sources of energy loss in a home. Air sealing targets gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the building envelope to reduce uncontrolled air leakage, improve comfort, and lessen the workload on heating and cooling systems. Attic floor insulation slows heat transfer between living areas and unconditioned attic spaces, keeping heat inside in winter and out in summer. Duct sealing and insulation prevents conditioned air from escaping into unconditioned spaces through leaky ducts, improving HVAC efficiency, maintaining more even indoor temperatures, and protecting indoor air quality. While each measure provides benefits individually, their combined effect is greater, making them most effective when implemented as a package.

metadata.doc_title: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements
metadata.section: 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing
metadata.measure_name: Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing

indoor temperatures, and protecting indoor air quality. While each measure provides benefits individually, their combined effect is greater, making them most effective when implemented as a package.

The recommended implementation sequence is based on building science principles. First, light air sealing is applied to achieve a 25% infiltration reduction, followed by duct sealing and insulating to reduce leakage to a maximum of 5% and achieve R-8 duct insulation, and finally upgrading attic floor insulation. This order ensures air leaks are addressed before insulation is installed, prevents ducts from being buried before sealing, and optimizes the performance of both insulation and the HVAC system. By following this sequence, field staff can more easily identify and seal problem areas and avoid rework.

Together, these measures improve comfort, lower energy bills, and enhance indoor air quality throughout the year. Air sealing stabilizes indoor temperatures and minimizes drafts, duct sealing reduces waste and protects against contaminants entering the system, and attic insulation locks in the conditioned air for longer periods. When applied together, they create a tighter, betterinsulated, and more efficient home, with benefits that are greater and more durable than any single measure alone.

Figure 3 shows the annual site energy consumption for the applicable housing stock split out by Building America climate zone (Antonopoulos, et al. 2022). As envelope improvements reduce loads, savings are seen in all climate zones. The largest magnitude savings are seen in the MixedHumid and the Cold climate zones. The reduction in heating load and associated energy consumption provides most of the savings in these climate zones. Note that for all climate zones, installing a two-stage GHP is the primary driver of savings, while additional envelope improvements further increase the savings. Looking more closely at individual end uses, all climate zones show an increase in electricity consumption for heating fans and pumps, and conversely all climate zones, except Subarctic, show savings from cooling.

Dwellings with existing electric heating are replacing electric resistance equipment, such as an electric furnace, with a more efficient GHP. Energy bills for applicable dwelling units are shown in this section. The average energy bill for the two-stage GHP with light envelope improvements is shown in Figure 6. On average, total energy bills decreased by 22% (over $500 per year) for the two-stage GHP with light envelope improvements compared to baseline dwelling units. All fuel costs decreased on average, with 2% savings on electricity bills, 66% savings on natural gas bills, 85% savings on propane bills, and 93% savings on fuel oil bills.

text:
Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER) With Light Envelope Improvements — 3.4  Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the two-stage GHP with light envelope improvements will have on electrical panels. The modeling assumptions and details about electric panels in ResStock can be found in the single-stage GHP documentation (Maguire, Fontanini, et al. 2026).

First, Figure 8 and Figure 9 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. Figure 8 shows in the first column (labeled 'All') that about 35% of all dwelling units have one or fewer breaker spaces available. Figure 9 shows in the first column that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. Hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

It is estimated that about 31% of dwelling units upgrading to a two-stage GHP with envelope improvements will experience either a capacity and/or space constraint, and the other 69% will experience no constraint. The next three figures show percentages of dwelling units for each state that would have some type of electric panel constraint after the two-stage GHP with envelope improvements is applied. Figure 11 shows a range of 6%-65% of dwelling units that would have either a capacity and/or space constraint after this upgrade package, with the largest prevalence of panel constraints occurring in colder states with high heating requirements. Specifically looking at space constraints, Figure 12 shows a smaller range from about 2% to 51% of dwelling units that would have a space constraint. Finally, Figure 13 shows a range of roughly 4% to 40% of dwelling units would have a capacity constraint.

In general, switching to a GHP system is more likely to face panel constraints in heatingdominated climates due to a substantial new electric load being introduced. Compared with the stand-alone two-stage GHP measure (Jeff Maguire 2026), which shows ranges of 11%-70% for either capacity and/or space constraints, 4%-54% for space constraints, and 7%-48% for capacity constraints, these results indicate that light envelope improvements help mitigate panel constraints.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover most high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model represents the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al., 2022).

Reyna et al. (Reyna, et al., 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson, et al., 2022).

This document focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (GHP) (4.4 Coefficient of Performance [COP], 30.9 Energy Efficiency Ratio [EER]) With Light Envelope Improvements. This measure combines a variable-speed GHP with light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation as a single package. Because this package is a combination of two other measures, this document focuses on the results associated with this combination of technologies, while individual measure documents for the variable-speed GHP and light envelope improvements package provide methodology and results for those measures.

This upgrade package demonstrates 39% modeled total site energy savings (4.62 quadrillion Btu [quads]) for the U.S. residential building stock. These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 80% stock natural gas heating savings (3.14 quads)
- 64% stock cooling savings (0.85 quads)
- 65% stock fuel oil heating savings (0.40 quads)
- 80% stock propane heating savings (0.36 quads)
- 23% stock electricity heating increase (0.20 quads).

Applicable This GHP measure in this package applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with air ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

The light envelope measures in this package apply according to the following criteria:

- Light air sealing measure applies to dwellings with:
- o Infiltration rate of 10 ACH50 or more
- Attic insulation measure applies to dwellings with:
- o Unfinished attic & less than R-49 attic floor insulation & in climate zone 1
- o Unfinished attic & less than R-60 attic floor insulation & in climate zones 2 through 8
- Duct sealing and insulation measure applies to dwellings with:
- o More than 6% duct leakage to outside
- o Less than R-6 duct insulation.

The GHP must be applicable in order for the dwelling unit to also be eligible for the light envelope measures.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 1  Technology Summary

This measure combines two separate measures into a single package. The first measure is a water-to-air GHP with a variable-speed compressor rated at a COP of 4.4 and an EER of 30.9. More details on GHPs and how they are modeled in ResStock 2025 Release 1, including the details of modeling the ground heat exchanger, are included in the single-stage GHP measure document (Maguire, et al., 2026). The details of how variable-speed GHPs with this rated efficiency are modeled are included in the variable-speed GHP measure document (Maguire, et al., 2026). The details of the light envelope improvement measure package are included in the light air sealing, attic insulation, and duct sealing improvement measure document (Brossman & White, 2026).

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.1  Applicability of a Variable-Speed GHP Measure

Using the same applicability criteria as the single-stage GHP and the stand-alone variable-speed compressor, the water-to-air vertical ground heat exchanger GHP upgrade measure applies to all dwellings with:

- Non-shared (in-unit) HVAC and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Shared (across multiple units) HVAC and a building height of <8 stories and any of the following heating fuels: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, or propane
- Dwelling units with ducts
- Dwelling units with soil thermal conductivity greater than 0.8 Btu/hr-ft-°F.

With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to roughly 71% of the existing building stock. 6.4% of the residential units that receive the GHP upgrade lack existing space cooling systems in the baseline and therefore receive a central cooling system via the GHP.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.2  Applicability of Light Envelope Improvements Package

The information in this section is repeated here from a previous report (Brossman, White, & Lou, 2026). While envelope improvements are included for any home receiving a variable-speed GHP, the baseline conditions must warrant an improvement for each component of the upgrade to apply.

For the light air sealing upgrades to apply, the infiltration rate of the baseline home must be at least 10 air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50). The light air sealing upgrade is then applied to reach a 25% infiltration reduction. More details on air sealing applicability can be found in the light air sealing measure document (Brossman, Phoung, & White, 2026).

For duct sealing and insulation, the upgrade case installs R-6 duct insulation if existing ducts have an insulation level of R-4 or worse. Ducts are sealed to 5% leakage if there is more than 6% leakage in the baseline. These improvements can be installed independently of each other, or both may apply if both the leakage and insulation criteria are met. More details on duct sealing and insulation applicability can be found in the duct improvement measure document (Lou, Liu, & Parker, 2026).

if both the leakage and insulation criteria are met. More details on duct sealing and insulation applicability can be found in the duct improvement measure document (Lou, Liu, & Parker, 2026).

For attic insulation, this measure upgrades attic floor insulation in unfinished attics where the existing R-value is more than 10 below the maximum level recommended by the IECC for each unit's climate zone. The post-retrofit Rvalue is set to reflect the maximum value recommended by code. For example, while the IECC recommends an R-value range of R-49 to R-60 for climate zone 2, dwelling units in this zone are upgraded to R-60 to represent the upper bound of achievable performance. This approach ensures that the modeled retrofit captures both the energy savings potential of code-compliant upgrades and the levels typically achieved in field implementations. More details on attic insulation applicability can be found in the attic insulation measure document (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2026).

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.3  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

The ResStock building stock energy model contains conditional probability distributions of building characteristics that are representative of the U.S. residential building stock (Reyna, et al., 2025). These are sampled to create a synthetic stock where each sample has an assigned option for each characteristic for each dwelling unit to be simulated. ResStock utilizes the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to translate these dwelling characteristics into building models ready to be simulated via OpenStudio ®  and EnergyPlus ®  through an HPXML file. For reference, the state of the OpenStudio-HPXML repository when the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset was created can be found here. Assumptions about the GHP upgrades that are not explicitly defined in ResStock are contained in the BuildResidentialHPXML measure.

For information on how OpenStudio-HPXML handles controls in ResStock Dataset 2025 Release 1 see here, and for how it handles HVAC distribution see here. Additional details on applying the variable-speed GHP measure are included in the relevant section of that measure document.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.4.1  GHP Sizing Methodology

The variable-speed GHP uses the same sizing methodology as the single- and two-stage GHPs (Maguire, et al., 2026) (Fontanini, et al., 2026). The design heating and cooling loads are calculated in accordance with Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) Manuals J (ACCA, 2016), and the equipment size is selected based on ACCA Manual S (ACCA, 2014) using a routine included in OpenStudio-HPXML. Note that because the GHP sizing routine includes accounting of the peak heating and cooling building loads, equipment sizes are decreased when envelope improvements are included. This means that for the combined package the equipment capacity, ground heat exchanger size, and associated cost for installing a GHP may be reduced compared to just installing a variable-speed GHP.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — Why sizing around envelope improvements matters:

This section is taken from the two-stage GHP with light envelope improvements document and repeated here (Brossman, White, & Lou, 2026). When the building envelope is improved (through measures such as added insulation, air sealing, or high-performance windows) the peak heating and cooling loads are reduced. This directly impacts the sizing calculation for the GHP, allowing for smaller-capacity equipment to meet the same comfort requirements and reducing the capital costs for the heat pump. Smaller systems also require less ground heat exchanger length, which further lowers installation costs and can improve system efficiency. By addressing the envelope before or during GHP sizing, the project avoids oversizing, reduces upfront and operating costs, and maximizes the long-term performance of the system.

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.4.2 Ground Heat Exchanger

The variable-speed GHP uses the same type of ground heat exchanger as the stand-alone variable-speed GHP measure. Both use thermally enhanced grout and pipe materials to improve heat transfer, and the loop is installed in a vertical, rectangular configuration.
