text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — Why the ground heat exchanger matters when adding envelope improvements:

The ground heat exchanger is one of the largest cost components of a GHP system because drilling and installing the vertical loops is labor- and equipment-intensive. When the building envelope is improved, the heating and cooling loads are reduced, which means the GHP can be smaller. A smaller GHP requires less heat exchange with the ground, allowing for shorter ground heat exchangers. This reduction in drilling length can significantly cut installation costs and make the overall system more affordable. Better insulation and air sealing can not only shrink the equipment size, but also shrink the number of vertical feet of drilling.

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing

measures that can be applied to existing buildings. This is similar to what might be done as part of weatherization upgrades to a home, where the easiest and most beneficial improvements are made.

This upgrade package integrates three coordinated energy efficiency measures: light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing and insulation, to address sources of energy loss in a home. Air sealing targets gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the building envelope to reduce uncontrolled air leakage, improve comfort, and lessen the workload on heating and cooling systems. Attic floor insulation slows heat transfer between living areas and unconditioned attic spaces, keeping heat inside in winter and out in summer. Duct sealing and insulation prevents conditioned air from escaping into unconditioned spaces through leaky ducts, improving HVAC efficiency, maintaining more even indoor temperatures, and protecting indoor air quality. While each measure provides benefits individually, their combined effect is greater, making them most effective when implemented as a package.

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 2.5  Attic Insulation, Light Air Sealing, and Duct Sealing

indoor temperatures, and protecting indoor air quality. While each measure provides benefits individually, their combined effect is greater, making them most effective when implemented as a package.

The recommended implementation sequence is based on building science principles. First, light air sealing is applied to achieve a 25% infiltration reduction, followed by duct sealing and insulating to reduce leakage to a maximum of 5% and achieve R-8 duct insulation, and finally upgrading attic floor insulation. This order ensures air leaks are addressed before insulation is installed, prevents ducts from being buried before sealing, and optimizes the performance of both insulation and the HVAC system. By following this sequence, field staff can more easily identify and seal problem areas and avoid rework.

Together, these measures improve comfort, lower energy bills, and enhance indoor air quality throughout the year. Air sealing stabilizes indoor temperatures and minimizes drafts, duct sealing reduces waste and protects against contaminants entering the system, and attic insulation locks in the conditioned air for longer periods. When applied together, they create a tighter, betterinsulated, and more efficient home, with benefits that are greater and more durable than any single measure alone.

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 3.1  Annual Stock Savings

Figure 1 shows the annual site energy consumption for all dwelling units, regardless of whether they got the upgrade, for the baseline and variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements package. Figure 2 shows the annual site energy consumption only for dwelling units that received the upgrade. For this upgrade, about 71% of the residential housing stock received the upgrade.

In each of the two figures, significant energy savings come from heating energy savings from natural gas, propane, and fuel oil. Cooling electricity also shows significant savings (even while adding cooling in 6% if households) from load reduction and higher efficiency cooling. Electric heating increases in both cases, and this is due to fuel switching from traditional heating systems to fully electric GHPs. Figure 1 shows 39% stock site energy savings, while Figure 2 shows 50% site energy savings in applicable dwelling units.

Figure 3 shows the annual site energy consumption for the applicable housing stock split out by Building America climate zone (Antonopoulos, Gilbride, Margiotta, Cragin, & Kaltreider, 2022). As envelope improvements reduce loads, savings are seen in all climate zones. The largest magnitude savings are seen in the Mixed-Humid and the Cold climate zones. The reduction in heating load and associated energy consumption provides most of the savings in these climate zones. Note that for all climate zones installing a variable-speed GHP is the primary driver of savings, while additional envelope improvements further increase the savings. Looking more closely at individual end uses, all climate zones show an increase in electricity consumption for heating fans and pumps, and conversely all climate zones, except Subarctic, also show savings from cooling.

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 3.2  Annual Energy Bill Impact for Applicable Dwelling Units Only

Energy bills for applicable dwelling units are shown in this section. The average energy bill for the variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements is shown in Figure 6. On average, total energy bills decreased by 30% (over $600 per year) for the variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements compared to baseline dwelling units. All fuel costs decreased on average, with 13% savings on electricity bills, 66% savings on natural gas bills, 85% savings on propane bills, and 93% savings on fuel oil bills.

Figure 6. Average annual energy bill for applicable dwelling units only broken out by fuel type

![Image](99820_images/image_000007_72cc21ee12a1ebb306098d656ca8f91a3f9f1c59344b0e23f1f3b05857cafe20.png)

Figure 7 shows average energy bills for applicable dwelling units only broken out by Building America climate zone. The variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements results in a lower average energy bill across all climate zones, with bills in the Subarctic region showing the largest magnitude savings (over $2,000 per year).

Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 3.3  GHP Borehole Length and Heating Capacity

The total borehole length of the ground heat exchanger and GHP capacity are shown in Table 1 for applicable dwelling units only. The total borehole length is the trench count of the geothermal loop multiplied by the length of one trench.

Table 1. GHP Borehole Length and Heating Capacity for Applicable Dwelling Units Only

| Percentile   |   Total Borehole Length [ft] |   Heating Capacity [kBtu/h] |
|--------------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| 10           |                          240 |                        16.9 |
| 25           |                          450 |                        32.0 |
| 50           |                          772 |                        52.1 |
| Mean         |                          886 |                        57.7 |
| 75           |                        1,188 |                        76.2 |
| 90           |                        1,670 |                       103.8 |

The mean is larger than the median in the total borehole length and the heating capacity, indicating the upper outliers are causing the data to trend upwards. Results for the variable-speed geothermal heat pump only can be viewed in the ResStock Measure Documentation: Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump document (Maguire, et al., 2026).

text:
Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER) with Light Envelope Improvements — 3.4  Electric Panel Impact

This section details the impact the variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements will have on electrical panels. The electric panel impact of this measure is the same as the stand-alone variable-speed GHP. The modeling assumptions and details about electric panels in ResStock can be found in the single-stage GHP documentation (Maguire, et al., 2026).

First, Figure 8 and Figure 9 show information about the ResStock 2025 Release 1 baseline housing stock electric panel distribution. Figure 8 shows in the first column (labeled 'All') that about 35% of all dwelling units 1 or fewer breaker spaces available. Figure 9 shows in the first column that 97.7% of electric panels have no existing capacity constraint for the baseline housing stock.

Capacity constraints in the existing baseline stock are due in part to the uncertainty associated with the modeling process, where the prediction of the panel size is not based on the presence of all major electric appliances. However, it's important to recognize that this level of uncertainty applies to all panel results, including those that look reasonable. Hence, the capacity-constrained homes in the baseline can be thought of as over-capacity homes that experience frequent flickering of lights or tripping of breakers if/when large appliances are turned on.

Figure 10 shows the distribution of panel constraints overall (left column) and then broken out by heating fuel for dwelling units that receive the variable-speed GHP with envelope improvements. It is estimated that about 31% of dwelling units upgrading to a variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements will experience either a capacity and/or space constraint, and the other 69% will experience no constraint. Looking more closely at the results, we see that dwelling units that are converting from natural gas, fuel oil, or propane heating fuels are far more likely (46%-62%) to face a panel constraint when switching to an all-electric GHP system. This compares to only 6.4% of dwellings that started with electric heating facing a panel constraint.

The next three figures show percentages of dwelling units for each state that would have some type of electric panel constraint after the variable-speed GHP with light envelope improvements is applied. Figure 11 shows a range of 6%-65% of dwelling units per state that would have either a capacity and/or space constraint after this upgrade package, with the largest prevalence of panel constraints occurring in colder states with high heating requirements. Specifically looking at space constraints, Figure 12 shows a smaller range from about 2% to 51% of dwelling units that would have a space constraint. Finally, Figure 13 shows a range of roughly 4% to 40% of dwelling units would have a capacity constraint.

In general, switching to a GHP system is more likely to face panel constraints in heatingdominated climates due to a substantial new electric load being introduced. Compared with the stand-alone variable-speed GHP measure (Maguire, et al., 2026), which shows ranges of 11%70% for either capacity and/or space constraints, 4%-53% for space constraints, and 7%-48% for capacity constraints, these results indicate that light envelope improvements help mitigate panel constraints.
